explanation: Spot on! Checking the label at these three key steps helps you catch any errors before the drug gets to the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why is it dangerous to administer a medication prepared by another nurse?

options.A: It takes away valuable learning time from student nurses
options.B: The pharmacy software will crash when scanning the barcode
options.C: You cannot verify its true contents or preparation accuracy
options.D: It violates hospital laundry and uniform policies

explanation: The person who prepares the medication must be the one who administers it to maintain complete safety accountability. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why does an intravenous (IV) medication work much faster than a swallowed pill?

options.A: It travels straight to the liver for immediate activation
options.B: It is manufactured using higher chemical concentrations
options.C: It avoids the lungs where oxygen slows down circulation
options.D: It enters the bloodstream directly without needing absorption

explanation: Exactly! Because IV meds skip the digestive tract and go straight into the blood, they start working almost instantly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which medication route involves placing a tablet under the tongue to dissolve?

options.A: Transdermal
options.B: Intradermal
options.C: Subcutaneous
options.D: Sublingual

explanation: Sublingual medications dissolve under the tongue where rich blood vessels allow quick absorption into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the main legal risk if a nurse forgets to document a medication right after giving it?

options.A: The hospital computer system will delete the patient file
options.B: The pharmacy will automatically double the next scheduled dose
options.C: The patient's insurance company will refuse to pay the bill
options.D: Legally, the medication is considered unadministered

explanation: In nursing law, if it isn't charted, it didn't happen! Always document promptly to protect your license and your patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h5)

question: What should a nurse do when a patient refuses to take a prescribed oral medication?

options.A: Document the refusal and notify the prescribing doctor
options.B: Hide the crushed pill inside sweet food without telling them
options.C: Force the medication gently by holding the patient's jaw
options.D: Leave the pill on the bedside table for them to take later

explanation: Competent patients have the right to refuse treatment, and the care team must be informed to adjust the plan. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse must do after discovering a medication error?

options.A: Call the hospital lawyer to explain what happened
options.B: Fill out the institutional incident report form right away
options.C: Assess the patient's vital signs and current physical condition
options.D: Hide the medication packaging so nobody notices the mistake

explanation: Patient well-being always comes first! Always check your patient's condition before worrying about paperwork. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to prevent medication errors?

options.A: Minimizing hallway conversations while calculating doses
options.B: Double-checking high-alert calculations with a colleague
options.C: Carefully reading medication labels three separate times
options.D: Rushing through drug rounds to finish ahead of schedule

explanation: Spot on! Rushing causes stress and mistakes. Taking your time is key to safe medication administration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T1#GNS122_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of instilling medication drops into the eye, ear, or nose?

options.A: To deliver slow-release nutrition directly into the blood
options.B: To completely flush out all natural body fluids
options.C: To provide direct local treatment to the affected area
options.D: To replace the need for all oral pain medications

explanation: Drops are applied straight to body cavities so the medicine works right where it is needed most. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why can eye or nose drops sometimes cause whole-body effects even though they are used locally?

options.A: Liquid drops always mix with stomach acids immediately
options.B: The skin barrier blocks most of the dose from staying local
options.C: The medicine absorbs quickly through nearby mucous membranes into the bloodstream
options.D: Drops travel directly down the spine to affect the brain

explanation: Mucous membranes in the eyes and nose have rich blood supplies that can absorb liquid medications into circulation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h1)

question: How should a nurse pull the ear pinna when giving ear drops to an adult patient?

options.A: Downward and forward
options.B: Downward and backward
options.C: Upward and backward
options.D: Straight outward by the lobe

explanation: Pulling the adult ear pinna up and back straightens the curved ear canal so the drops can reach the eardrum area. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h2)

question: Why must the ear pinna be pulled downward and backward for a child under three years old?

options.A: The eardrum sits at a completely different angle in infants
options.B: It prevents the child from turning their head sideways
options.C: Children have more earwax blocking the upper canal
options.D: Their ear canal is shorter and straighter compared to an adult

explanation: An infant's ear canal anatomy requires a downward and backward pull to properly align the passage for drops. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the main reason a medication dropper should never touch the patient's skin or eyelashes?

options.A: To prevent contaminating the entire medication bottle with germs
options.B: To stop the liquid from flowing out too fast
options.C: To keep the glass tip from breaking off inside the canal
options.D: To avoid causing a sudden sharp pain for the patient

explanation: Touching the eye or ear transfers bacteria to the dropper tip, which then contaminates the remaining liquid inside the bottle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h3)

question: A nurse accidentally touches a patient's eyelid with the tip of an eye drop bottle. What is the safest action to take?

options.A: Wipe the tip with a dry tissue and keep using it
options.B: Discard the bottle to prevent spreading infection
options.C: Rinse the bottle tip under hot tap water
options.D: Store the bottle in the refrigerator for twenty-four hours

explanation: Once a dropper tip touches a patient, it is considered contaminated and should not be used again to avoid infection. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h3)

question: What critical assessment must a nurse make before administering ear drops?

options.A: Check the patient's blood pressure and pulse
options.B: Confirm that the eardrum is intact
options.C: Test the patient's hearing using a tuning fork
options.D: Measure the exact width of the ear canal

explanation: Putting drops into an ear with a ruptured eardrum can cause severe pain and push infection deeper into the inner ear. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why is it important to check the medication label three times before instilling drops?

options.A: To follow hospital rules without any clear medical purpose
options.B: To catch any potential mistakes and ensure the right drug and dose are given
options.C: To make sure the expiration date is at least five years away
options.D: To help the patient memorize the name of their prescription

explanation: Triple-checking the label is a core safety habit that prevents giving the wrong medication or dose to a patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h4)

question: Where should eye drops be placed when instilling medication into the eye?

options.A: Underneath the upper eyelid margin
options.B: Into the inner corner near the nose
options.C: Into the lower conjunctival sac
options.D: Directly onto the center of the cornea

explanation: The conjunctival pocket holds the drop safely on the eye surface without harming the sensitive cornea. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why should a nurse apply gentle pressure to the nasolacrimal duct after giving eye drops?

options.A: To help spread the liquid evenly across the eyeball surface
options.B: To stop the patient from blinking too rapidly
options.C: To seal the eyelids shut until the medication dries completely
options.D: To keep the medication from draining into the nasal passage and causing systemic effects

explanation: Blocking the tear duct stops the medicine from entering the nose and bloodstream, keeping its action localized to the eye. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h5)

question: What can happen if ear drops are administered while they are too cold?

options.A: Infection of the outer ear
options.B: Dizziness and vertigo
options.C: Immediate hearing loss
options.D: Swelling of the earlobe

explanation: Cold liquid near the eardrum stimulates the inner ear balance centers, triggering sudden dizziness and nausea. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h6)

question: Why is it recommended to gently press on the tragus after instilling ear drops?

options.A: It prevents earwax from hardening further
options.B: It warms up the liquid drops inside the canal
options.C: It helps move the medication down into the ear canal
options.D: It seals the ear completely to block out loud noises

explanation: Pumping the tragus gently creates a mild suction effect that helps the drops travel down the canal toward the eardrum. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h6)

question: How should a patient breathe while receiving nasal drop medication?

options.A: By holding their breath
options.B: With deep chest breaths
options.C: Through their mouth
options.D: Slowly through their nose

explanation: Breathing through the mouth prevents the patient from accidentally inhaling the drops down into their lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h7)

question: Why must the dropper be aimed away from the center nasal septum during instillation?

options.A: To block the airflow in both nostrils equally
options.B: To avoid injuring the delicate tissues and causing bleeding
options.C: To make sure the liquid enters the mouth directly
options.D: To prevent the dropper tip from bending

explanation: The nasal septum has a fragile blood supply that can easily bleed if scraped by a dropper tip. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of an allergic reaction after administering eye drops?

options.A: A slight bitter taste in the back of the mouth
options.B: Mild coolness on the surface of the skin
options.C: Sudden swelling and itching around the eye
options.D: Temporary blurriness right after the drop falls

explanation: Swelling, intense itching, and hives indicate an allergic immune response to the medication ingredients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h8)

question: A patient reports severe burning and pain immediately after receiving ear drops. What is the nurse's first action?

options.A: Wait ten minutes to see if the pain goes away on its own
options.B: Stop the procedure and report the reaction to the doctor
options.C: Pack the ear canal tightly with sterile gauze
options.D: Reassure the patient and give a second dose right away

explanation: Severe pain means something is wrong, so the nurse must stop immediately and seek medical guidance. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h8)

question: What important detail must be included when charting medication drop administration?

options.A: The brand name of the box the bottle came in
options.B: The room temperature during the procedure
options.C: The exact weight of the glass dropper bottle
options.D: The specific eye, ear, or nostril treated

explanation: Recording the exact side and site ensures continuity of care and prevents treating the wrong side later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h9)

question: Why is it important to teach patients to finish all prescribed drops even if they feel better?

options.A: Stopping early can allow the infection to return stronger
options.B: Unused drops will expire quickly on the bathroom shelf
options.C: Leftover drops can cause severe poisoning if saved
options.D: Doctors require empty bottles brought back to the clinic

explanation: Stopping medication early before all bacteria or inflammation is cleared often causes the condition to flare up again. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h9)

question: What is the medical name for normal earwax?

options.A: Mucin
options.B: Tympanum
options.C: Cerumen
options.D: Sebum

explanation: Cerumen is just the fancy medical word for the natural wax our ears make to keep things clean and protected. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why would a nurse need to flush or irrigate a patient's ear?

options.A: To drain excessive fluid from the middle ear cavity
options.B: To remove stuck earwax or small foreign objects
options.C: To repair a torn eardrum using pressurized water
options.D: To treat an active bacterial infection deep in the inner ear

explanation: Ear irrigation is a safe way to wash out stubborn wax buildup or little things that got stuck in the outer ear. Great clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h1)

question: When should you NEVER perform an ear irrigation?

options.A: A torn (perforated) eardrum
options.B: Mild itching in the outer ear
options.C: A history of mild seasonal allergies
options.D: Excessive dry earwax buildup

explanation: Never put fluid into an ear with a hole in the eardrum! It can push water and infection straight into the middle ear. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h2)

question: A patient comes in with a small plastic bead stuck in their ear, but no pain. What is your very first step?

options.A: Immediately begin high-pressure irrigation to wash out the bead
options.B: Send the patient home without an examination
options.C: Instill cold water to freeze the plastic bead so it shrinks
options.D: Check the ear with an otoscope to look at the eardrum first

explanation: Always take a peek with your otoscope first! You need to make sure the eardrum is safe and intact before you introduce any water. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h2)

question: How warm should the water be when you prepare it for ear irrigation?

options.A: Ice cold
options.B: Room temperature only
options.C: Boiling hot
options.D: Body temperature (lukewarm)

explanation: Using lukewarm water matches body temperature. It keeps the patient comfortable and prevents terrible dizziness! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h3)

question: What happens if you accidentally use cold water to flush a patient's ear?

options.A: The earwax will instantly dissolve into liquid
options.B: The eardrum will automatically seal itself tighter
options.C: The patient may feel very dizzy and start vomiting
options.D: The water flow will stop completely

explanation: Cold water messes with the balance organs in the inner ear, triggering heavy dizziness and nausea (vertigo). Keep it warm! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h3)

question: How do you correctly straighten an adult's ear canal before flushing it?

options.A: Push the tragus inward over the opening
options.B: Tilt the head sharply toward the chest
options.C: Pull the earlobe straight downward
options.D: Pull the outer ear (pinna) upward and backward

explanation: For adults, pulling the pinna up and back straightens out the curvy ear canal so your water stream can reach the blockage easily. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h4)

question: Where should you aim the stream of water inside the ear canal?

options.A: Straight down the bottom floor of the canal
options.B: Directly at the center of the eardrum
options.C: Against the center of the wax plug only
options.D: Against the top or back wall of the canal

explanation: Aiming along the canal wall lets the water slip behind the wax and push it out gently, without blasting the delicate eardrum. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is your immediate action if the patient feels sharp pain while you are flushing their ear?

options.A: Push the syringe faster to clear the blockage
options.B: Lower the temperature of the water
options.C: Stop the irrigation procedure right away
options.D: Ask the patient to lie flat on the bed

explanation: Pain is a warning sign of injury! Stop immediately to protect your patient from further harm. You're doing great learning this. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h5)

question: What damage can happen if you push water into the ear canal with too much force?

options.A: Permanent loss of the sense of taste
options.B: Tearing (perforation) of the eardrum
options.C: Complete closure of the outer jaw bone
options.D: Instant growth of new ear cartilage

explanation: Too much pressure in a tight space can rupture the thin eardrum. Always use gentle, controlled pressure! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h5)

question: Which of these details is NOT needed in your nursing notes after an ear irrigation?

options.A: How the ear canal looked afterward
options.B: The amount and temperature of the fluid used
options.C: The brand name of the plastic syringe used
options.D: How well the patient tolerated the procedure

explanation: You need to document clinical facts like fluid amounts and patient reactions, but nobody needs to know the syringe brand name! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why do nurses check the ear canal with an otoscope after finishing an irrigation?

options.A: To check if the patient's hearing loss is permanent
options.B: To measure the exact length of the ear canal
options.C: To pump remaining air out of the middle ear space
options.D: To make sure the wax or object is actually gone

explanation: An otoscope check lets you double-check your work and confirm the ear canal is clean and the eardrum looks safe. Perfect finish! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T11#GNS122_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the main reason a nurse performs an eye irrigation?

options.A: To flush out chemicals or foreign bodies from the eye
options.B: To deliver antibiotic eye drops for a bacterial infection
options.C: To permanently dilate the pupil for a detailed eye exam
options.D: To measure the exact intraocular pressure of the globe

explanation: Great job thinking practically! Irrigation uses a steady stream of fluid to wash away dangerous substances or particles before they hurt the eye tissues. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why do you need to act immediately when a patient gets a chemical splash in the eye?

options.A: Chemicals quickly burn and damage delicate eye tissues
options.B: Waiting prevents the nurse from finding a neutralizing agent
options.C: Delayed washing allows the chemical to crystallize into a solid
options.D: Chemical splashes rapidly lower the normal body temperature

explanation: Time is precious here! Harsh substances start destroying eye cells right away, so washing them out fast stops permanent injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h1)

question: When should you NEVER perform routine eye irrigation?

options.A: Mild redness caused by ordinary environmental dust
options.B: A suspected penetrating injury or rupture of the eyeball
options.C: A chemical splash involving standard household bleach
options.D: A small speck of sand trapped under the lower eyelid

explanation: Remember: if the eyeball itself is cut open or ruptured, pushing fluid in will raise pressure and push the inside out. Always check for a puncture first! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h2)

question: A patient comes in with a metal flake stuck on the surface of their eye. Why is irrigation a good choice here?

options.A: Fluid pressure forces the metal deeper to hide the pain
options.B: Washing the eye replaces the need for a physical eye exam
options.C: Irrigation completely dissolves metal on contact
options.D: The fluid stream can safely flush away loose surface irritants

explanation: Spot on! If something is just resting loosely on the surface, a gentle, steady flow of liquid is a safe way to float it right out. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which fluid solution is preferred for a standard eye wash?

options.A: Hydrogen peroxide
options.B: Normal saline
options.C: Boric acid drops
options.D: Tap water only

explanation: Normal saline is isotonic, meaning it matches the natural fluid balance of the eye so it won't harm delicate cells while cleaning. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why should you avoid using plain distilled water for an eye wash?

options.A: Plain water freezes too quickly when exposed to room air
options.B: Isotonic solutions have a bright color to track the runoff
options.C: Distilled water instantly burns the skin around the eye
options.D: Distilled water causes fluid to move into cells and swell them

explanation: Plain water lacks salt balance (it's hypotonic), so it crosses into eye cells and causes them to swell and damage. Stick to saline! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h3)

question: How should you position your patient's head during an eye wash?

options.A: Tilted slightly toward the affected side
options.B: Tilted firmly toward the unaffected side
options.C: Positioned flat and facing straight up
options.D: Tilted backward as far as the neck allows

explanation: Tilting toward the bad side ensures the dirty runoff flows away off the face instead of spilling into the healthy eye. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why does a nurse test tear pH with paper before treating a chemical splash?

options.A: To determine if the patient needs local numbing eye drops first
options.B: To prove that the patient is experiencing a severe allergic reaction
options.C: To measure how severe the chemical exposure is and guide treatment
options.D: To check if the patient has a hidden bacterial eye infection

explanation: Checking the pH tells you if it was an acid or an alkali burn, and you keep washing until the pH goes back to normal. Smart nursing! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h4)

question: When starting an eye irrigation, where do you aim the stream of fluid?

options.A: Directly onto the center of the black pupil
options.B: At the outer corner, flowing inward toward the nose
options.C: Directly against the upper eyelid skin
options.D: At the inner canthus, flowing toward the outer canthus

explanation: Always flow from the inside corner (near the nose) toward the outside corner. This follows natural tear flow and keeps junk out of the tear ducts! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h5)

question: A student nurse is getting ready to irrigate an eye. Which action means they need a quick correction?

options.A: Placing a waterproof towel and a kidney basin under the cheek
options.B: Encouraging the patient to blink periodically during the wash
options.C: Resting fingers directly upon the patient's eyeball to hold it open
options.D: Holding the irrigation tubing about one inch away from the eye

explanation: Ouch! Always rest your fingers on the bony cheekbone or forehead, never directly on the eyeball, to prevent accidental pressure injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h5)

question: What is an important final step after finishing an eye irrigation for a chemical burn?

options.A: Rechecking the tear pH to ensure it has returned to normal
options.B: Rinsing the patient's entire face with rubbing alcohol
options.C: Instructing the patient to avoid blinking for two hours
options.D: Applying a tight eye patch with heavy pressure tape

explanation: Checking the pH one last time confirms that all the harmful chemical has been fully neutralized and washed away. Great wrap-up! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h6)

question: Why is charting the details of an eye irrigation so important in the patient's record?

options.A: It proves to the pharmacy department that sterile supplies were wasted
options.B: It provides a clear legal record of solution amount, duration, and patient response
options.C: It prevents the patient from receiving any further medical bills
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will regain full vision by tomorrow

explanation: Good documentation protects both you and the patient by proving exactly what care was given and how the patient responded. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which of these is a common complication if an eye irrigation is done carelessly?

options.A: Corneal abrasion from equipment or trapped debris
options.B: Permanent systemic high blood pressure
options.C: Total loss of the patient's sense of smell
options.D: Sudden fracture of the orbital cheekbone

explanation: Rough handling or dragging particles across the eye can scratch the delicate cornea. Always be gentle! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h7)

question: What should you do right away if a patient says their eye pain and blurriness are getting worse during an irrigation?

options.A: Stop the irrigation and notify the healthcare provider
options.B: Turn off the room lights and leave the patient alone to rest
options.C: Increase the fluid flow rate to wash the pain away faster
options.D: Ignore the complaint because pain is normal during a flush

explanation: Never ignore worsening pain! Stop right away and let the doctor know so they can check for further injury or complications. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T12#GNS122_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of drug legislation in nursing?

options.A: To increase the cost of essential medicines
options.B: Um, to reduce the workload of hospital pharmacists
options.C: To make medication administration slower
options.D: To protect the public and healthcare workers

explanation: Drug laws exist mainly to keep patients safe from harm and guide nurses on legal medication practices. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why must nurses follow strict legal boundaries when giving powerful medications?

options.A: Because the pharmacy department requires extra paperwork
options.B: Because these substances have a high risk of abuse and harm
options.C: To ensure that doctors do not prescribe any treatment
options.D: So that hospital management can monitor daily staffing

explanation: Strong medications carry serious risks like addiction or overdose, making strict rules necessary for patient safety. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h1)

question: What does the Drug Control Act primarily regulate?

options.A: The cleaning schedules of hospital wards
options.B: The daily salaries of nursing personnel
options.C: The handling and distribution of controlled substances
options.D: The construction of public healthcare clinics

explanation: The act focuses on controlling how dangerous drugs are moved, made, and supplied in the country. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h2)

question: How does the Drug Control Act directly affect daily nursing practice?

options.A: It decides which patients receive free medical care
options.B: It dictates the special handling rules for dangerous drugs
options.C: It sets the standard uniform code for hospital wards
options.D: It determines how many hours a nurse can work per week

explanation: The law sets clear rules on how nurses must store, give, and record potent medications. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which Nigerian agency is mainly responsible for fighting drug trafficking and hard drugs?

options.A: NAFDAC
options.B: FMOH
options.C: NMCN
options.D: NDLEA

explanation: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency handles illegal drug trafficking and illicit substances. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h3)

question: What is the main duty of NAFDAC regarding medications?

options.A: Providing free meals to hospitalized patients
options.B: Regulating drug manufacturing, importation, and quality
options.C: Issuing practicing licenses to individual bedside nurses
options.D: Managing the internal budget of teaching hospitals

explanation: NAFDAC ensures that all drugs sold or used in the country are safe, effective, and of good quality. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which schedule describes substances with NO accepted medical use and high abuse risk?

options.A: Schedule V
options.B: Schedule IV
options.C: Schedule I
options.D: Schedule II

explanation: Schedule I drugs are considered too dangerous and lack approved medical applications. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why are drugs like morphine classified under strict schedules even though they have medical uses?

options.A: They carry a high risk of dependence and abuse
options.B: They are extremely expensive to import from abroad
options.C: They can only be administered by specialized surgeons
options.D: They lose their potency very quickly in storage

explanation: Even though they relieve severe pain, strong opioids can easily lead to addiction if not closely monitored. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h4)

question: What should a nurse do if a medical doctor prescribes an obviously dangerous dose of a controlled drug?

options.A: Question the order and clarify with the prescriber before giving it
options.B: Throw the medication away without telling anyone
options.C: Ask another patient to take the extra dose instead
options.D: Administer the medication anyway since the doctor signed it

explanation: Nurses are legally responsible for the medications they administer and must question unsafe orders. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a legal duty of a nurse handling controlled drugs?

options.A: Changing the doctor's prescription order to match ward supplies
options.B: Reporting missing medication from the drug cupboard
options.C: Verifying the patient's identity before administration
options.D: Documenting every dose given accurately

explanation: Nurses cannot alter prescriptions; doing so is illegal and falsifies medical records. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h5)

question: How must controlled substances be stored on a hospital ward?

options.A: In an open metal tray on the main nurses' station desk
options.B: Inside the patient's bedside locker for easy access
options.C: In a double-locked secure cabinet with restricted key access
options.D: Inside the general refrigerator with food items

explanation: Double-locking prevents theft, diversion, and unauthorized access to dangerous drugs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is required when a nurse needs to discard a leftover portion of liquid morphine?

options.A: The hospital pharmacist must inspect the empty syringe
options.B: Another nurse must witness and co-sign the disposal
options.C: The patient must sign a form confirming the waste
options.D: The nurse can throw it away alone at the end of the shift

explanation: A second witness prevents falsification and ensures leftover drugs are not diverted for illegal use. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h6)

question: When should a nurse record the administration of a controlled drug in the register?

options.A: Whenever time permits during the weekly stock check
options.B: The following morning during the official handover
options.C: At the end of the working shift before going home
options.D: Immediately after administering the drug to the patient

explanation: Prompt documentation prevents errors, omissions, and discrepancies in the narcotic register. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h7)

question: What should a nurse do immediately if the physical count of pethidine does not match the register balance?

options.A: Add personal money to replace any missing tablets
options.B: Wait until the next shift to see if the count balances out
options.C: Report the discrepancy right away to the nursing supervisor
options.D: Cross out the wrong number and write a new one quietly

explanation: Missing drugs could indicate theft or error, requiring immediate official investigation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h7)

question: What administrative penalty can the Nursing and Midwifery Council impose for drug law violations?

options.A: A temporary transfer to a different medical department
options.B: Requiring the nurse to attend a basic computer class
options.C: Suspension or revocation of the nursing practicing license
options.D: Mandatory promotion to a hospital management position

explanation: Professional regulatory bodies protect the public by removing the licenses of unsafe practitioners. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h8)

question: Why do courts hand down severe punishments, including imprisonment, for drug diversion in hospitals?

options.A: Because pharmaceutical companies demand strict punishment
options.B: Because doctors refuse to work with nurses who make errors
options.C: Because stolen drugs fuel illegal abuse and endanger public safety
options.D: Because hospitals lose a lot of daily operating revenue

explanation: Diverted prescription drugs often end up on the street, worsening community addiction and public health risks. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of giving medications through the oral route?

options.A: It bypasses liver metabolism completely
options.B: It is the most convenient and common way
options.C: It guarantees 100 percent drug absorption
options.D: It works faster than intravenous injections

explanation: The oral route is favored because patients can usually swallow pills themselves, making it easy and convenient for long-term care. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why should a nurse avoid crushing an enteric-coated tablet?

options.A: It turns the solid pill into an unmixable powder
options.B: It changes the color of the liquid mixture
options.C: It causes the medication to dissolve too slowly
options.D: It ruins the special coating designed to protect the stomach

explanation: Enteric coatings protect the stomach lining from irritation or protect the drug from stomach acid; crushing destroys this barrier. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why must a nurse position a patient upright before giving oral medications?

options.A: It speeds up the first-pass metabolism in the liver
options.B: It allows the nurse to check the pulse more easily
options.C: Gravity helps the medication go down safely and prevents choking
options.D: It stops the stomach acid from rising into the throat

explanation: Sitting at a 90-degree angle uses gravity to guide the pill into the esophagus and protects the airway from accidental aspiration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: What vital sign must a nurse always check before administering certain heart medications like digoxin?

options.A: Body temperature
options.B: Respiratory rate
options.C: Oxygen saturation
options.D: Apical pulse rate

explanation: Certain cardiac drugs lower the heart rate, so nurses must measure the pulse beforehand to ensure it is safe to give. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: How many patient identifiers should a nurse check before giving a medication?

options.A: At least two identifiers
options.B: Three separate room numbers
options.C: Four family member approvals
options.D: Only one quick identifier

explanation: Using identifiers like the patient's name and hospital number ensures the right person receives the treatment. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: When is the best time for a nurse to document that a medication was given?

options.A: While walking down the hallway to the room
options.B: Right before taking the pills out of the drawer
options.C: At the very end of the entire work shift
options.D: Immediately after the patient swallows the drug

explanation: Documenting right away prevents accidental double-dosing and ensures an accurate record of care. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: Why should a nurse avoid using household kitchen spoons to measure liquid medications?

options.A: Using them makes the liquid spill on the table
options.B: Household spoons react chemically with liquid drugs
options.C: Kitchen spoons are too heavy for patients to hold
options.D: Kitchen spoons vary in size and give inaccurate doses

explanation: Household spoons are not standardized for medical measurements, which can lead to giving too much or too little medicine. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: Where should a nurse look when measuring liquid medication in a clear plastic cup?

options.A: At eye level with the bottom of the liquid meniscus
options.B: From underneath the table looking up through the plastic
options.C: From high above looking down at the top of the fluid
options.D: At the highest edge of the liquid touching the cup wall

explanation: Reading at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus ensures the exact volume of medication is measured. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why must a nurse stay at the bedside until the patient swallows all their medications?

options.A: To record the exact second the patient stops drinking water
options.B: To collect payment for the hospital prescription fees
options.C: To make sure the water cup is returned clean to the medication room
options.D: To confirm the patient actually takes the drugs and does not hide them

explanation: Staying at the bedside ensures compliance and safety, preventing patients from pocketing pills or missing doses. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take before preparing medications?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene
options.B: Check the hospital bed
options.C: Pour water into a cup
options.D: Open the patient chart

explanation: Hand hygiene is the primary step in infection control to prevent spreading germs to clean medication supplies. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: A confused elderly patient keeps holding pills in their cheek without swallowing them. What is this behavior called?

options.A: First-pass effect
options.B: Pouching
options.C: Aspiration
options.D: Enteric coating

explanation: Pouching happens when patients store food or medication in their cheek pockets instead of swallowing it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which food choice is generally NOT recommended when mixing crushed medication for an infant?

options.A: A small taste of flavored pudding
options.B: A spoonful of sweet applesauce
options.C: Daily milk or formula bottle feeds
options.D: A small drop of fruit puree

explanation: Mixing drugs into routine milk feeds can cause the infant to reject their primary nutrition if the taste changes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is the main reason a nurse performs a follow-up check after giving medication?

options.A: To ask the patient to sign the hospital billing forms
options.B: To evaluate if the drug is working and watch for side effects
options.C: To remind the doctor when the next shift starts
options.D: To clean up the leftover water cups from the bedside table

explanation: Follow-up monitoring ensures therapeutic effectiveness and catches early signs of adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)

question: What action should a nurse take immediately if a medication administration error occurs?

options.A: Ask the patient to keep quiet about the mistake
options.B: Hide the empty medicine cup in the trash can
options.C: Wait until the end of the month to see if harm happens
options.D: Report it to the doctor and nurse manager right away

explanation: Immediate reporting ensures the patient gets quick medical evaluation and treatment if an adverse effect develops. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)

question: Why would you give a drug through an injection (parenterally) instead of having the patient swallow it?

options.A: It requires no special technical skill.
options.B: It achieves much faster drug absorption.
options.C: It is completely painless for the patient.
options.D: It has zero risk of local tissue damage.

explanation: You got this! Injections bypass the digestive system straight into the bloodstream or tissues, meaning the medicine gets to work much quicker. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why do we have to be extra careful and double-check our work when giving injections?

options.A: Oral medications require much higher doses than injections.
options.B: Errors can cause rapid and severe harm because absorption is direct.
options.C: Hospital insurance policies mandate double-checking every dose.
options.D: The digestive system neutralizes all injectable substances.

explanation: Spot on! Once a drug is inside the body via injection, you can't take it back out. That's why accuracy is super important. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h1)

question: What is the proper technique for cleaning a patient's skin before giving an injection?

options.A: Use a circular motion starting from the center and moving outward.
options.B: Clean from the outer edges inward toward the exact puncture spot.
options.C: Wipe back and forth rapidly across the site with a dry gauze pad.
options.D: Apply warm soapy water and rinse with sterile tap water.

explanation: Well done! Starting from the center and swirling outwards pushes germs away from the exact spot where the needle will pierce the skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is the best way to prevent accidental needlestick injuries after giving an injection?

options.A: Carefully placing the plastic cap back onto the needle using two hands.
options.B: Dropping the uncapped needle directly into a rigid sharps box.
options.C: Leaving the used syringe on the bedside table until the end of the shift.
options.D: Breaking the needle off the syringe before throwing it in the trash.

explanation: Great job! Never try to recap a used needle—that is the number one cause of accidental pricks. Drop it straight into the safety box! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h2)

question: Which of these needle gauges is the thinnest?

options.A: 25 gauge
options.B: 30 gauge
options.C: 18 gauge
options.D: 20 gauge

explanation: You rock! Remember the golden rule of needles: the higher the gauge number, the thinner the actual needle diameter. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h3)

question: Why does medication given into a muscle absorb faster than medicine given under the skin?

options.A: Muscles are located closer to the outer surface of the skin.
options.B: Intramuscular needles are always made of thinner metal.
options.C: The liver metabolizes intramuscular drugs before they enter blood vessels.
options.D: Muscle tissue has a much richer blood supply than fatty tissue.

explanation: Exactly! Muscles have a bustling network of blood vessels, helping the medication hitch a quick ride into the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h3)

question: What is the main reason a nurse gives an intradermal injection (just under the top layer of skin)?

options.A: Delivering rapid pain relief during acute trauma.
options.B: Providing daily maintenance doses of intravenous fluids.
options.C: Vaccinating large populations against seasonal influenza.
options.D: Diagnostic testing like allergy or tuberculosis screenings.

explanation: Spot on! Because skin layers absorb very slowly here, it's the perfect spot to watch for a localized immune reaction like a TB test. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: When giving a routine subcutaneous insulin injection to an adult, how should you position the skin and needle?

options.A: Inject the medication directly into the dermis until a fluid bleb forms.
options.B: Push the needle straight down into the muscle at a 90-degree angle.
options.C: Stretch the skin flat and insert the needle at a 15-degree angle.
options.D: Pinch a skin fold and insert the needle at a 45 to 90-degree angle.

explanation: You got it! Pinching the fatty tissue makes sure your needle stays in the fat layer and doesn't accidentally dive into the muscle underneath. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which muscle site is generally considered the safest and most reliable for giving an intramuscular injection to an adult?

options.A: Ventrogluteal
options.B: Rectus femoris
options.C: Dorsogluteal
options.D: Deltoid

explanation: Brilliant! The ventrogluteal site is clear of major nerves and big blood vessels, making it a nurse's best friend for adult IM shots. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of using the Z-track technique when giving an intramuscular injection?

options.A: It seals the medication inside the muscle and prevents leakage into skin tissue.
options.B: It speeds up the absorption rate of irritating oily substances.
options.C: It allows the nurse to inject larger volumes of fluid into the deltoid.
options.D: It completely eliminates the pain associated with needle puncture.

explanation: Well done! Pulling the skin sideways before poking creates a zigzag path that traps irritating drugs safely down in the muscle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the biggest clinical advantage of giving a medication straight into a vein (intravenously)?

options.A: It requires minimal monitoring compared to oral medications.
options.B: It prevents rapid allergic reactions from occurring.
options.C: It carries zero risk of localized tissue irritation.
options.D: It provides immediate systemic availability of the medication.

explanation: You're doing great! Since IV medications go right into the bloodstream, they start working instantly—a lifesaver in emergencies. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: Why must you check if two drugs are compatible before adding an IV piggyback medicine into an existing line?

options.A: Hospital pharmacy software blocks incompatible infusions anyway.
options.B: Primary fluids neutralize the therapeutic effect of all antibiotics.
options.C: Incompatible drugs can form precipitates that block the catheter.
options.D: Mismatched drugs will automatically cause severe patient hypertension.

explanation: Spot on! Mixing the wrong drugs can cause chemical reactions that turn into solid gunk, clogging the line and endangering the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: A patient with a peripheral IV line says it hurts, and you notice the area is cool, pale, and swollen. What has likely happened?

options.A: Air embolism
options.B: Circulatory overload
options.C: Phlebitis
options.D: Infiltration

explanation: You got it! When the IV fluid slips out of the vein and leaks into the surrounding tissue, it makes the skin feel cool, tight, and swollen. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: Your patient suddenly starts wheezing, struggling to breathe, and breaking out in hives right after an IV medication starts. What is your very first action?

options.A: Stop the infusion immediately.
options.B: Slow the infusion rate to a keep-vein-open speed.
options.C: Notify the attending physician before taking action.
options.D: Document the vital signs in the patient chart.

explanation: Brilliant nursing instinct! Always stop the flow first to keep any more of the allergen from entering their system. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: When is the right time for a nurse to document a medication in the patient's chart?

options.A: Only if the patient experiences a negative side effect.
options.B: Before drawing up the medication in the treatment room.
options.C: Immediately after the medication is given.
options.D: At the end of the shift during the final handover report.

explanation: Exactly right! Documenting right away prevents accidental double-dosing by another nurse who might think the dose was missed. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why is it important to check up on your patient after giving an injection or IV medication?

options.A: It ensures the medication achieved its intended effect and checks for adverse reactions.
options.B: It proves to the hospital pharmacy that the correct vial was opened.
options.C: It satisfies legal billing requirements for injectable supplies.
options.D: It replaces the need to check vital signs prior to administration.

explanation: You nailed it! Because injections work fast, following up helps you catch any early side effects and make sure the patient is feeling better. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of intravenous therapy over oral medication administration?

options.A: It prevents medications from being filtered by the kidneys.
options.B: It is completely painless and requires no technical skill.
options.C: It provides immediate systemic availability by bypassing the digestive tract.
options.D: It eliminates all potential risks of systemic infection.

explanation: Giving medications directly into a vein places them instantly into the bloodstream, avoiding the delay of digestion and liver processing. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h1)

question: When is a nurse most likely to initiate intravenous therapy for a patient?

options.A: When the patient needs a rapid correction of severe dehydration.
options.B: When the patient is eating normally and taking daily multivitamin pills.
options.C: When topical skin cream is prescribed for a localized rash.
options.D: When a mild headache needs to be relieved over an eight-hour period.

explanation: Severe dehydration requires quick fluid volume restoration directly into the blood vessels, which can only be achieved effectively through IV therapy. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h1)

question: Which vein is located in the antecubital fossa and is often used for emergency access or blood draws?

options.A: Digital dorsal vein
options.B: Median cubital vein
options.C: Temporal scalp vein
options.D: Great saphenous vein

explanation: The median cubital vein sits right in the bend of the elbow, making it large, prominent, and easy to access quickly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h2)

question: Why is the antecubital fossa generally avoided for long-term peripheral IV maintenance?

options.A: Bending the elbow can easily kink and block the catheter.
options.B: Medications cannot reach the heart from upper arm veins.
options.C: Infusions run much slower through arm veins than hand veins.
options.D: The veins in this area have no nerve supply nearby.

explanation: Movement at the elbow joint puts constant stress on an IV catheter in the antecubital space, leading to infiltration or flow stoppage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h2)

question: Which IV solution is classified as isotonic and commonly used for fluid resuscitation?

options.A: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.B: 5% Dextrose in water
options.C: 3.0% Sodium Chloride
options.D: 0.45% Sodium Chloride

explanation: Normal Saline at 0.9% concentration matches body fluid osmolarity, keeping red blood cells stable while expanding blood volume. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h3)

question: What happens to body cells when a hypotonic IV solution is infused into the vascular system?

options.A: Fluid is pulled out of the cells into the bloodstream, causing them to shrink.
options.B: Water molecules stay completely inside the blood vessels with no movement.
options.C: Fluid moves from the blood vessels into the cells, causing them to swell.
options.D: Red blood cells immediately break apart and release all their hemoglobin.

explanation: Hypotonic solutions have a lower concentration of solutes than blood, so water shifts toward areas of higher solute concentration inside the cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h3)

question: Where should a nurse begin looking when selecting a site for peripheral IV insertion?

options.A: As close to the shoulder joint as physically possible
options.B: Directly in the antecubital fossa of the dominant arm
options.C: On the most distal areas of the non-dominant hand or forearm
options.D: On the lower extremities near the ankle joints

explanation: Starting low on the non-dominant arm preserves higher vein sites for future use if the current line fails or needs replacement. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h4)

question: Why must a nurse check a female patient's surgical history before placing an IV in her arm?

options.A: To confirm she is not currently allergic to standard soap.
options.B: To avoid placing an IV on the same side as a prior mastectomy.
options.C: To make sure she has never received a blood transfusion before.
options.D: To ensure her blood pressure can be measured safely on that arm.

explanation: Lymph node removal during a mastectomy impairs lymphatic drainage, making that arm vulnerable to swelling and severe infection if punctured. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h4)

question: What is the primary indicator that the needle has successfully entered the lumen of the vein during insertion?

options.A: The surrounding skin turns pale and cold to the touch.
options.B: The patient reports a warm, soothing sensation in the hand.
options.C: A flashback of blood appears in the catheter hub chamber.
options.D: The tourniquet drops off the patient's arm automatically.

explanation: Blood entering the flash chamber confirms that the needle tip is inside the blood vessel before advancing the plastic cannula. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h5)

question: What unit of measurement is typically used when programming an electronic infusion pump?

options.A: Drops per minute (gtt/min)
options.B: Milligrams per minute (mg/min)
options.C: Milliliters per hour (mL/hr)
options.D: Liters per 24 hours (L/day)

explanation: Electronic infusion pumps are calibrated to deliver exact volumetric amounts calculated in milliliters per hour. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why is a microdrip tubing set (60 gtt/mL) often chosen for infants or sensitive pediatric patients?

options.A: It eliminates the need to use an electronic infusion pump entirely.
options.B: It pumps fluids at a much faster speed than standard gravity tubing.
options.C: It allows for much smaller, more precise adjustments in fluid delivery.
options.D: It prevents air bubbles from ever entering the patient's bloodstream.

explanation: Microdrip sets produce tiny drops, making it easier to deliver precise fluid volumes and prevent accidental fluid overload in small patients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h6)

question: Which complication involves a vesicant medication leaking into the surrounding tissue and causing severe tissue damage?

options.A: Simple infiltration
options.B: Fluid overload
options.C: Air embolism
options.D: Extravasation

explanation: Extravasation specifically refers to the leakage of harsh, blistering drugs (vesicants) that destroy local tissue if not managed quickly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take when suspecting an IV site has infiltrated?

options.A: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter immediately.
options.B: Flush the catheter with sterile saline to clear any local blockage.
options.C: Apply a hot compress directly over the swollen site while the line runs.
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down by half and monitor for one hour.

explanation: Stopping the infusion prevents any more fluid from entering the damaged tissue space, protecting the patient from further injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h7)

question: How often should an IV insertion site covered with a transparent dressing be visually inspected by the nurse?

options.A: Whenever the patient complains of severe pain
options.B: Only once every seven days
options.C: Only when changing the IV solution bag
options.D: During every routine shift assessment

explanation: Frequent visual checks through transparent dressings allow nurses to catch early signs of redness, swelling, or infiltration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h8)

question: Why should a nurse apply pressure to an IV site immediately after withdrawing the catheter?

options.A: To ensure the plastic catheter tip remains intact inside the arm.
options.B: To push any remaining trapped air bubbles back up into the vein.
options.C: To stimulate rapid skin healing and eliminate scarring completely.
options.D: To stop bleeding and prevent hematoma formation at the site.

explanation: Applying direct pressure helps seal the puncture wound in the blood vessel wall, stopping external bleeding and preventing internal bruising. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h8)

question: What makes an IV fluid 'isotonic'?

options.A: It draws fluid out of the blood vessels and into the tissue cells
options.B: It contains large protein molecules that cannot cross membranes
options.C: It causes body cells to swell by forcing water inside them
options.D: It has the same particle concentration as blood plasma

explanation: You've got this! Isotonic fluids match the natural concentration of our blood, meaning they safely boost fluid volume without causing water to rush into or out of our cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why would a doctor order a hypotonic fluid like 0.45% Normal Saline?

options.A: To maintain a stable vein without altering any fluid balance
options.B: To rapidly replace large volumes of blood loss from trauma
options.C: To treat severe cellular dehydration by moving water into tissues
options.D: To pull excess fluid out of swollen brain cells and tissues

explanation: Think of hypotonic fluids as having fewer particles than blood. When a patient is super dehydrated, these fluids move out of the veins and into thirsty cells to plump them back up! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h1)

question: What is the safest way to check a patient's identity before starting an IV?

options.A: Look at the medication chart resting on the bedside table
options.B: Ask the client what room they are currently staying in
options.C: Check the client's identification band using two unique identifiers
options.D: Call out the client's full name and wait for a head nod

explanation: Safety first! Always use two patient identifiers (like name and hospital number on the ID band) to make sure you are giving the right treatment to the right person. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h2)

question: A patient with heart failure needs an IV infusion. What is your most important pre-infusion check?

options.A: Choosing a vein located in the dominant hand for comfort
options.B: Selecting the largest gauge needle available for rapid infusion
options.C: Warming the intravenous fluid bag to body temperature first
options.D: Listening to the client's lung sounds and checking baseline vital signs

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Heart failure patients struggle to handle extra fluid. Checking their lungs and vitals first gives you a baseline so you can catch early signs of fluid overload. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h2)

question: When inserting a peripheral IV catheter, what angle should your needle enter the skin?

options.A: 75 to 90 degrees
options.B: 5 to 10 degrees
options.C: 45 to 60 degrees
options.D: 15 to 30 degrees

explanation: An angle of 15 to 30 degrees is the sweet spot! It lets you slide right through the skin and gently catch the superficial vein without poking through the back wall. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why must you let the skin antiseptic dry completely before starting an IV stick?

options.A: To allow the chemical to fully destroy microorganisms on the skin
options.B: To ensure the vein stays plump and easy to palpate
options.C: To prevent the sticky dressing from sliding off wet skin
options.D: To stop the client from feeling a sharp burning sensation

explanation: Patience pays off! Antiseptics like chlorhexidine need a little contact and drying time to actually kill the germs on the skin before you puncture it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h3)

question: What does the 'drop factor' on an IV tubing package tell you?

options.A: The number of drops delivered in one milliliter of fluid
options.B: The maximum speed the fluid can flow through the line
options.C: The total number of milliliters the tubing can hold
options.D: The hours the administration set can remain sterile

explanation: You've got this. Drop factor tells you the size of the drops the tubing makes, which you need to know when calculating manual drip rates (gtt/min). [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h4)

question: An order reads: 1,000 mL normal saline over 8 hours. Your tubing drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. What is the flow rate?

options.A: 63 gtt/min
options.B: 15 gtt/min
options.C: 31 gtt/min
options.D: 125 gtt/min

explanation: Math made simple! Multiply total volume (1000) by drop factor (15) to get 15,000 drops, then divide by total minutes (480 mins). That gives you roughly 31 drops per minute. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h4)

question: How often should you change a clean, intact transparent IV dressing?

options.A: Every 24 hours
options.B: Every 7 days
options.C: Only when the IV line is removed
options.D: Every 14 days

explanation: Standard hospital guidelines recommend changing transparent peripheral IV dressings every 7 days unless they get dirty, loose, or wet. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why is it important to regularly check the connection joints of an IV setup?

options.A: To ensure the gravity roller clamp is set to the maximum speed
options.B: To check if the plastic tubing needs to be warmed with a heating pad
options.C: To make sure the manufacturer label matches the client's chart
options.D: To prevent accidental disconnection, fluid leakage, and bacterial entry

explanation: Keeping connections tight keeps the system sterile! It stops messy leaks and prevents nasty bacteria from sneaking into your patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the main difference between infiltration and extravasation?

options.A: Extravasation makes the skin feel very cold, whereas infiltration makes it feel hot
options.B: Infiltration only happens in the legs, while extravasation happens in the arms
options.C: Extravasation involves tissue-damaging vesicant drugs that can cause necrosis
options.D: Infiltration requires immediate surgical removal of the vein tissue

explanation: Both mean fluid leaked out of the vein, but extravasation is extra scary because the leaked drug is a 'vesicant' that can actually destroy the surrounding tissue and cause severe sores. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h6)

question: Your IV patient suddenly feels short of breath, has crackles in their lungs, and high blood pressure. What do you do first?

options.A: Slow the infusion rate, elevate the head of the bed, and notify the provider
options.B: Flush the line rapidly with a bolus of normal saline to check patency
options.C: Place the client flat on their left side and prepare for emergency intubation
options.D: Remove the IV cannula immediately and apply a cold ice pack to the limb

explanation: Classic signs of fluid overload! Slowing the fluids and sitting the patient up helps them breathe easier while you alert the doctor. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why must you always inspect the tip of an IV catheter after you remove it?

options.A: To determine what gauge size was used for the infusion
options.B: To measure the exact length of the vein inside the client's arm
options.C: To ensure the catheter tip broke off completely or remained intact
options.D: To check if any blood clots formed inside the plastic tubing

explanation: Always double-check that tiny plastic tip! Ensuring it's in one piece means no broken plastic fragment floated off into the patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the correct technique for pulling out a peripheral IV catheter?

options.A: Twist the hub rapidly while pulling outward with force
options.B: Lift the tip upward quickly at a 90-degree angle
options.C: Flush the line with saline right before pulling it out
options.D: Pull it out smoothly and parallel to the skin surface

explanation: Keep it smooth! Pulling the catheter out parallel to the skin prevents it from scraping or tearing the delicate inside lining of the vein. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why do hospitals nowadays rarely give whole blood to patients?

options.A: Whole blood carries no oxygen-carrying capacity
options.B: Patients usually only need specific blood components
options.C: Whole blood spoils within two hours of collection
options.D: Processing whole blood is too expensive for hospitals

explanation: Great job thinking like a clinician! Blood is separated into parts so patients get precisely what they lack—like just red cells or platelets—rather than getting components they don't need. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h1)

question: Why is double-checking the patient's ID band considered the absolute most important rule before a blood transfusion?

options.A: It ensures the hospital billing department charges the correct patient
options.B: It guarantees the blood donor receives proper compensation
options.C: It prevents clerical errors that can cause fatal incompatible reactions
options.D: It speeds up the time it takes to deliver blood from the lab

explanation: Spotting identity mistakes saves lives! Giving blood to the wrong person is a major cause of dangerous reactions, making this check vital. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which blood type is known as the universal red cell donor because almost anyone can safely receive it in emergencies?

options.A: Type AB positive
options.B: Type B negative
options.C: Type A positive
options.D: Type O negative

explanation: You've got this! Type O negative red cells have no main antigens, so they won't trigger an attack in most recipients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the main reason lab scientists perform a crossmatch before releasing blood?

options.A: To check for hidden antibodies and ensure true compatibility between donor and recipient
options.B: To determine the patient's exact height and weight for dosage calculations
options.C: To sterilize the blood product before it leaves the blood bank
options.D: To measure the exact volume of red blood cells in the donor bag

explanation: Crossmatching is like a test-drive in a test tube! It mixes donor cells with patient serum to catch any immune clashes early. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h2)

question: When should you take a patient's baseline vital signs when getting ready to give a blood transfusion?

options.A: Immediately before starting the transfusion
options.B: Only when the patient complains of fever
options.C: Six hours after the transfusion finishes
options.D: The evening before the procedure is scheduled

explanation: Taking vitals right before the infusion gives you a clear starting point so you can easily spot if anything changes later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h3)

question: How many nurses must check the blood bag details against the patient's ID band?

options.A: Two licensed nurses
options.B: Only one registered nurse
options.C: Any available hospital staff member
options.D: A nurse and a laboratory technician

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are better than one! Having two qualified nurses check together is a mandatory safety net. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h3)

question: Which IV fluid is the ONLY one safe to use alongside blood products?

options.A: Ringer's Lactate Solution
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 5% Dextrose in Water
options.D: Half-Normal Saline

explanation: Normal saline is isotonic and friendly to red blood cells, preventing them from bursting or clumping like other fluids might. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h4)

question: Why do nurses prefer using a large-bore cannula (like an 18-gauge) for blood transfusions?

options.A: It prevents the physical damage and destruction of red blood cells
options.B: It prevents the IV site from swelling or leaking into the tissues
options.C: It allows the nurse to infuse multiple medications at the same time
options.D: It reduces the need to check vital signs during the first fifteen minutes

explanation: Think of it like a wide pipe versus a tiny straw—narrow needles can squeeze and break fragile red blood cells, causing damage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h4)

question: How fast should you run a blood transfusion during the very first fifteen minutes?

options.A: As fast as the gravity pump can squeeze
options.B: Completely shut off until vitals stabilize
options.C: Exactly 500 milliliters per hour
options.D: Slowly, around 50 to 60 drops per minute

explanation: Starting slow is a smart safety habit! If a reaction starts, a slow rate means less bad blood enters the body before you catch it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h5)

question: Within how many hours must a single unit of packed red blood cells be completely infused?

options.A: Twelve hours
options.B: Four hours
options.C: Thirty minutes
options.D: Twenty-four hours

explanation: Keep an eye on the clock! Blood must finish within four hours so bacteria don't start multiplying in room temperature. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h5)

question: When is the best time to check the second set of vital signs after starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: After thirty minutes
options.B: At the very end of the bag
options.C: After two hours
options.D: After fifteen minutes

explanation: The 15-minute mark is crucial because most serious acute reactions happen right at the beginning of the infusion. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h6)

question: Your patient suddenly complains of lower back pain and chills mid-transfusion. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Ignore the symptoms unless the blood pressure drops significantly
options.B: Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the vein open with saline
options.C: Leave the room quickly to fetch the attending physician
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down and give prescribed paracetamol

explanation: Trust your instincts! Back pain and chills are classic warning signs of a hemolytic reaction—stop the infusion right away. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which symptom strongly points to an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Lower back or flank pain
options.B: Gradual weight loss over days
options.C: Excessive daytime sleepiness
options.D: Severe localized skin dryness

explanation: When red cells break down inside the body, the kidneys take a hit, which often shows up as sharp lower back or flank pain. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h7)

question: What usually causes Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)?

options.A: A mismatched ABO blood type between donor and recipient
options.B: Bacterial contamination of the red blood cells during storage
options.C: An allergic response to donor plasma proteins in the blood bag
options.D: Infusing blood too rapidly for the patient's cardiovascular system to handle

explanation: TACO happens when fluid goes in faster than a patient's heart can pump it, causing fluid backup in the lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h7)

question: What fluid should you use to flush the IV tubing after a blood transfusion is complete?

options.A: Plain Tap Water
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 5% Dextrose Water
options.D: Sterile Water for Injection

explanation: A normal saline flush nicely clears out any remaining blood products from the line without harming the patient's cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h8)

question: Which of these details is NOT necessary to write down in your notes after a blood transfusion?

options.A: The name of the blood donor's family members
options.B: The product serial number and volume given
options.C: The start and stop times of the infusion
options.D: The patient's post-transfusion vital signs

explanation: Donor privacy is key! Blood banks keep donor details strictly confidential, so they never appear in your patient's chart. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h8)

question: What does fluid balance mean in patient care?

options.A: Fluid intake is greater than output
options.B: Urine output equals total blood volume
options.C: Fluid intake equals fluid output
options.D: IV fluids match oral fluid intake

explanation: Fluid balance is achieved when the total volume of fluid entering the body matches the total volume leaving it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why is fluid balance monitoring especially critical for a patient with heart failure?

options.A: They lose all body fluids through sweating
options.B: Their hearts cannot pump excess fluid effectively
options.C: Their kidneys stop producing urine entirely
options.D: They always have high oral fluid intake

explanation: Compromised heart function makes it hard to handle extra fluid, quickly leading to dangerous fluid overload. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which patient group requires strict fluid intake and output monitoring?

options.A: Patients taking diuretic medications
options.B: Patients waiting for outpatient eye surgery
options.C: Patients with mild, healing skin scratches
options.D: Patients admitted for routine physical exams

explanation: Diuretics alter fluid excretion, making it necessary to track how much urine the patient passes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of keeping a strict fluid chart on a surgical ward?

options.A: Preventing the patient from needing IV access
options.B: Proving the patient is drinking enough plain water
options.C: Calculating the exact daily hospital food costs
options.D: Detecting early signs of fluid overload or dehydration

explanation: Careful tracking lets nurses spot dangerous imbalances before they cause severe harm. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h2)

question: Which item should be counted as part of a patient's fluid intake?

options.A: An intramuscular pain injection
options.B: An intravenous blood transfusion
options.C: A solid tablet pain medication
options.D: A dry solid piece of toast

explanation: Blood products and IV fluids introduce liquid directly into the vascular system and must be counted as intake. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h3)

question: A patient drinks a mug of tea, receives an IV antibiotic piggyback, and eats a plate of rice. What counts as fluid intake?

options.A: The tea and the IV antibiotic
options.B: Only the IV antibiotic
options.C: Only the mug of tea
options.D: The tea, IV antibiotic, and rice

explanation: Liquids consumed orally and fluids given intravenously are recorded as intake, while solid food is excluded. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h3)

question: Which type of fluid output is typically easiest to measure accurately in a hospital ward?

options.A: Urine collected in a graduated container
options.B: Moisture lost through normal breathing
options.C: Fluid lost from weeping skin wounds
options.D: Sweat lost during a mild afternoon fever

explanation: Urine can be easily captured and measured using marked collection containers or catheter drainage bags. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h4)

question: Why are normal losses from breathing and light sweating called insensible fluid losses?

options.A: They only happen when the patient is unconscious
options.B: They do not affect the body's overall fluid balance
options.C: They cannot be measured directly with standard equipment
options.D: They are completely harmless to the human body

explanation: Insensible losses evaporate continuously into the air and through the skin without leaving a pool of liquid to measure. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h4)

question: What is the correct way to read fluid volume in a graduated cylinder?

options.A: Looking down from a standing position
options.B: Holding the cylinder up to a bright light
options.C: At eye level on a flat surface
options.D: Tilting the container at a 45-degree angle

explanation: Reading at eye level on a flat surface prevents parallax errors and ensures the measurement is correct. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h5)

question: How do nurses accurately measure fluid output from a heavy surgical dressing or pad?

options.A: Estimating the stain size using a common ruler
options.B: Squeezing the fluid out into a measuring cup
options.C: Asking the patient how much fluid they think leaked
options.D: Weighing the wet item and subtracting the dry weight

explanation: Weight is the most reliable way to quantify fluid soaked into solid materials, where one gram roughly equals one milliliter. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h5)

question: What standard unit of measurement is used on a hospital fluid intake and output chart?

options.A: Kilograms
options.B: Liters
options.C: Milliliters
options.D: Ounces

explanation: Milliliters provide the precise detail needed to track small fluid shifts safely. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h6)

question: A patient drinks a six-ounce cup of juice. How many milliliters should the nurse record on the chart?

options.A: 60 milliliters
options.B: 180 milliliters
options.C: 300 milliliters
options.D: 120 milliliters

explanation: Multiplying six ounces by thirty milliliters per ounce gives a total volume of 180 milliliters. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h6)

question: What does a positive fluid balance indicate for a patient over a twenty-four-hour period?

options.A: Output was greater than intake
options.B: The patient lost too much body weight
options.C: Intake and output were perfectly even
options.D: Intake was greater than output

explanation: A positive balance means more fluid entered the body than was eliminated, leaving a surplus behind. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h7)

question: A patient has a total fluid intake of 2,200 milliliters and a total output of 1,500 milliliters. What is their net balance?

options.A: Negative 700 milliliters
options.B: Positive 3,700 milliliters
options.C: Negative 3,700 milliliters
options.D: Positive 700 milliliters

explanation: Subtracting 1,500 output from 2,200 intake leaves a remaining surplus of 700 milliliters. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h7)

question: Which nursing action compromises the accuracy of a fluid balance chart?

options.A: Waiting until the end of the shift to guess and write down intake amounts
options.B: Involving the patient and family in reporting oral drinks
options.C: Converting all cup and bowl volumes into milliliters promptly
