options.B: It carries oxygenated blood directly from the lungs
options.C: It is too small to yield an adequate blood sample
options.D: It has thick muscular walls that resist needle entry

explanation: Be cautious with the basilic vein—major nerves and the brachial artery run right beside it, so care is needed to avoid accidental injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h2)

question: In which of these situations should you definitely AVOID drawing blood from that arm?

options.A: A patient with a mild headache
options.B: A fasting patient scheduled for routine labs
options.C: An arm with an active dialysis fistula
options.D: An adult over the age of sixty

explanation: Never touch an arm with an active dialysis fistula! Doing so can damage their vascular access and put the patient in serious danger. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h3)

question: A patient had a right-sided mastectomy last year. Which arm should you use for venepuncture?

options.A: On the right arm
options.B: On the left arm
options.C: In the right hand veins only
options.D: Either arm without preference

explanation: Always avoid the arm on the side of a previous mastectomy because lymph flow there is compromised, making infections much harder to fight off. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the main reason we tie a tourniquet before doing venepuncture?

options.A: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the hand
options.B: To numb the puncture site and reduce pain
options.C: To disinfect the skin surface before needle entry
options.D: To engorge and make the veins more visible

explanation: The tourniquet gently slows down blood returning to the heart, causing the veins to pop up nicely so they are easier to see and feel. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why do blood collection sample tubes come with different colored tops?

options.A: They contain different chemical additives for specific tests
options.B: They indicate the date the tubes were manufactured
options.C: They show which department ordered the laboratory test
options.D: They represent the different sizes of the patient's veins

explanation: Those color codes are lifesavers! They tell you which additive (like anticoagulants or clot activators) is inside for specific lab investigations. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why must you wait for the skin antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the needle?

options.A: To make the skin tougher so the needle enters smoothly
options.B: To ensure the tourniquet stays firmly in place on the skin
options.C: To prevent the adhesive bandage from sticking too early
options.D: To allow the chemical to kill microorganisms and prevent sample damage

explanation: Patience is key! Giving the antiseptic time to dry lets it kill germs properly and stops wet alcohol from stinging the patient or ruining the blood sample. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which of these actions goes against safe infection control practice during venepuncture?

options.A: Recapping used needles using a two-handed technique
options.B: Disposing of the needle directly into a rigid sharps bin
options.C: Performing hand hygiene before putting on clean gloves
options.D: Cleaning the insertion site in a circular outward motion

explanation: Never use two hands to recap a needle! That is a quick way to get an accidental needlestick injury. Always use one hand or drop it straight into the sharps box. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h5)

question: At what angle should you typically insert the venepuncture needle into the skin?

options.A: 45 to 60 degrees
options.B: 15 to 30 degrees
options.C: 5 to 10 degrees
options.D: 75 to 90 degrees

explanation: A gentle angle of 15 to 30 degrees lets you slide smoothly into the vein without accidentally poking right through the other side! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h6)

question: At what point in the procedure should you release the tourniquet?

options.A: Immediately after the first blood tube is filled
options.B: Before pulling the needle out of the vein
options.C: Before inserting the needle into the skin
options.D: After applying the adhesive bandage to the arm

explanation: Remember to release the tourniquet before taking the needle out. This stops extra blood from leaking out and prevents a nasty bruise from forming. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h6)

question: What does 'sample hemolysis' mean in the laboratory?

options.A: The rupture of red blood cells releasing contents into serum
options.B: The formation of a painful bruise underneath the skin
options.C: The rapid clotting of blood inside the vacuum tube
options.D: The complete absence of blood flow into the collection tube

explanation: Hemolysis happens when delicate red blood cells burst open, coloring the serum pink or red and messing up test results like potassium levels. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is your best first step if a painful bruise (hematoma) starts swelling up while you are trying to find a vein?

options.A: Remove the tourniquet and withdraw the needle at once
options.B: Apply an ice pack directly over the needle while it remains inside
options.C: Push the needle deeper to secure better placement in the vein
options.D: Leave the tourniquet tight and attach a larger vacuum tube

explanation: If a hematoma starts forming, stop right away! Remove the tourniquet and pull out the needle to keep the patient comfortable and prevent more bleeding under the skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why should you tell your patient NOT to bend their elbow right after getting blood drawn?

options.A: It forces the needle site to bleed faster than normal
options.B: It increases the risk of bruising and hematoma formation
options.C: It stops the remaining blood from flowing into the fingers
options.D: It causes the adhesive bandage to fall off the arm

explanation: Bending the arm puts pressure on the fresh puncture spot, which pops the clot loose and causes blood to leak underneath the skin into a nasty bruise. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h8)

question: When is the absolute right time to label your blood collection tubes?

options.A: At the bedside immediately after collection
options.B: At the nurses' station at the end of the shift
options.C: After returning from the hospital laboratory counter
options.D: Before entering the patient's room for the procedure

explanation: Always label your tubes right there at the bedside before you leave the patient. Never wait, because mixing up blood samples can have serious consequences! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the main reason we usually apply creams or ointments directly to the skin?

options.A: To bypass the digestive tract entirely
options.B: To achieve a localized effect at the site
options.C: To replace intravenous fluid therapy
options.D: To provide rapid systemic distribution

explanation: Most topical creams are meant to work right where you put them—treating skin issues locally without flooding the whole body with medicine. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h1)

question: How do transdermal patches differ from ordinary skin creams?

options.A: Transdermal patches are applied exclusively to mucous membranes
options.B: Patches only treat localized surface skin infections
options.C: Transdermal patches are designed for systemic absorption
options.D: Standard creams always enter the bloodstream faster than patches

explanation: While regular creams usually stay local, patches slowly deliver medicine through the skin and into the bloodstream to treat the entire body. Brilliant thinking! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which type of topical preparation is best for dry, thick, or scaly skin because it locks in moisture?

options.A: Lotion
options.B: Gel
options.C: Aqueous solution
options.D: Ointment

explanation: Ointments are oil-heavy, creating a protective blanket that stops moisture from escaping. Perfect for dry, scaly skin patches! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h2)

question: You need to treat an inflamed, hairy skin area with a non-greasy topical treatment. What should you pick?

options.A: Ointment
options.B: Gel
options.C: Heavy paste
options.D: Thick cream

explanation: Gels are water-based and dry quickly without feeling heavy or oily, making them super easy to apply on hairy areas. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h2)

question: Which layer of the skin acts as the main shield blocking most drugs from easily entering the body?

options.A: Stratum corneum
options.B: Sweat gland ducts
options.C: Dermal blood vessels
options.D: Subcutaneous fat layer

explanation: The stratum corneum is the tough outer layer of your epidermis that naturally keeps foreign substances out. Great job remembering your anatomy! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h3)

question: If you are applying a strong steroid cream, which body part will absorb it the fastest?

options.A: The sole of the foot
options.B: The face
options.C: The palm of the hand
options.D: The forearm

explanation: Facial skin is much thinner than the skin on our palms or soles, so medicines absorb through it much quicker. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is an important step before putting a fresh layer of ointment on a patient's skin?

options.A: Apply a drying alcohol swab over the entire lesion
options.B: Scrub the area vigorously with an antiseptic brush
options.C: Warm the skin using a high-heat therapeutic lamp
options.D: Gently cleanse the skin to remove old medication

explanation: Always wash away old residue gently! This prevents buildup, stops irritation, and lets the fresh medicine do its job properly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why should a nurse check the target skin area before applying a prescribed cream?

options.A: To check for signs of breakdown or unexpected infection
options.B: To measure the exact surface area in square centimeters
options.C: To test the electrical conductivity of the skin cells
options.D: To determine if the patient has a systemic fever

explanation: A quick look helps you catch any new irritation or worsening infection before adding more medicine. Patient safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why must nurses wear gloves or use a tool when applying certain topical medications?

options.A: To keep the patient's room completely sterile
options.B: To prevent absorbing the medication through their own skin
options.C: To prevent the patient from feeling cold during touch
options.D: To ensure the medication absorbs faster into the patient

explanation: Powerful drugs like hormone creams can soak right through your bare hands if you aren't wearing gloves. Always protect yourself too! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h5)

question: What is a crucial safety rule when applying a new transdermal patch?

options.A: Remove the old patch before placing the new one
options.B: Place the new patch directly on top of the old patch
options.C: Cut the new patch in half to adjust the daily dose
options.D: Apply the patch to a hairy area for better adhesion

explanation: Leaving an old patch on while putting on a new one can cause an accidental overdose because of extra medicine absorption. Safety check passed! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which of these makes a topical medication much more likely to absorb into the bloodstream and cause toxicity?

options.A: Washing the skin thoroughly with mild soap and water
options.B: Applying the cream over large areas of broken skin
options.C: Rotating the application site with every dose
options.D: Using a clean tongue depressor to spread the ointment

explanation: When skin is broken, its natural protective barrier is gone, letting too much medicine flood into the bloodstream. Good clinical awareness! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal local reaction to a topical drug?

options.A: Contact dermatitis at the site
options.B: Local burning or stinging
options.C: Anaphylactic shock originating in the lungs
options.D: Pruritus and skin redness

explanation: Anaphylactic shock is a serious whole-body allergic emergency, whereas local reactions only happen right where you applied the cream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h6)

question: What should you tell a patient about how much topical cream to use?

options.A: Apply a thick layer so it cures the condition faster
options.B: Use only the exact amount prescribed by the doctor
options.C: Stop using the cream as soon as symptoms disappear
options.D: Double the dose if the skin looks very dry or scaly

explanation: More isn't always better! Piling on extra cream won't speed up healing, but it can cause skin thinning and side effects. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h7)

question: Why shouldn't patients cover skin creams with airtight plastic wraps unless a doctor tells them to?

options.A: It prevents the cream from ever touching the skin surface
options.B: It can trap excessive moisture and increase drug absorption dangerously
options.C: It stops the patient from feeling any local pain relief
options.D: It causes the skin to become permanently discolored

explanation: Airtight wraps act like an oven, trapping heat and moisture, which forces too much medicine into the body all at once. Spot on! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h7)

question: What does 'asepsis' mean in your daily nursing practice?

options.A: The complete destruction of all life forms on human skin
options.B: The chemical disinfection of hospital floors and walls
options.C: The total absence of disease-producing microorganisms
options.D: The administration of prophylactic antibiotics before surgery

explanation: Great job! Asepsis simply means keeping an environment or item free from harmful germs that cause infections. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h1)

question: You are about to use a sterile pack, but you are not completely sure if the seal was broken. What should you do?

options.A: Assume it is contaminated and discard or re-sterilize it
options.B: Check if the expiration date on the package is still valid
options.C: Use it only for non-invasive bedside procedures
options.D: Wipe it down with alcohol and proceed with the task

explanation: When in doubt, throw it out! In sterile technique, any uncertainty means the item is no longer safe to use. Better safe than sorry! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which of these routine ward procedures strictly requires surgical asepsis (sterile technique)?

options.A: Taking a routine blood pressure reading
options.B: Administering oral medications
options.C: Assisting a patient to brush their teeth
options.D: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter

explanation: Spot on! Inserting a catheter goes straight into the bladder—a sterile body cavity—so we must use strict sterile technique to keep bacteria out. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the main goal of practicing medical asepsis (clean technique) on the ward?

options.A: To sterilize multi-use equipment between patients
options.B: To destroy all bacterial spores on the patient's skin
options.C: To reduce the number of pathogens and stop their spread
options.D: To create a completely germ-free surgical environment

explanation: You got it! Medical asepsis is all about reducing the number of germs and stopping them from traveling around the ward. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h2)

question: When you wash your hands thoroughly, which part of the chain of infection are you directly blocking?

options.A: Mode of transmission
options.B: Infectious reservoir
options.C: Portal of entry
options.D: Susceptible host

explanation: Exactly! Handwashing washes away germs before they can hitch a ride from one surface or patient to another. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h3)

question: You cover an open surgical wound with a sterile dressing. Which part of the infection chain are you primarily blocking?

options.A: Infectious agent
options.B: Infectious reservoir
options.C: Portal of entry
options.D: Portal of exit

explanation: Well done! A sterile dressing acts like a shield, stopping new germs from getting into the vulnerable, open tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is widely considered the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infections in any hospital?

options.A: Performing proper hand hygiene
options.B: Administering daily multivitamins
options.C: Changing bed linen every morning
options.D: Wearing sterile gloves for all tasks

explanation: Spot on! Good old-fashioned hand hygiene is your number one weapon against hospital-acquired infections. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h4)

question: You finish helping a patient and notice visible blood on your bare hands. What is your immediate next step?

options.A: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and running water
options.B: Apply an alcohol-based hand rub and rub briskly
options.C: Put on clean gloves without washing the hands
options.D: Wipe the hands clean with a dry paper towel

explanation: Right! When hands are visibly soiled with blood or body fluids, soap and water are a must because alcohol rubs can't wash away the physical dirt. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h4)

question: When taking off your personal protective equipment (PPE) after a procedure, which item should come off first?

options.A: Mask
options.B: Gloves
options.C: Eyewear
options.D: Gown

explanation: You got it! Gloves are usually the dirtiest item, so taking them off first stops you from spreading germs to your face or clothing. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why must you always clean your hands immediately after taking off your PPE?

options.A: To cool down your skin after wearing heavy protective gear for a long time
options.B: To prevent the uniform from smelling like hospital disinfectants
options.C: To remove any microorganisms that may have transferred to your hands during removal
options.D: To prepare your skin for putting on the next set of gloves

explanation: Brilliant! Germs can easily sneak onto your skin while you peel off dirty gear, so hand hygiene right after doffing is a must. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h5)

question: When opening a sterile pack, which part of the sterile drape or wrapper is always considered contaminated?

options.A: The portion closest to the patient
options.B: The top surface facing upwards
options.C: The outer one-inch border
options.D: The exact center of the drape

explanation: Spot on! That outer edge touches non-sterile surfaces when packaged, so we always treat the outer one-inch margin as unsterile. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h6)

question: During a sterile procedure, a sterile instrument slips and drops below the level of the tabletop. What should you do?

options.A: Ask another staff member if they saw it touch the floor
options.B: Pick it up quickly and use it if it looks clean
options.C: Consider it contaminated and discard it
options.D: Wipe it with an antiseptic wipe before continuing

explanation: You got it! If an item drops below your waist or out of your direct sight, you can't guarantee its sterility anymore. Toss it out! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is one of the biggest challenges to infection control in busy Nigerian healthcare settings?

options.A: The complete absence of infectious agents
options.B: Overcrowded wards and limited resources
options.C: An excess of disposable sterile supplies
options.D: Patients refusing all forms of medication

explanation: True talk! High patient numbers and scarce supplies make infection control tough, which is why Nigerian nurses have to be extra resourceful. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h7)

question: You are working in a busy ward where running water has temporarily stopped. What is the best way to keep up with infection control?

options.A: Wear the same pair of gloves for all patients to save supplies
options.B: Use stored clean water and alcohol rubs correctly between patients
options.C: Skip hand hygiene until running water is restored to the clinic
options.D: Reuse single-use syringes after rinsing them in warm water

explanation: Brilliant problem-solving! Using safe stored water and alcohol rubs keeps your hands clean and keeps your patients safe even when the plumbing acts up. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the main goal of medical asepsis in the ward?

options.A: To kill all bacterial spores
options.B: To replace hand hygiene completely
options.C: To sterilize all medical instruments
options.D: To reduce the number of germs

explanation: Medical asepsis is all about cutting down the number of germs and stopping them from spreading. Surgical asepsis, on the other hand, aims for complete sterility. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h1)

question: When must you clean your hands when wearing gloves?

options.A: Only when the gloves look dirty or torn
options.B: After removing them, but never before
options.C: Before putting them on and after taking them off
options.D: Only before putting on a fresh pair

explanation: Always wash or sanitize your hands before donning gloves and right after doffing them! Gloves can get tiny tears, and your hands can easily pick up germs during removal. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which routine nursing task calls for clean examination gloves?

options.A: Measuring a patient's resting blood pressure
options.B: Handing a clean meal tray to a patient
options.C: Adjusting nasal cannula oxygen flow
options.D: Emptying a urinary catheter drainage bag

explanation: Urine is a body fluid, so you definitely want glove protection to avoid exposure when emptying that drainage bag. Simple and safe! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h2)

question: You are about to check the oral temperature of a patient whose skin is intact. What should you do about gloves?

options.A: Skip gloves because skin is intact and no fluids are expected
options.B: Wear standard examination gloves just in case
options.C: Put on sterile surgical gloves
options.D: Wear heavy-duty utility gloves

explanation: For routine checks involving unbroken skin and no body fluids, gloves aren't needed. This saves precious hospital supplies and time! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h2)

question: What is a major difference between standard examination gloves and surgical gloves?

options.A: Surgical gloves are strictly sterile and have longer cuffs
options.B: Examination gloves are always thicker and tougher
options.C: Examination gloves come in precise numbered hand sizes
options.D: Surgical gloves are only used for drawing blood

explanation: Surgical gloves are sterile and feature longer cuffs to cover your gown sleeves, keeping the operating field completely germ-free. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h3)

question: When should you choose sterile surgical gloves instead of regular exam gloves?

options.A: When performing a procedure inside a sterile body cavity
options.B: During routine physical checks on unbroken skin
options.C: Whenever touching a patient with an infection
options.D: When cleaning up a blood spill on the floor

explanation: Whenever you enter a sterile space or use sterile instruments, you need sterile gloves to keep bacteria out. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h3)

question: Which glove material gives you a great feel (tactile sensitivity) but can cause nasty allergies?

options.A: Nitrile
options.B: Neoprene
options.C: Vinyl
options.D: Latex

explanation: Natural rubber latex fits like a second skin, but protein allergies make it a risk for both healthcare workers and patients. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h4)

question: You need cheap gloves for quick, low-risk tasks where tearing isn't a big worry. Which material is best?

options.A: Latex
options.B: Vinyl
options.C: Surgical
options.D: Nitrile

explanation: Vinyl is budget-friendly and latex-free, making it ideal for quick, low-risk chores where you don't need heavy-duty strength. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the very first thing you must do before putting on examination gloves?

options.A: Open the outer wrapper
options.B: Perform hand hygiene
options.C: Check the patient's skin
options.D: Wipe down your work table

explanation: Always clean your hands first! Putting gloves on unwashed hands traps germs right against your skin. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why does wearing the correct glove size matter so much in clinical work?

options.A: It prevents tearing and keeps your fingers nimble
options.B: It stops the material from causing latex allergies
options.C: It keeps the gloves completely sterile
options.D: It means you don't have to wash your hands afterwards

explanation: Gloves that are too tight will easily rip, while oversized gloves make it hard to grip things. Finding your right size is key! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h5)

question: When taking off dirty gloves, where should your very first move begin?

options.A: Tearing the palm area to loosen a tight fit
options.B: Pulling straight from the fingertips
options.C: Grasping the outside of the cuff and peeling downward
options.D: Snapping the wristband outward with a quick flick

explanation: Pinching the outer cuff lets you peel the glove inside out, trapping all the nasty germs safely on the inside. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h6)

question: Why do you hold the first removed glove inside the palm of your remaining gloved hand?

options.A: To stop the latex from releasing powder into the air
options.B: To easily peel off the second glove without touching its dirty outside
options.C: To keep the first glove clean so you can use it again
options.D: To save space in the waste bin

explanation: Ball up the first glove in your palm so your bare fingers can safely slide under the clean inner cuff of the second glove. Clever and safe! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which of these is a dangerous and incorrect practice with disposable medical gloves?

options.A: Cleaning your hands before putting them on
options.B: Choosing nitrile instead of latex
options.C: Washing and reusing them between patients
options.D: Changing them after every single patient

explanation: Disposable gloves are strictly single-use! Washing them ruins their protective barrier and spreads germs around the ward. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h7)

question: Which situation is an example of cross-contamination from poor glove habits?

options.A: Not wearing gloves to take a pulse on an arm
options.B: Touching a computer keyboard with gloves you wore during wound care
options.C: Washing your hands right after taking off both gloves
options.D: Choosing a larger glove size to avoid thumb tears

explanation: Using dirty gloves on shared equipment like keyboards transfers patient germs to surfaces where other staff can pick them up. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h7)

question: Under standard precautions, when should a nurse wear gloves?

options.A: Whenever you give oral medications to older adults
options.B: Whenever there is a chance of touching blood or body fluids
options.C: During every single interaction with any patient
options.D: Only when caring for patients in isolation rooms

explanation: Standard precautions apply to everyone. If you expect contact with moist body substances, glove up! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h8)

question: A patient is in contact precautions for a resistant bug. What is the rule for gloves in this room?

options.A: Wear gloves only if the patient is bleeding
options.B: Keep the same pair on for your whole shift
options.C: Put on gloves before entering the room and remove them before leaving
options.D: Wear gloves only if doing a surgical dressing change

explanation: For contact precautions, put on your gloves right before you step into the room, and take them off before you step out to contain the germs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T10#GNS122_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the main difference between a wound dressing and a bandage?

options.A: A dressing is only for bone fractures, and bandages are for skin cuts.
options.B: A bandage absorbs drainage, while a dressing provides structural support.
options.C: A bandage is always sterile, whereas dressings are never sterile.
options.D: A dressing touches the wound directly, while a bandage holds the dressing in place.

explanation: Think of it this way: the dressing is the sweet layer right on the open skin soaking up fluids, while the bandage wraps around it to keep everything secure. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why do modern nurses prefer keeping a wound environment moist?

options.A: It leaves the wound completely open to fresh air safely.
options.B: It keeps the body from producing any fluid at all.
options.C: It stops all bacterial growth on the skin completely.
options.D: It lets skin cells repair faster and helps prevent harsh scarring.

explanation: Skin cells love moisture! They glide across a moist wound bed way faster than trying to crawl across a dry, crusty scab. Great nursing knowledge to keep in your pocket. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which type of wound is created under clean, controlled hospital conditions?

options.A: Contaminated laceration
options.B: Traumatic abrasion
options.C: Intentional wound
options.D: Infected ulcer

explanation: An intentional wound is just a planned surgical cut made by a surgeon using strict sterile steps. Nice and straightforward! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h2)

question: How do partial-thickness and full-thickness wounds differ in how they heal?

options.A: Partial-thickness wounds heal by skin cell regeneration, while full-thickness wounds need granulation tissue and a scar.
options.B: Full-thickness wounds never form scar tissue like shallow cuts do.
options.C: Partial-thickness wounds go all the way into the muscle layer.
options.D: Partial-thickness wounds always need skin grafts, but full-thickness ones heal on their own.

explanation: When a wound goes deep (full-thickness), the body has to build new tissue from the bottom up to fill the gap before it can close. You're learning clinical anatomy like a pro! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h2)

question: Which dressing material comes from seaweed and turns into a soft gel when it meets heavy wound fluid?

options.A: Cotton gauze
options.B: Alginate dressing
options.C: Hydrocolloid pad
options.D: Transparent film

explanation: Alginates are made from seaweed and are superstars at soaking up heavy drainage while forming a comfy gel. Pretty cool nursing trivia! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h3)

question: A patient has a deep pressure ulcer on their heel that is draining a lot of fluid. Which dressing is best to handle it?

options.A: Transparent film
options.B: Dry cotton gauze
options.C: Foam dressing
options.D: Paper tape

explanation: Foam dressings are fantastic at cushioning fragile skin while soaking up moderate-to-heavy drainage. Spot on! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h3)

question: What do we call wound drainage that is clear and watery?

options.A: Sanguineous
options.B: Fibrinous
options.C: Purulent
options.D: Serous

explanation: Serous fluid comes from plasma—think of the clear liquid you see in a minor blister. Easy terminology to lock down! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h4)

question: When should you usually give a patient their pain medication before a scheduled dressing change?

options.A: Right after you finish the dressing change
options.B: About 30 minutes before the procedure
options.C: Only if the patient starts crying
options.D: Two hours before so it wears off

explanation: Giving pain meds about half an hour early gives the drug time to kick in right when you start cleaning sensitive tissue. Patient comfort is key! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h4)

question: When you are cleaning a wound, what is the safest direction to wipe?

options.A: From the outer edges inward to the center
options.B: From the cleanest area to the dirtiest area
options.C: In a wild circular motion all over the skin
options.D: From the bottom of the wound straight up

explanation: Always move from clean to dirty! This golden rule stops you from dragging germs from the surrounding skin right back into the open wound. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h5)

question: What must you do if an unsterile object accidentally touches your sterile field while setting up?

options.A: Throw away the whole field and set up a fresh sterile kit.
options.B: Spray antiseptic over the area and wait two minutes.
options.C: Wipe the spot with alcohol and keep going.
options.D: Ignore it if the object looked clean enough.

explanation: Safety first! If a sterile field is touched by something unsterile, its clean status is broken and you have to start fresh. Better safe than sorry in infection control. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h5)

question: What should you do if an old gauze dressing is stuck tightly to a healing wound?

options.A: Leave the old gauze stuck and put new dressings on top.
options.B: Moisten it gently with sterile normal saline to loosen it.
options.C: Soak the whole patient in hot soapy water.
options.D: Rip it off quickly with a fast jerk to save time.

explanation: Never rip dry gauze off! A little sterile saline softens the dried fluid and protects that precious new skin underneath. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h6)

question: Right after finishing a sterile dressing change, what final detail should you write on the dressing tape?

options.A: The hospital's insurance billing code.
options.B: The date, time, and your initials.
options.C: The patient's diagnosis and room number.
options.D: A friendly smiley face for the patient.

explanation: Labeling your work lets the rest of the healthcare team know exactly when the dressing was changed and who did it. Professional habit unlocked! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h6)

question: Which of these details do you need to write in your nursing notes after a dressing change?

options.A: Wound size, color, and how much drainage you saw
options.B: The exact financial cost of the gauze packs
options.C: What the patient's family members think about it
options.D: The brand name of soap the patient uses at home

explanation: Documentation must stay clinical and objective so everyone can track whether the wound is actually getting better. You're thinking like a registered nurse! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h7)

question: What does healthy pink or red granulation tissue tell you about a wound?

options.A: A severe bacterial infection has taken over the site.
options.B: The wound is healing nicely with new blood vessel growth.
options.C: The tissue is dying and needs immediate surgery.
options.D: The dressing material is causing an allergic reaction.

explanation: Granulation tissue is packed with tiny new blood vessels. Seeing that healthy pink/red color is a huge nursing win! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h7)

question: What is the term for a surgical emergency where internal organs pop out through an opened surgical wound?

options.A: Ecchymosis
options.B: Dehiscence
options.C: Evisceration
options.D: Maceration

explanation: Evisceration is a scary medical emergency where organs protrude past the incision line. It needs immediate sterile coverage and a surgeon right away! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h8)

question: What is your very first nursing action if an abdominal wound suddenly pops open and organs are exposed?

options.A: Cover the organs with sterile saline-soaked dressings and call the surgeon.
options.B: Use your gloved fingers to push the organs back inside.
options.C: Wrap a tight binder around the belly to squeeze the organs back in.
options.D: Leave the wound completely open to the fresh air.

explanation: Keep those exposed organs moist with sterile saline gauze so they don't dry out while you call for emergency surgical help. Emergency handled like a champ! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T11#GNS122_U2_T11_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of removing sutures after a wound has healed?

options.A: To restart the bleeding process for better healing
options.B: To prevent foreign body inflammation and scarring
options.C: To measure the exact depth of the subcutaneous tissue
options.D: To allow the application of topical antibiotics

explanation: Leaving thread in the skin too long causes unnecessary local irritation, inflammation, and permanent marks across the scar line. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do sutures need to be taken out instead of left inside the body permanently?

options.A: Skin cells will permanently grow over the thread and trap it in bone.
options.B: Non-absorbable threads act as foreign objects that can trigger infection.
options.C: The body will naturally dissolve all types of suture material within a week.
options.D: Permanent synthetic threads interfere with normal skin sensation forever.

explanation: Non-absorbable materials do not break down inside the body and will cause chronic irritation or abscess formation if left indefinitely. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which body area generally requires the earliest suture removal due to a rich blood supply?

options.A: The lower leg
options.B: The lower back
options.C: The knee joint
options.D: The face

explanation: Facial skin heals very fast because of abundant blood circulation, so sutures are removed early to avoid permanent track marks. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h2)

question: A patient had surgery on their knee joint two days ago. When should the nurse expect these sutures to be removed?

options.A: In 30 days minimum
options.B: In 14 days or more
options.C: In 7 to 8 days
options.D: In 3 to 5 days

explanation: Joint areas experience constant pulling and stretching, requiring a longer healing time and delayed suture removal to prevent reopening. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h2)

question: What should a nurse do if they inspect a wound and notice the edges are still gaping apart?

options.A: Stop the procedure and notify the medical doctor.
options.B: Irrigate the open area with normal saline and remove them anyway.
options.C: Apply strong adhesive tape across the gap and pull the rest.
options.D: Proceed with removing half of the sutures carefully.

explanation: Gaping edges mean the wound has not healed properly, and removing the support will cause the incision to open completely. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h3)

question: Which health condition can significantly delay the normal wound healing process?

options.A: Primary hypertension
options.B: Acute tension headache
options.C: Uncontrolled diabetes
options.D: Mild seasonal allergies

explanation: High blood sugar impairs circulation and white blood cell function, which slows down tissue repair and delays safe suture removal. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h3)

question: What specific tool is commonly used to snip skin threads during suture removal?

options.A: Bandage scissors or suture-removal scissors
options.B: Heavy orthopedic wire cutters
options.C: Standard surgical scalpel handle only
options.D: Disposable plastic tweezers

explanation: Specialized scissors or small curved blades are designed with a tiny hook to slide under the tight thread safely without cutting the skin. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why must the skin around the incision be cleansed with an antiseptic before cutting the threads?

options.A: To numb the local skin nerve endings completely
options.B: To dissolve the remaining knot so scissors are not needed
options.C: To remove surface bacteria and prevent deep infection
options.D: To stain the thread so it is easier to see

explanation: Cleansing eliminates germs sitting on the skin surface, ensuring they do not enter the tiny tract when the thread is pulled through. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h4)

question: When pulling a cut interrupted suture out of the skin, which direction should the nurse pull the thread?

options.A: Away from the wound line
options.B: Straight down into the subcutaneous fat
options.C: In a fast circular motion
options.D: Toward the opposite side of the wound

explanation: Pulling the thread away from the incision prevents the exposed, germ-carrying part of the thread from dragging through the delicate healing tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h5)

question: What is the correct way to handle a continuous (running) suture during removal?

options.A: Cut the knot and pull the main strand so the loops slide out.
options.B: Cut every single loop in half and pull them all out sideways.
options.C: Leave the knots intact and push them deeper under the skin.
options.D: Unravel the entire line manually without using any scissors.

explanation: Continuous sutures are linked together as a single chain, so cutting the proper segments allows the whole strand to glide out smoothly. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h5)

question: What should the nurse apply across the incision after removing sutures to provide extra support?

options.A: Sterile adhesive strips
options.B: Tight elastic bandages
options.C: Thick plaster of paris
options.D: Wet saline gauze pads

explanation: Adhesive closure strips help hold the skin edges together gently while the deeper layers continue gaining strength after suture removal. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h6)

question: Why is it important to carefully inspect the removed threads and the incision site?

options.A: To ensure no small pieces of thread were left inside the skin
options.B: To count the exact number of stitches for insurance records
options.C: To prove to the patient that the procedure is finished
options.D: To save the old thread pieces for laboratory testing

explanation: Retained suture fragments act as foreign bodies that can trigger a delayed local infection or inflammatory reaction inside the tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is wound dehiscence?

options.A: The total numbness of nerves near the surgical site
options.B: The normal darkening of skin color around a healing cut
options.C: The rapid growth of new hair follicles over a scar
options.D: The partial or complete opening of a wound incision

explanation: Dehiscence happens when the edges of a healing wound separate and pull apart, requiring immediate medical attention. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h7)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of a localized infection following suture removal?

options.A: Mild itching around the adhesive strips
options.B: Temporary skin numbness near the cut
options.C: Pus drainage and spreading skin warmth
options.D: Fading pink color of the scar line

explanation: Pus and warmth indicate bacterial multiplication and active inflammation, which signal that the wound is becoming infected. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h7)

question: Why would a nurse choose the intradermal route for giving a medication?

options.A: Allergy and sensitivity testing
options.B: Large volume fluid replacement
options.C: Long-term antibiotic therapy
options.D: Rapid systemic pain relief

explanation: You've got this! Intradermal injections go just under the top layer of skin, which makes them perfect for checking things like TB or allergies. They aren't meant for fast whole-body treatment. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why do intramuscular (IM) injections absorb faster than subcutaneous ones?

options.A: Muscle tissue has a much richer blood supply
options.B: The skin barrier is thinner over muscle sites
options.C: Injections into muscle bypass the liver completely
options.D: Needles used for muscle are always smaller

explanation: Think of blood vessels as busy highways! Because muscles have way more blood vessels than fatty tissue underneath the skin, the medicine gets swept right up into the bloodstream much faster. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h1)

question: Which muscle site is generally considered the safest and most recommended for adult IM injections?

options.A: Dorsogluteal
options.B: Deltoid
options.C: Ventrogluteal
options.D: Vastus lateralis

explanation: Great clinical choice! The ventrogluteal site is a superstar because it stays far away from major nerves and big blood vessels, making it the safest spot on an adult for deep shots. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h2)

question: You need to give a routine vaccine to a healthy 12-month-old baby. Which injection site is best?

options.A: Dorsogluteal
options.B: Ventrogluteal
options.C: Vastus lateralis
options.D: Deltoid

explanation: Spot on! The vastus lateralis (thigh muscle) is nice and plump in little infants, making it the go-to, safe spot for routine baby immunizations. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h2)

question: When looking at needle sizes, what does a higher gauge number tell you?

options.A: The bevel angle is sharper
options.B: The needle length is longer
options.C: The needle width is smaller
options.D: The barrel capacity is larger

explanation: Needle gauges can trick people, but just remember: the bigger the gauge number, the tinier and thinner the actual needle! A 27-gauge is super fine, while an 18-gauge is quite thick. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h3)

question: Which needle size and length is standard for an adult intramuscular injection?

options.A: 25 gauge, 1/2 inch needle
options.B: 27 gauge, 3/8 inch needle
options.C: 22 gauge, 1.5 inch needle
options.D: 31 gauge, 5/8 inch needle

explanation: You need a longer needle and a wider opening (like a 22-gauge, 1.5-inch) to bypass skin and fat and reach deep down into adult muscle tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h3)

question: Why must you use a filter needle when drawing medication out of a glass ampoule?

options.A: To catch microscopic glass fragments
options.B: To prevent the plunger from sticking
options.C: To filter out air bubbles in the liquid
options.D: To neutralize chemical impurities

explanation: Snap! Snapping open that glass top creates tiny, invisible glass shards. A filter needle acts like a tiny shield, catching those shards so they never make it into the syringe. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h4)

question: Why do nurses inject a little bit of air into a closed medication vial before pulling out the liquid?

options.A: To increase the potency of the drug
options.B: To mix the medication with sterile gas
options.C: To prevent a vacuum and ease withdrawal
options.D: To sterilize the rubber stopper surface

explanation: Vials are sealed tight. If you don't pump a little air in first, you end up fighting a vacuum trying to pull the liquid out. Air creates pressure that makes drawing the med smooth and easy! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h4)

question: Why should you let the alcohol swab dry completely on the skin before giving an injection?

options.A: To keep the patient from feeling a cold sensation
options.B: To make sure the skin markings remain clearly visible
options.C: To let the chemical achieve maximum antimicrobial action
options.D: To prevent the needle from slipping out of place

explanation: Patience pays off! Alcohol needs a few seconds of drying time to actually kill the germs. Plus, injecting through wet alcohol stings fiercely—ouch! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h5)

question: At what angle should you insert a subcutaneous injection for an average adult?

options.A: 45 to 90 degrees
options.B: Exactly 180 degrees
options.C: 15 to 30 degrees
options.D: 90 degrees only

explanation: You've got flexibility here! Depending on how much fatty tissue the patient has and how long your needle is, either a 45-degree or a 90-degree angle works great for sub-Q shots. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the main clinical reason for using the Z-track method during an IM injection?

options.A: To speed up the systemic absorption rate of local anesthetics
options.B: To prevent irritating medication from leaking into subcutaneous tissue
options.C: To eliminate the need for skin antisepsis before the procedure
options.D: To reduce the overall depth required for deep muscle penetration

explanation: Z-track is a smart trick! By pulling the skin sideways before sticking, you create a zigzag path that locks harsh or staining medicines deep in the muscle where they belong. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h6)

question: When should you release the pulled skin tissue when doing a Z-track injection?

options.A: Immediately before pushing the plunger down
options.B: Before cleansing the skin site with an alcohol swab
options.C: After the needle has been completely withdrawn
options.D: While the needle is still inside the muscle tissue

explanation: Keep holding that skin until the needle is completely out! Letting go only after the needle is gone ensures the track zips shut and traps the medicine inside. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h6)

question: What is the very first thing you should do right after giving an injection?

options.A: Break the needle off the syringe barrel before throwing it in the trash
options.B: Activate the safety device and drop the syringe into a sharps container
options.C: Recap the needle firmly using both hands to protect housekeeping staff
options.D: Place the exposed needle on the bedside tray until documentation is done

explanation: Safety first! Never recap needles with two hands. Pop the safety shield on and drop the whole syringe straight into the sharps box to avoid nasty needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h7)

question: What complication can happen if you give an intramuscular injection too low on the back of the hip?

options.A: Lipodystrophy
options.B: Cellulitis of the dermis
options.C: Systemic air embolism
options.D: Sciatic nerve damage

explanation: Watch out for that sciatic nerve! Aiming too low or too close to the middle on the posterior hip can hit this huge nerve, causing terrible pain and walking issues for the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h7)

question: When is the right time to chart an injection you just gave your patient?

options.A: Only if the patient reports an adverse reaction
options.B: At the end of the 8-hour shift
options.C: Before drawing the drug from the vial
options.D: Immediately after giving the injection

explanation: Always document right away! Doing it immediately keeps your records accurate and lets the rest of the healthcare team know the patient's exact medication status. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h8)

question: Why do nurses stick around and monitor a patient for about 30 minutes after certain shots or vaccines?

options.A: To ensure the patient does not walk around too soon
options.B: To verify that the medication has been fully absorbed
options.C: To measure the exact change in body temperature
options.D: To watch for acute allergic or anaphylactic reactions

explanation: Better safe than sorry! Severe allergic reactions usually pop up fast. Keeping an eye on your patient during that first half-hour means you can jump in with emergency help if needed. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T13#GNS122_U2_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of placing a drainage tube in a surgical wound?

options.A: To measure the exact blood pressure of the local tissue bed
options.B: To remove fluid or air and prevent dangerous accumulation
options.C: To deliver strong liquid antibiotics directly into the tissue
options.D: To keep the surgical incision completely open for daily inspection

explanation: Drains are used to clear out blood, serum, or air that can collect inside a body cavity, which helps lower infection risk and pressure. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h1)

question: Why is a closed drainage system generally preferred over an open system?

options.A: It relies entirely on patient movement rather than gravity or suction
options.B: It never requires emptying or measuring by the nursing staff
options.C: It dissolves completely inside the body over a few days
options.D: It greatly reduces the chance of external bacteria entering the wound

explanation: Closed systems keep the drainage contained within sealed tubing and collection bags, making it harder for germs from the outside environment to reach the healing tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h1)

question: Why must a gravity drainage bag always be positioned below the level of the wound?

options.A: To use gravity to pull fluid out and prevent it from flowing back
options.B: To make it easier for the patient to walk around the unit
options.C: To keep the collection bag hidden from the patient's direct view
options.D: To stop the tubing from becoming permanently kinked or twisted

explanation: If the collection container is higher than the wound, fluid inside the tubing can flow backward into the body cavity, introducing bacteria and causing infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h2)

question: Which finding around a drainage tube insertion site is a sign of a potential infection?

options.A: Clear pink fluid on the outer dressing
options.B: Purulent discharge and foul odor
options.C: A small amount of dried blood at the stitch
options.D: Soft skin that feels cool to the touch

explanation: Pus and bad smells are classic indicators that bacteria are multiplying at the wound site, signaling a developing infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the main risk of aggressively stripping surgical drainage tubes?

options.A: It can create a strong vacuum that damages delicate internal tissue
options.B: It always causes the collection container to crack and leak fluid
options.C: It permanently ruins the plastic so it can no longer collect blood
options.D: It stops the patient from feeling any post-operative surgical pain

explanation: Stripping generates high negative pressure inside the tube, which can suck delicate tissue into the drainage holes and cause injury or bleeding. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h3)

question: What does milking a drainage tube involve?

options.A: Disconnecting the drainage bag completely and washing the inside with soap
options.B: Injecting large volumes of sterile water upward into the wound site
options.C: Twisting the tube tightly until the fluid stops flowing completely
options.D: Gently squeezing and releasing the tubing downward to push clots along

explanation: Milking is a gentle technique used to clear minor blockages by compressing the tubing progressively toward the collection container. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h3)

question: A nurse notices that a surgical drain has produced 300 mL of bright red blood in the last hour. What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.A: Strip the tubing vigorously to clear out any remaining blood clots
options.B: Elevate the collection bag above the level of the patient's wound
options.C: Document the normal finding and check the patient again tomorrow
options.D: Notify the surgeon immediately because this suggests active hemorrhage

explanation: A sudden, large volume of bright red drainage indicates heavy bleeding inside the body, which requires urgent medical intervention. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h4)

question: When measuring fluid from a drainage container, how should the nurse read the volume accurately?

options.A: By guessing the amount based on how full the bulb looks
options.B: By weighing the container on a bathroom scale while wet
options.C: By holding the container high up near the ceiling lights
options.D: At eye level with the liquid resting on a flat surface

explanation: Reading fluid levels at eye level on a flat surface prevents parallax errors and ensures the measurement recorded on the chart is correct. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h4)

question: When cleaning the skin around a drainage tube, what is the correct direction to wipe?

options.A: Strictly from the bottom of the wound up toward the top
options.B: Back and forth rapidly across the entire wound surface
options.C: From the outer edges of the tape inward toward the tubing
options.D: In a circular motion starting at the tube and moving outward

explanation: Cleaning from the cleanest area (the insertion site) toward the dirtier outer skin prevents dragging outside bacteria closer to the wound opening. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h5)

question: Which type of gauze is specially designed to fit snugly around a surgical drain?

options.A: Split-drain gauze with a pre-cut slit
options.B: Elastic compression bandage wraps
options.C: Large roller gauze wrapped around the limb
options.D: Non-absorbent plastic mesh sheeting

explanation: Split-drain gauze features a factory-made cut that allows it to wrap around the tube without overlapping or leaving gaps in protection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h5)

question: A patient's surgical drain has accidentally fallen out onto the bed sheets. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Rinse the fallen tube with tap water and tape it to the skin
options.B: Cover the insertion site immediately with a sterile dressing
options.C: Leave the open hole uncovered to let the remaining fluid drain out
options.D: Put sterile gloves on and push the tube right back into the wound

explanation: Placing a sterile dressing over the hole protects the exposed tissue from bacteria, and you should never reinsert a fallen drain because it is no longer sterile. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the most likely cause when fluid leaks constantly around the outside of a drainage tube?

options.A: Normal healing of the deeper muscle layers inside
options.B: The collection bag hanging below the level of the bed
options.C: The patient drinking too much water during the night
options.D: A loose seal or saturation of the current dressing

explanation: Leakage around the tube entry site often happens when the dressing is too full to hold more fluid or when the seal around the tube is compromised. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h6)

question: Why is the patient instructed to take a deep breath and hold it while a chest or abdominal drain is removed?

options.A: To distract the patient so they do not feel any sharp pain
options.B: To help the remaining fluid rush out faster before sealing
options.C: To relax the outer muscles so the tube slips out without resistance
options.D: To increase internal pressure and prevent air from entering the body

explanation: Holding a deep breath raises internal pressure, which stops air from being drawn into the body cavity through the open tract as the tube comes out. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h7)

question: What type of dressing is typically applied immediately after a drainage tube is pulled out?

options.A: An airtight sterile dressing
options.B: A wet saline compress wrap
options.C: An open gauze pad without tape
options.D: A rigid plastic protective shell

explanation: An occlusive or airtight sterile dressing is placed over the fresh wound site to seal the opening and protect it from outside bacteria while it closes. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h7)

question: Why do nurses use isolation techniques in the ward?

options.A: To speed up the patient's physical recovery
options.B: To prevent the spread of harmful microorganisms
options.C: To completely cure the underlying disease
options.D: To reduce the cost of hospital medications

explanation: Isolation acts like a shield to stop germs from jumping between patients, staff, and visitors. Great job keeping the ward safe! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h1)

question: Who is protected when a nurse properly uses isolation precautions?

options.A: Only the doctors working in the ward
options.B: Only the patient who is currently sick
options.C: Patients, healthcare workers, and visitors
options.D: Hospital management and administrators

explanation: Infection control keeps everyone in the hospital safe and sound—patients, your colleagues, and loved ones who come to visit! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h1)

question: How do isolation methods mainly stop infections from spreading?

options.A: By destroying the causative agent inside the body
options.B: By blocking the mode of transmission
options.C: By eliminating all reservoirs on the hospital ward
options.D: By making the host completely immune to disease

explanation: By putting up physical barriers like gloves, masks, and private rooms, we cut off the path germs use to travel to new hosts. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h2)

question: In infection control, what do we call a 'reservoir'?

options.A: A person who is immune to the infection
options.B: The route by which a germ leaves the body
options.C: A place where pathogens live and multiply
options.D: The physical barrier used to block germs

explanation: Think of a reservoir as a cozy home for germs. It can be a human, an animal, or even a damp surface where they grow and wait to spread. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h2)

question: Which patients should receive Standard Precautions?

options.A: Every patient in the healthcare setting
options.B: Only patients with weak immune systems
options.C: Only patients admitted to the emergency room
options.D: Only patients with confirmed infections

explanation: Always treat every patient with Standard Precautions! We treat everyone as if they could carry an infection, keeping both them and us safe. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h3)

question: When do you need to add Transmission-Based Precautions?

options.A: When a specific infection is known or suspected
options.B: When the nurse starts a new morning shift
options.C: When standard handwashing fails to work
options.D: When the patient requests a private room

explanation: You add these special precautions (like gowns or masks) on top of standard ones whenever you're dealing with a specific germ. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h3)

question: What special mask is a must-have for Airborne Precautions?

options.A: Disposable plastic apron
options.B: Clean non-sterile gloves
options.C: Standard surgical mask
options.D: N95 respirator mask

explanation: Tiny germs floating in the air need an N95 respirator to filter them out before they reach your lungs. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h4)

question: A patient is admitted with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis. What do you do right away?

options.A: Contact precautions
options.B: Droplet precautions
options.C: Standard precautions only
options.D: Airborne precautions

explanation: TB travels easily through tiny air particles. Setting up airborne precautions and grabbing an N95 protects everyone immediately. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h4)

question: When leaving an isolation room, what is the very first piece of PPE you take off?

options.A: Gloves
options.B: Goggles
options.C: Gown
options.D: Mask

explanation: Your gloves have touched the most germs, so they come off first! Always peel them off carefully before touching anything else. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h5)

question: Why is the order of removing your PPE so important?

options.A: It prevents self-contamination from dirty gear onto clean skin
options.B: It keeps the patient's room looking tidy
options.C: It ensures the equipment can be washed and reused safely
options.D: It saves time during busy hospital shifts

explanation: Following the right steps ensures that the germs on your outer gear don't accidentally end up on your face or skin. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h5)

question: What does 'cohorting' mean in the ward?

options.A: Placing patients with the same infection in the same room
options.B: Training new nursing students in isolation procedures
options.C: Sharing medical equipment between different hospital wards
options.D: Moving a patient to a room with negative air pressure

explanation: When single rooms run out, grouping patients with the exact same infection together is a smart way to manage space and safety. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h6)

question: What special room feature do you need for a patient on Airborne Precautions?

options.A: Negative pressure airflow
options.B: An attached private sunroom
options.C: Open windows for natural breeze
options.D: Positive pressure ventilation

explanation: A negative pressure room pulls air in instead of blowing it out into the hallway when the door opens, trapping germs inside. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h6)

question: How do patients in strict isolation often feel emotionally?

options.A: Indifference to hospital staff
options.B: Loneliness and anxiety
options.C: Relief from daily visitors
options.D: Excitement about privacy

explanation: Being cut off from normal human contact behind barriers can make patients feel very lonely and worried. Empathy goes a long way here! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h7)

question: How can you best support a patient feeling down due to isolation?

options.A: Limit all conversations to essential medical updates only
options.B: Keep the room door tightly closed at all hours of the day
options.C: Schedule regular visits and encourage communication with family
options.D: Advise the patient to sleep most of the day away

explanation: A friendly chat, a reassuring smile, and helping them connect with family helps beat the loneliness of isolation. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h7)

question: What is considered the single most effective habit to stop the spread of infection?

options.A: Changing hospital scrubs hourly
options.B: Proper hand hygiene
options.C: Wearing sterile gloves all day
options.D: Using strong chemical sprays

explanation: Good old handwashing (or using alcohol rub) at the right moments is your absolute best defense against spreading germs! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a correct way to handle hospital waste?

options.A: Sealing biohazard bags securely before carrying them out
options.B: Disposing of sharp needles in designated puncture-proof boxes
options.C: Leaving overfilled waste bags open in the hallway
options.D: Wearing gloves when touching soiled linen or dressings

explanation: Leaving dirty waste bags open in public view is a major hazard! Always seal and dispose of waste safely. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of barrier nursing?

options.A: To completely cure chronic infectious diseases
options.B: To stop pathogens from spreading between people
options.C: To speed up the healing of surgical wounds
options.D: To replace the need for routine handwashing

explanation: Barrier nursing uses physical blocks to prevent germs from moving from one person or surface to another. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h1)

question: Why are hospital-acquired infections a major concern for nurses using barriers?

options.A: Wards lack enough cleaning supplies
options.B: Hospital germs are easily spread to vulnerable patients
options.C: Patients bring all their own germs from home
options.D: Doctors rarely wash their hands

explanation: Sick patients in hospitals have lowered immune defenses, making them very easy targets for spreading germs if barriers are missed. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h1)

question: The place where a microorganism normally lives and multiplies is called what?

options.A: A susceptible host
options.B: A reservoir
options.C: A portal of entry
options.D: A transmission route

explanation: A reservoir provides a safe home for pathogens to survive and multiply before finding a new host. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h2)

question: How does washing your hands thoroughly break the chain of infection?

options.A: It removes the susceptible host entirely
options.B: It eliminates the initial reservoir
options.C: It stops the mode of transmission
options.D: It destroys the infectious agent completely

explanation: Hand hygiene removes germs from your hands, preventing them from traveling from one patient or surface to another. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h2)

question: Which type of isolation is used to protect a patient with a very weak immune system?

options.A: Strict contact isolation
options.B: Respiratory isolation
options.C: Protective isolation
options.D: Standard isolation

explanation: Protective or reverse isolation guards patients who cannot fight off everyday germs by keeping outside microorganisms away from them. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h3)

question: A patient with a wound infected by a multi-drug resistant organism needs which type of precaution?

options.A: Respiratory isolation
options.B: Protective isolation
options.C: Contact isolation
options.D: Airborne isolation

explanation: Resistant germs in open wounds are typically passed through physical touch, making contact isolation necessary. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h3)

question: Who should be cared for using standard precautions in a hospital?

options.A: Every patient, regardless of their diagnosis
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Only patients with confirmed viral infections
options.D: Only individuals coughing or showing rashes

explanation: Standard precautions are universal and must be applied to all patients because infection status is not always known upfront. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h4)

question: When are transmission-based precautions added to patient care?

options.A: Only after laboratory tests prove the patient is cured
options.B: When the hospital runs out of standard gloves
options.C: When a specific contagious disease is suspected or confirmed
options.D: Whenever a visitor enters the isolation room

explanation: Transmission-based precautions are extra steps added on top of standard rules when dealing with specific, easily spread germs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h4)

question: When putting on a full set of PPE, which item is typically put on first?

options.A: The face mask
options.B: The eye goggles
options.C: The gown
options.D: The gloves

explanation: The gown is put on first to cover your clothing, followed by masks, eye protection, and gloves last. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h5)

question: Why must you perform hand hygiene immediately after taking off your gloves?

options.A: Hospital policy requires washing hands twice per hour
options.B: Gloves make your hands smell unpleasant
options.C: Microorganisms may have transferred to your skin during removal
options.D: It helps the skin dry out after sweating inside rubber

explanation: Even with careful removal, tiny tears or contact with the outside of gloves can transfer germs to your hands. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h5)

question: Where should used injection needles and sharp blades be discarded?

options.A: Puncture-proof sharps containers
options.B: Red infectious linen laundry bags
options.C: Open cardboard boxes near sinks
options.D: Standard black plastic waste bins

explanation: Sharps must go directly into rigid, puncture-resistant containers to prevent accidental needle pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h6)

question: What is the main reason for frequently cleaning high-touch surfaces in an isolation room?

options.A: To prevent germs from surviving on objects and spreading
options.B: To prevent medical equipment from rusting
options.C: To make the floor shiny and slip-resistant
options.D: To keep the room smelling fresh for visitors

explanation: Pathogens can live on dry surfaces for hours or days, making regular disinfection vital to stopping indirect spread. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h6)

question: How do patients in isolation often feel due to lack of human contact?

options.A: Relieved and relaxed
options.B: Indifferent and calm
options.C: Lonely and anxious
options.D: Energetic and joyful

explanation: Being cut off from normal social interaction and seeing staff in heavy gear frequently causes emotional distress. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h7)

question: A patient in strict isolation cries because no one wants to touch them without gear. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Assure them that the infection is not serious at all
options.B: Remove your gown and gloves to prove you care
options.C: Tell them the rules are necessary and leave the room quickly
options.D: Acknowledge their feelings and spend time talking calmly with them

explanation: Validating emotions and offering supportive conversation helps reduce the psychological toll of isolation while keeping safety intact. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h7)

question: What is a key daily responsibility of the nurse regarding barrier nursing?

options.A: Writing new infectious disease policies
options.B: Testing hospital water supplies daily
options.C: Ordering all hospital cleaning supplies
options.D: Ensuring proper compliance with infection control rules

explanation: Nurses must actively monitor and maintain infection control standards during every shift to protect patients and staff. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h8)

question: What should a nurse do if a visitor enters an isolation room without wearing the required PPE?

options.A: Ignore it if they promise not to touch the patient
options.B: Ask another staff member to handle the situation later
options.C: Report the visitor to hospital security immediately
options.D: Politely stop them, explain the rules, and help them put on PPE

explanation: Educating visitors and ensuring they wear correct gear prevents breaches in the barrier system. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h8)

question: What is the main goal of using aseptic technique in the ward?

options.A: To prevent pathogen contamination during clinical procedures
options.B: To cure patients who already have active bacterial infections
options.C: To completely eliminate all microbes from the hospital environment
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of hospital-acquired illnesses

explanation: You've got this! Aseptic techniques are just safe practices we use to stop harmful germs from getting into clean or sterile parts of the body during procedures. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is infection control a team duty for all healthcare workers?

options.A: Because cleaning supplies are distributed equally among departments
options.B: Because a single mistake by any staff member can put a patient at risk
options.C: Because only doctors are allowed to handle sterile equipment
options.D: Because hospital management requires daily written reports from nurses

explanation: Spot on! Keeping patients safe is a team effort. Because we all work together around the patient, one small slip by anyone can let germs spread—so every member's vigilance counts. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which of these everyday nursing actions is an example of medical asepsis?

options.A: Performing an open surgical operation in the theatre
options.B: Wiping down a bedside table with a disinfectant wipe
options.C: Putting on sterile surgical gloves and a gown
options.D: Inserting a urinary catheter using a sterile kit

explanation: Great job! Medical asepsis is all about clean habits—like wiping down surfaces to cut down on germs. Surgical asepsis is what we save for deep, sterile procedures. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h2)

question: When should you as a nurse switch to surgical asepsis instead of medical asepsis?

options.A: Before giving oral medication to a patient in the general ward
options.B: During any procedure that enters a normally sterile body cavity
options.C: After finishing a routine bed bath for an adult patient
options.D: Whenever entering a patient room with a known respiratory infection

explanation: You're doing great! Whenever we do invasive things like passing a catheter or assisting in theater, we need total sterility to protect deep body tissues from infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h2)

question: What should you do if you are unsure whether a sterile package is still clean?

options.A: Use the item quickly before anyone notices the error
options.B: Treat the item as contaminated and get a new one
options.C: Ask another nurse to guess if the item is still safe
options.D: Wipe the outside package with alcohol and use it anyway

explanation: Safety first! In nursing, if there is ever any doubt about an item's sterility, we assume it's contaminated and grab a fresh one. Never gamble with a patient's safety. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why is the outer one-inch border of a sterile field considered unsterile?

options.A: Because nurses are only allowed to touch the exact center of the tray
options.B: Because air currents move faster along the edges of a paper wrap
options.C: Because the manufacturer marks that area with special invisible ink
options.D: Because it is likely to touch unsterile surfaces during setup and handling

explanation: Makes sense, right? That outer edge is bound to brush against your hands or the table surface while you open it, so we treat it as a safe buffer zone that's no longer sterile. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop the spread of infections in the hospital?

options.A: Taking daily antibiotics
options.B: Wearing sterile gloves
options.C: Using room air filters
options.D: Proper hand hygiene

explanation: Simple yet powerful! Washing or sanitizing your hands properly is your number one shield against carrying germs from patient to patient. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h4)

question: You just removed a dirty dressing from a draining wound while wearing gloves. What is your immediate next step after taking them off?

options.A: Put on a fresh pair of clean gloves
options.B: Touch the clean patient chart safely
options.C: Perform hand hygiene immediately
options.D: Write the nursing notes in the chart

explanation: Always clean your hands right after taking off gloves! Microbes can easily slip through tiny, unseen tears in gloves, so hand hygiene seals the deal. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h4)

question: When opening a wrapped sterile package on your tray, which flap should you open first?

options.A: The left side flap of the paper wrap
options.B: The right side flap of the paper wrap
options.C: The flap furthest away from the body
options.D: The flap closest to the nurse's chest

explanation: You've got this! Opening the far flap first means your hands won't have to reach directly across the clean items you just exposed. Smart and safe! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why must you never leave a set-up sterile field unattended on the ward?
