options.A: Because sterile drapes automatically fold up after five minutes
options.B: Because the sterile items will melt if exposed to room air
options.C: Because someone might contaminate it without your knowledge
options.D: Because hospital regulations fine nurses who walk away from trays

explanation: Spot on! If you walk away, someone might unknowingly brush against it or contaminate it, ruining your sterile setup. Stay close to your work! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which of these hospital items is considered critical and needs full sterilization?

options.A: A surgical scalpel blade
options.B: A reusable blood pressure cuff
options.C: A stethoscope chest piece
options.D: A bedside plastic commode

explanation: Brilliant! Scalpels cut deep into sterile body tissues, so they must be 100% free of all germs and spores through proper sterilization. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main difference between disinfection and sterilization?

options.A: Sterilization is only used on patient skin, while disinfection is used on metal tools
options.B: Disinfection uses high-pressure steam, while sterilization uses simple soap and water
options.C: Sterilization destroys all microorganisms and spores, while disinfection reduces their numbers
options.D: Disinfection kills bacterial spores, while sterilization only kills active living fungi

explanation: Think of it this way: sterilization wipes out *everything* including tough spores, while disinfection just lowers the germ count on surfaces to a safe level. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h6)

question: What do we mean by a healthcare-associated infection (HAI)?

options.A: An infectious disease that doctors catch from patients in the clinic
options.B: An infection acquired by a patient while receiving treatment in a hospital
options.C: A chronic illness that people inherit from their parents at birth
options.D: A skin rash caused by wearing dirty uniforms outside the ward

explanation: You're doing awesome! An HAI is simply an infection a patient picks up while receiving care in the hospital—something they didn't have when they first checked in. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which of these actions is NOT a way nurses help prevent healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Prescribing strong antibiotic medications to every new patient
options.B: Changing surgical wound dressings according to hospital policy
options.C: Using sterile technique during invasive urinary catheter insertions
options.D: Practicing consistent hand hygiene before and after patient contact

explanation: Spot on! Nurses don't prescribe drugs, and giving antibiotics to everyone would cause dangerous drug resistance rather than stop infections. Good catch! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which patients in a hospital setting require the use of standard precautions?

options.A: All patients regardless of their diagnosis
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Only patients who have open wounds
options.D: Only patients with confirmed infectious diseases

explanation: Standard precautions are designed for every patient interaction because infection status is not always known upon admission. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h1)

question: Standard precautions apply to which of these body fluids in the ward?

options.A: Sweat from a patient exercising in physical therapy
options.B: Clean tap water used for bed baths
options.C: Saliva and wound drainage from a post-operative client
options.D: Tears collected after an eye examination

explanation: Spot on! Standard precautions cover all body fluids—except sweat. Saliva and wound drainage can carry germs, so we always protect ourselves. You are thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the most effective single measure to prevent the spread of infections in a hospital?

options.A: Changing bed linens twice daily
options.B: Wearing sterile gloves for every task
options.C: Performing proper hand hygiene
options.D: Spraying patient rooms with disinfectants

explanation: Hand hygiene remains the single most impactful action a nurse can take to break the chain of infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h2)

question: When must a nurse choose soap and water over an alcohol-based hand rub?

options.A: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.B: Before entering a patient room for vital signs
options.C: After touching an intact patient gown
options.D: Immediately before administering oral medication

explanation: Alcohol rubs do not clean away physical dirt or certain spore-forming bacteria effectively, requiring mechanical washing with soap and water. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which piece of PPE is primarily used to protect the nurse's clothing from splashes of body fluids?

options.A: A surgical mask
options.B: Sterile shoe covers
options.C: A face shield
options.D: A protective gown

explanation: Gowns cover the uniform and skin of the torso to block fluid splashes during high-risk procedures. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h3)

question: You are about to flush out a deep infected wound that might splash fluid. What PPE do you need to wear?

options.A: Sterile gloves and a gown without eye protection
options.B: Gloves, a gown, a mask, and eye protection
options.C: A mask and shoe covers only
options.D: Gloves and a surgical cap only

explanation: Brilliant! Wound splashing is unpredictable. Covering your hands, body, mouth, and eyes keeps you totally protected. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the main reason we teach patients respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette?

options.A: Reducing the cost of cleaning medical equipment
options.B: Preventing foodborne illnesses among patients
options.C: Containing respiratory pathogens at the source
options.D: Purifying the air inside closed hospital wards

explanation: Spot on! Cough etiquette stops germs right where they start—catching them in a tissue or elbow before they can fly into the air. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h4)

question: What should a patient do right after coughing into a disposable tissue?

options.A: Place the tissue in their pocket for later use
options.B: Leave the tissue on the bedside table
options.C: Hand the tissue directly to the attending nurse
options.D: Throw the tissue in the trash and clean their hands

explanation: Correct! Tossing the tissue straight into the bin and cleaning up stops those sneaky germs from spreading to bed tables or other people. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the safest way to handle a used injection needle?

options.A: Break the needle off the syringe by hand
options.B: Drop it immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container
options.C: Recap it firmly using both hands before walking away
options.D: Place it inside a regular plastic waste bin

explanation: You've got it! Never mess around with used needles. Drop them straight into the sharps box to avoid accidental pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h5)

question: Why do we strongly advise against using both hands to recap a needle?

options.A: It damages the sharpness of the needle tip
options.B: It makes the syringe difficult to read
options.C: It greatly increases the risk of an accidental needle-stick injury
options.D: It takes too much time during an emergency

explanation: Spot on! Trying to guide a cap back on with two hands is a recipe for poking your own finger. Safety rules are written in blood—let's protect those fingers! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which high-touch surface in a patient room requires frequent routine disinfection?

options.A: Bedside tables and bed rails
options.B: The inside of closed closet drawers
options.C: Carpeted flooring under the bed
options.D: The ceiling tiles above the bed

explanation: High-touch items like bed rails and tables are frequently contaminated by hands and require regular cleaning. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h6)

question: How should a nurse handle bed sheets that are stained with blood?

options.A: Handle them with minimal agitation and bag them securely
options.B: Wash them by hand in the patient bathroom sink
options.C: Leave them on the floor until housekeeping arrives
options.D: Shake them out thoroughly to remove loose debris

explanation: You nailed it! Shaking dirty linens sends dust and germs flying everywhere. Roll them up gently and bag them safely! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T3#GNS122_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main goal of sterilization?

options.A: The removal of visible blood stains from metal surfaces
options.B: The elimination of dust and organic dirt from equipment
options.C: The complete removal or destruction of all microbial life
options.D: The reduction of harmful bacteria to safe levels on skin

explanation: Sterilization is all about getting rid of every single germ and tough spore so nothing is left alive. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is sterilization stricter and more powerful than standard disinfection?

options.A: It only applies to items that touch intact human skin
options.B: It can be completed in a few seconds using simple wipes
options.C: It targets and kills bacterial spores as well as vegetative cells
options.D: It is performed using mild soaps and warm running water

explanation: Disinfection kills a lot of germs, but tough bacterial spores can survive it. Sterilization goes the extra mile to destroy those resilient spores completely! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which of these steps must you always do first before disinfecting or sterilizing equipment?

options.A: Packaging
options.B: Cleaning
options.C: Disinfection
options.D: Sterilization

explanation: Always wash off blood, dirt, and tissue first! If dirt is left on the tool, it shields the germs from the disinfecting or sterilizing agents. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h2)

question: A nurse wipes down a bedside table with a chemical disinfectant. What is the expected result?

options.A: Most pathogenic germs are killed, but bacterial spores may survive
options.B: The surface becomes completely sterile for surgical procedures
options.C: All living microorganisms and tough spores are completely destroyed
options.D: Only visible dust and physical dirt are physically washed away

explanation: Disinfectants are great for cleaning surfaces and killing most harmful germs, but they don't always wipe out tough bacterial spores. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h2)

question: You are getting instruments ready for a deep abdominal surgery. How must these tools be processed?

options.A: Low-level disinfection
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: High-level disinfection
options.D: Thorough soap washing

explanation: Any tool going into sterile body tissue or blood vessels is a critical item and absolutely must be sterilized! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h3)

question: An item touches a patient's unbroken skin during a routine check-up. According to Spaulding's rules, what level of processing does it need?

options.A: Low-level disinfection
options.B: No processing is required
options.C: Sterilization
options.D: High-level disinfection

explanation: Items that only touch intact skin are non-critical and just need basic low-level disinfection between patients. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h3)

question: What does an autoclave mainly use to achieve full sterilization?

options.A: Dry scorching hot air
options.B: Toxic formaldehyde gas
options.C: Ultraviolet light rays
options.D: Moist heat under pressure

explanation: Autoclaves use pressurized steam, which packs enough heat to rapidly destroy all germs and spores. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why might a nurse choose dry heat sterilization instead of an autoclave for certain sharp tools or powders?

options.A: Dry heat uses steam pressure to penetrate thick plastic wrappers
options.B: Dry heat takes only two minutes to complete a full cycle
options.C: Dry heat is much cheaper to operate than electricity
options.D: Dry heat does not cause rusting or damage to moisture-sensitive items

explanation: Steam can rust fine metal edges or ruin powders. Dry heat is a wonderful alternative when you need to avoid moisture! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which chemical agent requires a special airing-out (aeration) period because it leaves toxic gas behind?

options.A: Ordinary liquid soap
options.B: Hydrogen peroxide
options.C: Ethylene oxide
options.D: Standard tap water

explanation: Ethylene oxide is a strong sterilizing gas, but items need to sit in a special aeration chamber afterward to clear out lingering toxic fumes. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is a big plus of using hydrogen peroxide gas plasma compared to older gas methods?

options.A: It works instantly without needing any special packaging
options.B: It can be performed easily using standard washbasins
options.C: It operates at low temperatures and leaves no toxic residue
options.D: It is the cheapest method available for hospital wards

explanation: Gas plasma is gentle on delicate equipment and breaks down into harmless water and oxygen, skipping the long wait for aeration. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which check is considered the ultimate gold standard to confirm your autoclave cycle actually worked?

options.A: Biological indicators containing resistant bacterial spores
options.B: Checking the machine door seal for visible steam leaks
options.C: Reviewing the nurse's handwritten checklist after a shift
options.D: A quick visual check of the external packaging tape color

explanation: Using actual resistant spores in biological indicators gives us the absolute best proof that the machine killed the toughest germs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main drawback of relying only on a chemical indicator strip on the outside of a sterile pack?

options.A: It can tell the exact internal temperature reached deep inside the metal tray
options.B: It permanently destroys the bacterial spores hidden inside the pack
options.C: It requires a laboratory incubator to read the final color change
options.D: It only shows that the pack was exposed to heat or gas, not that it is truly sterile

explanation: Color changes on the outside just prove the pack went into the machine; they don't guarantee every single germ inside was destroyed. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h6)

question: What does 'event-related sterility' mean for packaged instruments sitting in storage?

options.A: Sterility depends entirely on the specific time of day it was processed
options.B: Instruments lose their sterility the moment they are placed on a shelf
options.C: All items automatically expire exactly seven days after autoclaving
options.D: Items remain sterile until the packaging is damaged or exposed to moisture

explanation: Instead of worrying about a strict calendar expiration date, packs stay sterile as long as the packaging remains safe and dry! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h7)

question: A nurse picks up a sterile surgical tray from the supply room and notices the outer paper wrapper is damp. What should she do?

options.A: Dry the outside wrapper carefully with a clean towel and use it
options.B: Check the chemical indicator strip and use the tray if the color changed
options.C: Consider the item contaminated and return it for re-sterilization
options.D: Open the package immediately before the moisture spreads further

explanation: Moisture on packaging acts like a sponge, pulling bacteria right through the barrier. It's best to safely reprocess it! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T4#GNS122_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the main goal of disinfecting items in the ward?

options.A: To destroy most harmful germs on surfaces and non-living objects
options.B: To prevent allergic reactions from contact with medical tools
options.C: To eliminate all living cells and bacterial spores completely
options.D: To remove visible dirt and organic matter with water and soap

explanation: Great job thinking like a nurse! Disinfection is focused on knocking out pathogens on tables, beds, and equipment, though tough bacterial spores might still survive. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h1)

question: How is disinfection different from sterilization?

options.A: Sterilization takes less time than standard chemical disinfection
options.B: Disinfection is only performed on human skin and living tissues
options.C: Disinfection does not destroy all bacterial spores like sterilization does
options.D: Sterilization uses chemical agents while disinfection only uses heat

explanation: Spot on! Sterilization is the heavy-duty process that wipes out every single trace of life, including tough spores. Disinfection cleans up most germs, but leaves spores behind. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why must a nurse always clean an instrument before disinfecting it?

options.A: To sterilize the equipment without using heat or gas
options.B: To dry the medical instrument so it does not rust
options.C: To remove organic matter that can block chemical disinfectants
options.D: To instantly kill all bacterial spores present on the surface

explanation: Think of dirt or dried blood as a shield for germs! Cleaning washes away that organic barrier so your disinfectant can actually reach and kill the bacteria. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which process completely destroys ALL microbial life, including tough spores?

options.A: Cleaning
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: Sanitization
options.D: Disinfection

explanation: You nailed it! Only true sterilization goes all the way to wipe out every single microorganism and stubborn spore. Simple disinfection can't do that. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h2)

question: What level of cleaning is needed for items that only touch intact, healthy skin?

options.A: High-level disinfection
options.B: Intermediate-level disinfection
options.C: Low-level disinfection
options.D: Complete sterilization

explanation: Makes total sense! Items like blood pressure cuffs that only touch unbroken skin carry a very low infection risk, so basic low-level disinfection is plenty. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h3)

question: A nurse is preparing a flexible endoscope that touches mucous membranes. What level of germ control does this need?

options.A: Standard mechanical cleaning
options.B: Low-level disinfection
options.C: Routine surface wiping
options.D: High-level disinfection

explanation: Right on! Anything touching mucous membranes is 'semi-critical' and needs high-level disinfection to knock out almost all pathogens, keeping our patients safe. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h3)

question: How do alcohol-based disinfectants actually kill germs?

options.A: Forming hard crystals inside the bacterial nucleus
options.B: Blocking the respiratory system of the patient
options.C: Dissolving cell membranes and denaturing proteins
options.D: Lowering the room temperature to freeze pathogens

explanation: Alcohol is a tiny powerhouse! It rapidly tears apart the outer fatty layer of the germ and scrambles its vital proteins so it can't survive. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why is mixing a chemical disinfectant to the correct ratio so important?

options.A: Incorrectly mixed solutions may fail to kill target microorganisms
options.B: Water content prevents the disinfectant from evaporating too fast
options.C: Diluted solutions will automatically achieve complete sterilization
options.D: Stronger mixtures are always safer for hospital equipment surfaces

explanation: Measurements matter in nursing! Too much water makes the solution useless against germs, while guessing too strong can ruin expensive hospital gear. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h4)

question: What happens when organic matter like blood is left on a surface during disinfection?

options.A: It turns the disinfectant into a complete sterilizing agent
options.B: It neutralizes the chemical and shields microbes from contact
options.C: It helps the disinfectant spread more evenly over tools
options.D: It speeds up the chemical reaction time on the surface

explanation: Blood and body fluids are tricky—they absorb the disinfectant and act like a little bunker, protecting the bacteria hiding underneath. Always wash first! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why must you respect the 'wet contact time' when using a disinfectant?

options.A: Wet surfaces look cleaner to patients and visiting family members
options.B: Water helps the active ingredient evaporate faster to save cleaning time
options.C: Keeping the surface wet prevents dust from settling on medical equipment
options.D: The chemical needs adequate time to interact with and destroy microbial structures

explanation: Disinfection isn't instant magic; it's a chemical reaction! Wiping it dry too soon cuts the process short and lets germs survive. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h5)

question: When wiping a bedside table in the ward, what direction should a nurse move?

options.A: From the cleanest area to the dirtiest area
options.B: Starting at the floor and moving upward
options.C: From the bottom edges up to the top center
options.D: In random circles across the entire surface

explanation: Smart nursing habit! Moving from clean to dirty ensures you aren't dragging grime and germs right back onto the spotless parts of the table. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do before handling chemical disinfectants?

options.A: Performing hand hygiene and putting on protective gear
options.B: Informing the head physician about the cleaning schedule
options.C: Warming the chemical solution in a microwave oven
options.D: Testing the disinfectant flavor on a sterile cotton swab

explanation: Safety first! Protecting your own skin, hands, and airways from harsh chemicals is a must before you start cleaning up the ward. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h6)

question: What dangerous hazard happens when bleach and ammonia are mixed together?

options.A: Complete neutralization with zero chemical residue
options.B: Release of toxic and potentially lethal gases
options.C: Instant creation of a high-level sterilizing foam
options.D: Rapid freezing of the surrounding floor surface

explanation: Never mix cleaning chemicals! Combining bleach and ammonia creates poisonous chloramine gases that can severely damage your lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h7)

question: A nurse notices that a disinfectant storage room has no windows or airflow. What immediate danger does this pose?

options.A: Rapid growth of bacterial spores inside the closed storage containers
options.B: Automatic expiration of every chemical bottle within twenty-four hours
options.C: Immediate freezing of all liquid disinfectants stored on the shelves
options.D: Accumulation of harmful chemical fumes leading to staff respiratory irritation

explanation: Good catch! Without proper ventilation, strong chemical vapors build up in the air and can make nursing staff very sick when they breathe them in. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T5#GNS122_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of decontamination in a healthcare setting?

options.A: To ensure that expired drugs are safely disposed of in the incinerator
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing new medical instruments
options.C: To make hospital wards smell fresh and clean for visitors
options.D: To break the chain of infection and protect patients and staff

explanation: Decontamination removes or destroys harmful microorganisms to stop them from spreading to vulnerable patients and healthcare workers. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why are patients with surgical wounds or catheters at higher risk if equipment is poorly decontaminated?

options.A: They usually stay in the hospital longer than other patients do
options.B: They produce more body heat which helps bacteria multiply faster
options.C: Their immune systems completely stop working during recovery
options.D: Their natural body barriers are breached, allowing germs to enter easily

explanation: Surgical wounds and catheters bypass the body's normal physical defenses, providing a direct entry point for pathogens. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which decontamination process is required to completely destroy bacterial spores?

options.A: Washing
options.B: Cleaning
options.C: Disinfection
options.D: Sterilization

explanation: Only sterilization is powerful enough to destroy all microbial life, including tough bacterial spores. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why must an instrument be thoroughly cleaned before it undergoes disinfection or sterilization?

options.A: Cleaning agents instantly sterilize the instrument without needing an autoclave
options.B: Leftover organic matter and dirt can shield germs from the chemical or heat
options.C: Dry blood makes the metal instruments much heavier to carry
options.D: Patients will complain if the instruments look dull or stained

explanation: Organic debris like blood and tissue acts as a physical barrier that prevents disinfectants and steam from reaching the microorganisms underneath. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h2)

question: According to the Spaulding classification, what level of processing is required for surgical instruments?

options.A: Basic washing with soap
options.B: High-level disinfection
options.C: Sterilization
options.D: Low-level disinfection

explanation: Surgical instruments are classified as critical items because they enter sterile tissues, so they must be fully sterilized. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h3)

question: A nurse is preparing to use a blood pressure cuff on a patient with unbroken skin. How should this item be classified and processed?

options.A: Semi-critical item requiring high-level chemical disinfection
options.B: Critical item requiring high-pressure steam sterilization
options.C: Non-critical item requiring low to intermediate-level disinfection
options.D: Sterile item requiring single-use disposal packaging

explanation: Blood pressure cuffs touch only intact skin, making them non-critical items that only need routine low or intermediate disinfection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is considered the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infections in a hospital?

options.A: Hand hygiene
options.B: Wearing sterile gowns
options.C: Using room air filters
options.D: Spraying chemical disinfectants

explanation: Washing hands or using alcohol-based hand rub is universally recognized as the most effective action to stop infection transmission. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why do standard precautions apply to every single patient in the ward, even those not diagnosed with an infection?

options.A: Patients get offended if healthcare workers wear gloves only for some beds
options.B: Some patients may carry infections without showing any symptoms yet
options.C: Hospital management requires it only for statistical record keeping
options.D: It is too difficult for nurses to remember different rules for different people

explanation: Standard precautions assume any body fluid can carry pathogens because asymptomatic carriers can transmit infections unknowingly. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take with a surgical instrument immediately after a procedure is finished?

options.A: Wrap it tightly in sterile cloth for storage
options.B: Soak the instrument in strong bleach overnight
options.C: Place it directly into the clean instrument cabinet
options.D: Remove gross soil and blood to prevent drying

explanation: Wiping off heavy blood and tissue right away keeps it from drying onto the metal, which makes later cleaning much harder. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h5)

question: Where should sterilized instruments be kept after they have been processed and wrapped?

options.A: Directly on the floor of the utility room
options.B: Inside a warm, humid washing sink basin
options.C: On an open counter in the busy main hallway
options.D: In a clean, dry, and dust-free storage area

explanation: Proper storage protects sterilized packs from moisture, dust, and contamination until they are needed for the next patient. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why is it a mistake to wipe a chemical disinfectant off a surface immediately after spraying it?

options.A: Leaving it wet makes the table look shiny and polished to visitors
options.B: The chemical needs a specific contact time to successfully kill the germs
options.C: The cleaning cloth will instantly dissolve if it touches wet disinfectant
options.D: Quick drying causes the chemical to release poisonous gases into the room

explanation: Disinfectants require time to act against pathogens; wiping them away prematurely prevents complete disinfection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which chemical compound is commonly used for disinfecting blood spills on hard surfaces due to its quick action and low cost?

options.A: Liquid paraffin oil
options.B: Normal saline solution
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide cream
options.D: Sodium hypochlorite

explanation: Sodium hypochlorite, commonly known as bleach, is an affordable and effective disinfectant for clearing up blood spills. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which specific vaccination is especially critical for healthcare workers who handle decontamination and sharps?

options.A: Rabies vaccine
options.B: Tetanus toxoid
options.C: Hepatitis B
options.D: Yellow fever

explanation: The Hepatitis B vaccine is essential for protecting staff against bloodborne pathogen exposure from contaminated instruments and needles. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h7)

question: What type of protective equipment is recommended when working with harsh chemical disinfectants that might splash?

options.A: Paper surgical caps and cloth masks
options.B: Open sandals and thin cotton gowns
options.C: Sterile surgical gloves and boots
options.D: Face shields and waterproof aprons

explanation: Face shields protect the eyes and mucous membranes from chemical splashes, while waterproof aprons protect clothing and skin. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h7)

question: Where should used hypodermic needles and scalpel blades be disposed of immediately after use?

options.A: Black domestic waste bins
options.B: Puncture-resistant safety boxes
options.C: Cardboard packaging boxes
options.D: Open plastic wash basins

explanation: Sharps must always go into dedicated, puncture-proof safety containers to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h8)

question: Why is waste segregation at the point of generation considered so important in healthcare facilities?

options.A: It reduces the physical weight of general rubbish bins
options.B: It allows the hospital to recycle all medical waste into children's toys
options.C: It ensures hazardous infectious waste is treated correctly before final disposal
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for cleaning hospital floors

explanation: Separating waste immediately prevents infectious materials from mixing with ordinary household rubbish, protecting everyone from accidental contamination. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T6#GNS122_U2_T6_h8)

question: What is the main job of the CSSD in a hospital?

options.A: Dispensing prescription medications to wards
options.B: Processing and sterilizing reusable medical equipment
options.C: Disposing of hazardous chemical waste
options.D: Managing patient admission records

explanation: The Central Sterilizing Supply Department (CSSD) is like the hospital's powerhouse for cleanliness! They clean, package, sterilize, and distribute all the medical tools used across the wards. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why is the CSSD so important for infection control?

options.A: It breaks the chain of infection by providing sterile instruments
options.B: It administers routine vaccinations to hospital staff
options.C: It isolates patients with contagious airborne diseases
options.D: It monitors patient antibiotic resistance patterns daily

explanation: By making sure every tool is thoroughly decontaminated and germ-free, CSSD stops infections from spreading from one patient to another. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h1)

question: What kind of air pressure is kept in the CSSD washing and decontamination room?

options.A: Neutral air pressure
options.B: Negative air pressure
options.C: Positive air pressure
options.D: Variable air pressure

explanation: Think of negative pressure like a vacuum that sucks air in. It pulls air into the room instead of blowing it out, keeping dirty germs trapped safely inside the washing area. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h2)

question: Why does the CSSD follow a strict one-way workflow?

options.A: To make it easier for staff to walk around the department
options.B: To ensure sterilizers are close to the main entrance
options.C: To prevent clean items from crossing paths with dirty items
options.D: To reduce the electricity consumed by heavy machinery

explanation: A one-way flow makes sure that freshly cleaned and sterilized supplies never bump into or cross paths with dirty instruments. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h2)

question: What is the main use of an ultrasonic cleaner in the CSSD?

options.A: Killing bacterial spores using high heat
options.B: Removing microscopic debris using sound waves
options.C: Applying a protective rust-proof coating
options.D: Drying moisture from surgical hinges

explanation: Ultrasonic cleaners use high-frequency sound waves to create tiny scrubbing bubbles that blast hidden dirt out of tiny instrument hinges and joints. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why must an instrument be properly cleaned before going into the autoclave?

options.A: Dried blood and tissue can block the sterilizing agent from reaching the surface
options.B: Remaining moisture causes the electrical elements to short-circuit
options.C: Organic dirt makes the metal too heavy for the sterilization tray
options.D: Dirty instruments will permanently stain the inside of the machine

explanation: If blood or tissue is left on a tool, it acts like a shield protecting the germs. The steam won't be able to reach them to kill them! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h3)

question: When should instruments be checked for cleanliness and damage?

options.A: Directly after removal from the autoclave
options.B: Only when the surgeon complains about a tool
options.C: As soon as the items arrive dirty from the ward
options.D: After cleaning and before packaging

explanation: Staff inspect instruments right after they are washed and dried. This ensures no hidden dirt or broken parts slip through before they are wrapped up. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the most important feature of a good surgical instrument wrap?

options.A: It must change color to black when exposed to sunlight
options.B: It must completely block all air and moisture permanently
options.C: It must let the sterilizing agent in while blocking microbes
options.D: It must dissolve in water during the washing cycle

explanation: A good wrap has a clever design: it lets steam or gas pass through to clean the tools, but keeps tiny bacteria out after the process is done. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the most common and trusted way to sterilize metal surgical tools?

options.A: Boiling in water for twenty minutes
options.B: Steam under pressure in an autoclave
options.C: Ultraviolet radiation in a glass cabinet
options.D: Immersion in liquid bleach solution

explanation: The autoclave is the workhorse of the CSSD! Using high-pressure steam is fast, affordable, and extremely reliable for metal instruments. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why must wrapped instrument trays be loaded loosely inside a steam sterilizer?

options.A: To allow steam to circulate freely around every package
options.B: To stop the external indicator tape from melting off
options.C: To prevent the heavy metal trays from breaking the door
options.D: To make unloading faster for the nursing assistant

explanation: If the packs are crammed too tightly together, the steam can't reach every surface, leaving pockets where germs can survive. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which monitoring tool gives the absolute proof that bacterial spores have been killed?

options.A: Chemical indicator tape
options.B: Biological indicators
options.C: Digital pressure gauges
options.D: External pack labels

explanation: Biological indicators use real, highly resistant harmless spores to test if the autoclave truly destroyed all living microorganisms. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is the main limitation of a chemical indicator strip placed inside an instrument tray?

options.A: It can only be read using an ultraviolet microscope
options.B: It dissolves completely if the steam pressure gets too high
options.C: It only measures the external room temperature of the storage area
options.D: It shows that conditions for sterilization occurred, but not that spores are dead

explanation: Chemical strips change color when exposed to heat or steam, which proves the machine got hot enough. However, they don't test actual germ survival like biological tests do. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h6)

question: What stock rotation rule should be followed when storing sterile supplies?

options.A: Last-in, first-out
options.B: Random selection
options.C: First-in, first-out
options.D: Alphabetical order

explanation: Just like in a pharmacy or supermarket, 'First-In, First-Out' (FIFO) means older stock gets used first so nothing sits on the shelf long enough to expire. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h7)

question: Why is it important to let a hot sterilized pack cool down inside the autoclave before touching it?

options.A: Hot metal instruments will bend out of shape if exposed to room air
options.B: The packaging material will immediately catch fire if moved too quickly
options.C: Cooling down resets the chemical indicator strip color back to normal
options.D: Touching it while hot can draw moisture through the wrapper and contaminate the contents

explanation: Touching a hot, damp pack creates condensation. Water droplets act like an elevator for bacteria, letting them slip right through the wrapper! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h7)

question: What personal protective equipment is a must when working in the CSSD decontamination room?

options.A: Waterproof gowns, utility gloves, and face shields
options.B: Dust masks and cotton lab coats
options.C: Sterile surgical gloves and sterile cloth gowns only
options.D: Lead aprons and radiation dosimeter badges

explanation: Decontamination staff deal with splashes of dirty water, blood, and harsh chemicals, so waterproof gear and face shields are essential to stay safe. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h8)

question: What should you do immediately if you get a needle-stick injury from a used surgical tool?

options.A: Wait until the end of the shift before telling the supervisor
options.B: Wash the wound quickly and ignore it if there is no bleeding
options.C: Report the incident and follow the facility's post-exposure protocol
options.D: Soak the injured finger in strong chemical disinfectant

explanation: Never brush off a sharps injury! Report it right away so you can get quick medical checks and preventive care if needed. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T7#GNS122_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the main job of the Theatre Sterile Supply Unit (TSSU)?

options.A: Disposing of hazardous biological waste from wards
options.B: Manufacturing single-use surgical equipment
options.C: Processing, sterilizing, and distributing medical instruments
options.D: Conducting pre-surgery patient assessments

explanation: You've got this! The TSSU is the heartbeat behind every clean surgery. Its main job is to safely clean, sterilize, and hand out surgical tools so patients stay infection-free. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why do hospitals prefer a centralized TSSU instead of letting individual wards clean their own surgical tools?

options.A: It reduces the cost of purchasing brand new instruments
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for chemical disinfectants
options.C: It allows nurses to spend more time at the patient bedside
options.D: It ensures consistent and strict quality control standards

explanation: Great thinking! When trained specialists handle sterilization in one central place, you can trust that every single instrument goes through the exact same high safety checks every time. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which area in the TSSU uses negative air pressure?

options.A: Preparation zone
options.B: Decontamination zone
options.C: Sterile storage zone
options.D: Packaging zone

explanation: Spot on! The dirty (decontamination) zone has negative air pressure so that air flows inward, trapping germs and stopping them from floating out into cleaner rooms. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why must work inside the TSSU always flow in one direction?

options.A: To reduce the electricity consumption of heavy sterilizing machines
options.B: To prevent clean and sterile items from mixing with dirty ones
options.C: To make it easier for nursing students to clean the floors
options.D: To speed up the physical movement of heavy instrument trays

explanation: Exactly! Keeping a one-way workflow ensures items only move forward from dirty to clean, protecting patients from cross-contamination. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h2)

question: When first rinsing used surgical instruments, why should you use cool water instead of hot water?

options.A: Hot water causes proteins to bake onto the metal surface
options.B: Cool water makes the instruments easier to grip with gloves
options.C: Cool water is cheaper for hospital utility budgets
options.D: Hot water damages the outer coating of stainless steel

explanation: You're learning fast! Heat actually cooks blood and proteins, making them stick like glue to the metal. Always start with cool water to rinse them right! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h3)

question: A nurse notices dried blood on a clamp coming out of the washer. What should be done?

options.A: The cleaning process was incomplete and the instrument must be re-washed
options.B: The instrument is permanently stained but still safe to use
options.C: The autoclave cycle reached too high a temperature
options.D: The packaging material was sealed incorrectly

explanation: Spot on! If you still see dirt or blood, the washing stage failed. Any leftover organic matter blocks sterilization, so back to the wash it goes! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h3)

question: What should you do with a surgical instrument that has a broken ratchet during inspection?

options.A: Removed from circulation immediately
options.B: Stored in the sterile room for minor procedures
options.C: Sent straight to the sterilization autoclave
options.D: Wrapped tightly in a double linen layer

explanation: You got it! Damaged tools won't work right during surgery and tiny cracks can hide bacteria. Pull them out of use right away. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why must the packaging used for steam sterilization be porous (able to let air and steam through)?

options.A: To ensure the wrapper dissolves completely inside the machine
options.B: To make the heavy trays lighter for nurses to carry
options.C: To let air escape so the package smells fresh when opened
options.D: To allow the sterilizing agent to penetrate and reach the instruments

explanation: Brilliant! Steam needs to touch every single surface of the tools inside to actually kill the germs. Porous wraps let the steam in safely. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the most trusted and widely used method of sterilization in the TSSU?

options.A: Boiling in water for ten minutes
options.B: Washing with strong liquid bleach
options.C: Ultraviolet light exposure cabinets
options.D: Steam under pressure in an autoclave

explanation: You're doing great! The autoclave is the gold standard because hot steam under pressure quickly destroys all germs and tough spores. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h5)

question: What do biological indicators test for when placed inside a sterilizer?

options.A: The total weight of the metal trays loaded into the chamber
options.B: The correct color change of paper tape on instrument packs
options.C: The actual destruction of highly resistant bacterial spores
options.D: The exact temperature of the room surrounding the machine

explanation: Spot on! Biological indicators use real, super-tough live spores to prove that the machine is strong enough to kill the hardest-to-beat germs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h5)

question: In the TSSU, what does the inventory rule 'FIFO' stand for?

options.A: Filtered-Instrument, Filtered-Object
options.B: Final-Item, Final-Order
options.C: Fast-Inspection, Fast-Operation
options.D: First-In, First-Out

explanation: Correct! FIFO means the supplies that arrived first get used first, keeping items from sitting on shelves past their expiration dates. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h6)

question: A nurse drops a sterile instrument pack on the theatre floor before opening it. What is the correct next step?

options.A: Place the pack back on the shelf for the next procedure
options.B: Open the pack and check if the metal inside looks clean
options.C: Return the pack to the TSSU for complete reprocessing
options.D: Wipe the outside wrapper with alcohol and use it anyway

explanation: You've got this! Once a sterile pack hits the floor, its protective barrier is compromised. You can't trust it anymore—send it back for complete re-sterilization. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT safe for staff working in the TSSU decontamination zone?

options.A: Putting on face shields and eye protection
options.B: Wearing waterproof protective aprons
options.C: Wearing open-toed sandals for comfort
options.D: Using heavy-duty utility gloves

explanation: Great catch! Open-toed shoes leave your feet exposed to falling sharps and dirty splashes. Always wear closed, protective shoes in the wash area! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why is Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) so important specifically in the TSSU decontamination zone?

options.A: Hospital management requires it only for decorative uniformity
options.B: It prevents dust from settling on the clean instruments
options.C: The temperature in that specific room is extremely high
options.D: Staff are exposed to blood splashes, contaminated water, and sharp tools

explanation: Spot on! Because you are washing blood-stained, used instruments, PPE acts as your shield against splashes, dirty water, and accidental needle pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T8#GNS122_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why do nurses wear masks in the hospital?

options.A: To keep warm in air-conditioned rooms
options.B: To prevent patients from seeing the nurse's facial expressions
options.C: To eliminate the need for hand washing
options.D: To stop airborne and droplet germs from spreading

explanation: Masks act as a shield to keep harmful germs from traveling through the air between patients and staff. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the main difference between droplet and airborne germs?

options.A: Airborne germs only spread outdoors
options.B: Airborne germs cannot infect healthcare workers
options.C: Droplet germs need negative pressure rooms
options.D: Droplet germs travel on heavy particles that fall quickly, while airborne germs stay floating longer

explanation: Think of it by weight! Heavier droplets drop fast to the ground, but tiny airborne particles float around longer and need stronger masks. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the main job of a regular surgical mask?

options.A: To supply extra oxygen
options.B: To filter out tiny microscopic viruses completely
options.C: To block large splashes, sprays, and droplets
options.D: To provide a tight, air-sealed fit around the face

explanation: Surgical masks are great shields against everyday hospital splashes and sprays, even though they don't seal tightly around your face. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h2)

question: Why can't a regular surgical mask protect you against true airborne diseases like TB?

options.A: The loose fit lets air and tiny germs slip in through the edges
options.B: The material dissolves in humid hospital rooms
options.C: They only block bacteria, never viruses
options.D: They are only made for patients to wear

explanation: Since surgical masks aren't tightly sealed, air takes the easiest path—right around the sides instead of through the filter! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h2)

question: What percentage of tiny particles must an N95 respirator filter out?

options.A: Exactly 50 percent
options.B: At least 95 percent
options.C: 100 percent without exception
options.D: Up to 80 percent maximum

explanation: The '95' in N95 simply means it catches a minimum of 95 percent of test particles. Simple and reliable! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h3)

question: A male nurse with a thick beard is caring for a patient with TB. What should he do?

options.A: Shave his beard so the N95 can seal properly
options.B: Wear an N95 right over his beard
options.C: Wear a standard surgical mask instead
options.D: Double-mask with two surgical masks

explanation: Facial hair prevents that crucial tight seal. Shaving ensures the N95 can properly protect him from airborne germs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h3)

question: What kind of mask do you need when entering a patient's room who is on droplet precautions?

options.A: No mask is ever required
options.B: A cloth fashion face covering
options.C: A powered air-purifying respirator
options.D: A standard surgical mask

explanation: For droplet precautions, a standard surgical mask is all you need to block those larger splashes and secretions. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why do nurses wear masks during sterile procedures like putting in a central line?

options.A: To comply with fire safety codes
options.B: To protect the nurse from inhaling meds
options.C: To stop the nurse's germs from contaminating the sterile field
options.D: To keep their face warm in cold rooms

explanation: Here, the mask protects the patient! It stops your own mouth and nose bacteria from getting into the sterile area. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the quick check a nurse does every time they put on an N95 to check the seal called?

options.A: Qualitative sweet test
options.B: Sterile pressure scan
options.C: Manufacturer inspection
options.D: User seal check

explanation: It is a quick self-check you do every single time you put on your respirator to make sure it is sitting right. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h5)

question: Why do healthcare workers need to do an N95 fit test every year?

options.A: Weight changes or dental work can change how the mask seals
options.B: Manufacturers change their plastic formulas yearly
options.C: Hospital rules just want to renew licenses
options.D: Filters expire chemically after one year

explanation: Our faces change over time! A fit test ensures your mask still seals safely against your unique face shape. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h5)

question: Which part of a used mask is safe to touch when taking it off?

options.A: The metal nose bridge exterior
options.B: The bottom edge near the chin
options.C: The straps, ties, or ear loops
options.D: The front center filtration panel

explanation: Always grab the straps! The front of the mask holds onto trapped germs and should never be touched directly. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h6)

question: Why should you wash your hands right after taking off your mask?

options.A: To reactivate hand sanitizer lotions
options.B: To remove germs that may have touched your hands if you brushed the outer mask
options.C: To prevent mask elastic from marking your fingers
options.D: To cool your skin down after a long shift

explanation: Hand hygiene right after removal breaks the chain of infection just in case your fingers brushed against outer germs. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h6)

question: Why is pulling your mask down around your neck during a break a bad idea?

options.A: It violates fashion codes
options.B: It stretches out the elastic bands forever
options.C: It contaminates the clean inside of your mask with germs from your neck skin
options.D: It blocks blood flow to your head

explanation: Pulling it to your neck exposes the inner lining to skin oils and germs, which you then breathe right back in! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h7)

question: Your surgical mask becomes damp and sweaty during a busy shift. What should you do?

options.A: Leave it on because moisture helps filtration
options.B: Flip it inside out so the dry side faces out
options.C: Remove and discard it, clean your hands, and put on a fresh one
options.D: Wipe it with paper towels and pocket it

explanation: Once a mask gets damp, its filter barrier stops working well. Swap it out for a fresh one to stay safe! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T9#GNS122_U2_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of injection safety in clinical practice?

options.A: Ensuring no harm comes to the patient or nurse during the procedure
options.B: Reducing the overall cost of purchasing hospital medical supplies
options.C: Speeding up the time it takes to administer daily medication rounds
options.D: Eliminating the need to wear gloves when handling clean syringes

explanation: Injection safety focuses entirely on protecting both recipients and healthcare providers from physical harm and infections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why do nurses carry a major responsibility in maintaining injection safety?

options.A: They purchase all medical equipment used in the healthcare facility
options.B: They are responsible for manufacturing sterile needles in the hospital
options.C: They dictate the national health policies regarding infectious waste
options.D: They are the primary healthcare workers who administer injections to patients

explanation: Nurses are directly responsible for preparing and administering injections, placing them at the center of safety protocol execution. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h1)

question: When does the practice of injection safety actually begin?

options.A: Washing the patient's entire body with antibacterial soap and water
options.B: Recapping the needle tightly to ensure it stays sterile on the tray
options.C: Notifying the hospital director of the intended medication route
options.D: Deciding if an injection is truly necessary compared to oral medication

explanation: Think of safety as starting before you even pick up a syringe. If a patient can take oral medication instead, avoiding that needle prick is the safest first step! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which of these best captures the full picture of injection safety?

options.A: It is limited to washing hands before opening a packaged syringe
options.B: It covers everything from deciding on the route to safe disposal of waste
options.C: It focuses solely on preventing needlestick injuries among medical doctors
options.D: It only refers to the exact moment the needle enters the patient's skin

explanation: Injection safety isn't just one quick action. It's a complete journey—from checking if the injection is needed, to giving it cleanly, to throwing away the sharps properly. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h2)

question: What dangerous practice must nurses avoid to protect themselves from needlestick injuries?

options.A: Wearing clean gloves
options.B: Recapping used needles
options.C: Performing hand hygiene
options.D: Using safety-engineered devices

explanation: Recapping used needles is a primary cause of accidental needlestick injuries in clinical settings and must be avoided. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h3)

question: A nurse finishes giving an intramuscular injection to a patient. What is the safest immediate action regarding the used syringe?

options.A: Place the cap back on the needle using two hands before walking to the bin
options.B: Break the needle off the syringe by hand to save space in the disposal box
options.C: Drop the unsheathed needle and syringe directly into a rigid sharps container
options.D: Leave the syringe on the bedside table until the end of the shift

explanation: Immediate disposal of the unsheathed device into a puncture-resistant container prevents accidental injuries to staff and patients. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which bloodborne viruses are most commonly transmitted through unsafe injection practices?

options.A: Malaria, Typhoid, and Cholera
options.B: Influenza, Measles, and Chickenpox
options.C: Tetanus, Rabies, and Yellow Fever
options.D: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV

explanation: Unsafe injections are a major vector for transmitting bloodborne infections like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h4)

question: How do painful abscesses and bacterial infections usually happen after an injection?

options.A: Due to the natural chemical reaction of the medication inside the blood
options.B: As a normal side effect of every vaccine given in the muscle
options.C: Because the patient did not take oral antibiotics before the injection
options.D: Through contaminated equipment or poor skin preparation introducing bacteria

explanation: Abscesses happen when germs get introduced into the skin or muscle. This is why thorough hand washing, clean gear, and proper skin wiping are so important! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the main reason we practice standard precautions in everyday nursing?

options.A: To prevent the transmission of infections between patients and staff
options.B: To ensure medications dissolve faster in the patient's bloodstream
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital cleaning supplies
options.D: To eliminate the need for documenting medication administration

explanation: Standard precautions are your trusty shield! They keep both you and your patients safe from passing germs back and forth during care. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h5)

question: How should a nurse properly clean a medication vial septum before drawing up fluid?

options.A: Blow air heavily onto the rubber top to cool and clean it
options.B: Wipe the rubber top with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry
options.C: Wipe the top with a dry paper towel immediately before insertion
options.D: Run the entire glass bottle under hot tap water for one minute

explanation: Swabbing the septum with alcohol and letting it dry naturally reduces surface bacteria prior to needle insertion. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h5)

question: What key physical features must a proper sharps container have?

options.A: Transparent and open at the top
options.B: Biodegradable and water-soluble
options.C: Puncture-resistant and leak-proof
options.D: Made of soft, flexible cardboard

explanation: Sharps bins have to be tough! Being puncture-resistant and leak-proof ensures that needles won't poke through and fluids won't spill out while waiting for disposal. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h6)

question: What action should a nurse take when a sharps container reaches its designated fill line?

options.A: Leave it open on the counter until the end of the working week
options.B: Seal and close the container securely for safe disposal
options.C: Push the needles down firmly with a gloved hand to create more space
options.D: Transfer some of the used needles into a regular plastic trash bag

explanation: Containers must be closed and replaced once they reach the fill line to prevent accidental overflows and needle injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T1#GNS122_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the main goal of a safe injection according to the WHO?

options.A: To completely eliminate the use of oral medications in the hospital
options.B: To prevent harm to the patient and worker without creating dangerous waste
options.C: To ensure medications are absorbed twice as fast into the bloodstream
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing disposable syringes

explanation: A safe injection protects everyone: the patient getting the drug, you as the nurse giving it, and the community from bad waste disposal. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h1)

question: Why is an unsafe injection a big deal in public health?

options.A: It almost always leads to immediate surgical site infections
options.B: It causes severe allergic reactions in every patient who receives it
options.C: It can easily transmit serious bloodborne infections to healthy individuals
options.D: It guarantees that the administered drug will not work properly

explanation: Unsafe practices bypass the skin's natural defenses, which can directly spread heavy infections like HIV and hepatitis into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h1)

question: What is the main cause of spreading infections through unsafe injections?

options.A: Reusing single-use syringes without proper sterilization
options.B: Using the wrong size needle for subcutaneous injections
options.C: Administering expired medications into the muscle
options.D: Failing to wear sterile surgical gowns during an injection

explanation: Never reuse single-use syringes! Doing so transfers tiny amounts of contaminated blood straight to the next person. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h2)

question: A patient gets a painful, pus-filled swelling where they received an injection days ago. What happened?

options.A: An allergic reaction to the cotton wool used afterward
options.B: A normal immune response to the medication formula
options.C: A localized bacterial infection introduced during the procedure
options.D: Systemic failure of the patient's cardiovascular system

explanation: When hygiene slips, bacteria can hitch a ride on the needle and cause a painful abscess right in the tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h2)

question: Who does the WHO injection safety strategy aim to protect?

options.A: Patients, healthcare workers, and the surrounding environment
options.B: Hospital administrators, pharmacists, and medical equipment sellers
options.C: Patient comfort, medication speed, and low treatment costs
options.D: Drug manufacturing companies, shipping agents, and local clinics

explanation: Think of the safety triad: protect the patient, protect yourself (the healthcare worker), and keep the environment safe from hazardous waste. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h3)

question: Why does the WHO stress having a steady supply of injection equipment?

options.A: Having extra supplies makes nurses finish their shifts much faster
options.B: Patients refuse treatment if clinics do not show them brand new boxes
options.C: Shortages often force workers to reuse single-use devices out of desperation
options.D: Government regulations require clinics to store at least ten years of stock

explanation: When clinics run out of disposables, it puts immense pressure on nurses. Reliable supplies keep everyone safe from risky workarounds. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h3)

question: What is the single most effective way to prevent hospital-acquired infections?

options.A: Proper hand hygiene
options.B: Using face shields
options.C: Wearing sterile gowns
options.D: Taking daily antibiotics

explanation: Simple handwashing or using an alcohol rub is your superpower against germs. Never skip it! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h4)

question: When should you clean your hands when giving an injection with gloves?

options.A: After the injection is finished, but never before putting gloves on
options.B: Only if the gloves tear or develop visible holes during use
options.C: Only when entering a patient room for the very first time that day
options.D: Before putting on gloves and immediately after taking them off

explanation: Gloves can have tiny invisible holes, and hands easily pick up germs when taking gloves off. Always clean your hands on both ends! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h4)

question: What makes an auto-disable syringe special?

options.A: Measure the exact weight of the patient receiving the drug
options.B: Automatically mix powdered medication with sterile water
options.C: Dissolve completely in water after a few minutes
options.D: Prevent the syringe from being used more than once

explanation: Auto-disable syringes have a clever built-in block that jams the plunger after one use, making accidental or intentional reuse impossible. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h5)

question: Why is it unsafe to change the needle but keep using the same syringe barrel for another injection?

options.A: New needles never fit securely onto used plastic syringe tips
options.B: The plastic material of the barrel melts when exposed to air twice
options.C: The fluid path and internal parts of the syringe are already contaminated
options.D: The second medication will chemically react and turn into a solid block

explanation: Once a needle touches a patient or medication vial, the inside of the syringe barrel is no longer sterile. Don't risk it! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h5)

question: When should you seal and replace a sharps disposal box?

options.A: When it is completely filled to the absolute brim
options.B: Whenever the outer cardboard gets slightly dusty
options.C: When it is three-quarters full
options.D: At the end of every single calendar month

explanation: Stop at the three-quarter mark! Waiting until it's overflowing invites accidental needle pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h6)

question: Which of these actions with a used sharps box is dangerous and completely wrong?

options.A: Storing the closed box in a designated utility room
options.B: Labeling the box with the date it was sealed shut
options.C: Placing the box within arm's reach of the injection site
options.D: Shaking or emptying the box to reuse it for more waste

explanation: Never shake or try to empty a sharps box. That puts you and others at direct risk of needle injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h6)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you accidentally suffer a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Soak the finger in pure household bleach for ten minutes
options.B: Wait until the end of the shift to report it to the supervisor
options.C: Apply a tight tourniquet above the injury site immediately
options.D: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water

explanation: Stay calm! Wash the area right away with soap and running water to rinse away germs before they settle in. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h7)

question: Why should you avoid scrubbing a fresh needle-stick wound too hard?

options.A: It causes the wound to bleed much more than it is supposed to
options.B: It can cause skin abrasions and help pathogens enter the bloodstream faster
options.C: It ruins the shape of the skin and prevents proper medical documentation
options.D: It neutralizes the cleaning effect of the soap and water mixture

explanation: Be gentle with your skin. Vigorous scrubbing creates tiny micro-tears that actually help germs enter your bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h7)

question: What is a major challenge for injection safety in resource-limited settings like Nigeria?

options.A: An excessive surplus of modern safety-engineered syringes
options.B: Supply chain disruptions and shortages of safety devices
options.C: Complete lack of any national health guidelines or policies
options.D: Patients refusing to accept any injections from trained nurses

explanation: When clinics face stockouts of safety gear and syringes, it makes ideal infection control a tough daily battle for nurses. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h8)

question: If nurses on a ward keep leaving used needles uncapped on trays, what is the best way to fix this habit?

options.A: Issue written warning letters to every single nurse working in the ward
options.B: Ban all injections in the facility until staff members remember the rules
options.C: Conduct training sessions and place safety boxes closer to the point of use
options.D: Wait for the next annual hospital inspection to report the problem

explanation: Making safety gear easy to reach and providing supportive training works much better than punishment for changing clinical habits. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T10#GNS122_U3_T10_h8)

question: Why do we actively monitor injection safety devices in the ward?

options.A: To prevent the transmission of bloodborne infections
options.B: To measure the speed of nursing staff during shifts
options.C: To track the monthly financial budget of the pharmacy
options.D: To calculate the total electricity consumed by equipment

explanation: Spot on! Tracking these tools ensures safety devices are used right, keeping both patients and us safe from nasty infections like HIV and hepatitis. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h1)

question: What makes needle-stick injuries so scary for us on the clinical floor?

options.A: They automatically disqualify a nurse from clinical duty
options.B: They cause immediate systemic allergic reactions
options.C: They can transmit serious bloodborne pathogens easily
options.D: They always lead to permanent nerve damage in the hand

explanation: Exactly. A used needle carries patient blood straight into your bloodstream, which is a major risk for infections. Always handle sharps with care! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h1)

question: What is the main goal of filling out that monthly injection safety monitoring form?

options.A: To schedule annual leave periods for the clinical team
options.B: To evaluate the bedside nursing skills of newly hired staff
options.C: To guarantee an uninterrupted supply of safety devices
options.D: To determine the salary scales for hospital administrators

explanation: You got it! The form helps us keep an eye on stock levels so our clinic never suddenly runs out of syringes and safety boxes. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h2)

question: Why do we track wastage rates on our monthly injection safety form?

options.A: It automatically increases the monthly government drug allocation
options.B: It helps managers justify future procurement requests and reduce loss
options.C: It replaces the need for keeping a physical pharmacy inventory
options.D: It punishes nurses who accidentally drop sterile items

explanation: Spot on! Tracking broken or wasted items shows management where supplies are leaking, helping us order better next time. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h2)

question: Which of these details is typically recorded in the stock inventory part of the safety form?

options.A: The personal home address of every patient
options.B: Opening balance and quantities used
options.C: Detailed medical diagnoses of injection recipients
options.D: Daily weather conditions at the facility

explanation: Correct! The stock section is strictly about numbers: what we started with, what we used, and what is left. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h3)

question: Why is signing off at the very end of the monitoring form compulsory?

options.A: It proves that the nursing supervisor worked overtime hours
options.B: It allows the central store to bill individual patients directly
options.C: It serves as a legal waiver for expired medical supplies
options.D: It establishes accountability for the accuracy of the reported data

explanation: You nailed it. A signature means someone is taking responsibility to verify that the numbers written down are actually correct. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h3)

question: When is the best time to record numbers for your monthly injection safety report?

options.A: On a daily basis in the ward logbook
options.B: Whenever a patient makes a formal complaint
options.C: From memory at the very end of the year
options.D: Only when an inspector visits the clinic

explanation: Exactly! Jotting things down daily saves you from guessing games at month-end and keeps your records accurate. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the biggest risk of trying to estimate your injection usage from memory?

options.A: It automatically invalidates the nurse's practicing license
options.B: It causes immediate physical damage to safety boxes
options.C: It doubles the financial cost of purchasing new syringes
options.D: It distorts supply chain forecasts and leads to future stockouts

explanation: Spot on! If our recorded guesses are wrong, the central store will send the wrong quantity, leading to frustrating shortages. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h4)

question: What makes an auto-disable (AD) syringe special?

options.A: It locks or breaks after a single use to prevent reuse
options.B: It changes color when exposed to direct sunlight
options.C: It can be sterilized in boiling water up to ten times
options.D: It has a detachable needle that can be safely recapped

explanation: Correct! AD syringes jam or break right after the first injection so nobody can accidentally reuse them on another patient. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h5)

question: Up to what level should you fill a safety box before closing it for disposal?

options.A: Emptied out daily regardless of level
options.B: Sealed only when the outer cardboard tears
options.C: Never filled beyond the three-quarter line
options.D: Packed completely to the very top rim

explanation: You got it! Stopping at the three-quarter mark ensures protruding needles don't accidentally prick anyone passing by. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h5)

question: After calculating your paper totals for the month, what should a nurse do next?

options.A: Immediately throw away all the old daily logbooks
options.B: Order double the normal amount of safety boxes
options.C: Perform a physical count of the remaining stock in the storeroom
options.D: Send the unverified report directly to the federal ministry

explanation: Spot on! Always cross-check your paper math with what is actually sitting on the storeroom shelves. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h6)

question: You check the storeroom and notice your physical syringe count doesn't match the logbook. What's the best move?

options.A: Change the logbook numbers to make them match perfectly without checking
options.B: Record the discrepancy and add a brief explanation in the remarks column
options.C: Hide the leftover syringes so nobody notices the mistake
options.D: Ignore the difference since small errors do not matter in healthcare

explanation: Exactly. Honesty is key in nursing; noting the gap allows supervisors to look into it properly instead of sweeping errors under the rug. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h6)

question: Which of these is a major red flag that supervisors look out for during a data audit?

options.A: Reporting zero waste while consumption numbers are very high
options.B: Having more than two nurses sign the document
options.C: Submitting the monthly report on the exact final day
options.D: Using blue ink instead of black ink on the monitoring form

explanation: Spot on! In a busy clinic, zero waste is almost impossible. It usually means the numbers were guessed or made up. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h7)

question: Why is retraining better than punishing staff when errors pop up in data collection?

options.A: Staff members prefer being disciplined over learning new skills
options.B: Retraining is always cheaper than buying new paper forms
options.C: Punitive measures violate international supply chain laws
options.D: Punishment encourages staff to hide mistakes rather than fix them

explanation: You got it! When people are terrified of punishment, they fake records to look flawless, which ruins the reliability of our health data. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h7)

question: Where does a primary health clinic in Nigeria send its monthly injection safety report first?

options.A: The Local Government Area (LGA) focal officer
options.B: The international donor agency headquarters
options.C: The nearest private pharmaceutical distributor
options.D: Directly to the Federal Minister of Health

explanation: Correct! Reports start locally at the LGA level before moving upward to the state and federal tables. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h8)

question: Why do we follow a step-by-step reporting ladder for injection safety data?

options.A: It allows individual nurses to bypass hospital management
options.B: It prevents state and federal officers from seeing local clinic errors
options.C: It ensures that paperwork stays inside the hospital indefinitely
options.D: It allows data to be properly aggregated for national procurement planning

explanation: Spot on! Gathering data upward gives the country the accurate totals it needs to buy and distribute supplies for everyone. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T11#GNS122_U3_T11_h8)

question: What is the main reason we use injection safety supplies in the hospital?

options.A: To make hospital storage rooms look neat and organized
options.B: To protect patients and nurses from blood-borne infections
options.C: To reduce the cost of buying drugs
options.D: To speed up intravenous fluid administration

explanation: You got this! Injection safety items like proper syringes and safety boxes are specifically designed to stop infections like HIV and hepatitis from spreading during procedures. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T12#GNS122_U3_T12_h1)

question: Why does running out of basic injection gear cause dangerous situations on the ward?

options.A: Hospital management will automatically close down the clinic
options.B: Staff might feel tempted to reuse single-use syringes out of desperation
options.C: Nurses will completely stop writing patient notes
options.D: Patients will refuse to take any medications

explanation: Spot on! When supplies run dry, desperate situations can lead to unsafe shortcuts like reusing disposable syringes, which puts everyone at risk. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T12#GNS122_U3_T12_h1)
