explanation: You've got this! Reusing syringes transfers tiny traces of blood and germs from person to person, spreading serious viruses like HIV and hepatitis. Always use a fresh syringe! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why do many people in local communities prefer getting injections from informal medicine shops?

options.A: Oral medications are completely unavailable in cities
options.B: Government policy requires informal shops to give shots
options.C: They believe injections work much faster than pills
options.D: Injections are always cheaper than tablets

explanation: It's a common belief that shooting medicine straight into the body heals you faster than swallowing a pill. As nurses, patient education on safe administration is key here! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h1)

question: What does 'parenteral route' mean when talking about how diseases spread?

options.A: Entry through a break in the skin via needles or sharps
options.B: Inhalation of airborne droplets through the nose
options.C: Ingestion of contaminated food or drinking water
options.D: Spread through direct skin-to-skin physical contact

explanation: Think of parenteral as bypassing the skin barrier completely—usually when a contaminated needle or sharp punctures the tissue directly. Simple and clear! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h2)

question: Why can a needle look perfectly clean yet still carry a dangerous virus?

options.A: Microscopic traces of infected blood remain inside the hollow bore
options.B: Skin bacteria react with the metal to create new pathogens
options.C: The virus travels through the air surrounding the needle
options.D: Plastic needles absorb viruses and release them later

explanation: Even if you can't see it, an invisible film of fluid inside a needle hub holds enough viral particles to cause a new infection. That's why we never reuse needles! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which organ in the body is the main target for both Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C?

options.A: The lungs
options.B: The pancreas
options.C: The kidneys
options.D: The liver

explanation: Spot on! Both hepatitis B and C viruses attack liver cells, causing inflammation and long-term damage if left untreated. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h3)

question: A patient is shocked to test positive for Hepatitis C years after getting an unsterile injection. Why did it take so long to show up?

options.A: The virus often hides in the body silently for a long time before causing symptoms
options.B: The virus only becomes active when a person eats contaminated food
options.C: Hepatitis C instantly destroys the immune system within twenty-four hours
options.D: Antibodies against the virus disappear completely after a few months

explanation: Hepatitis C is known as a silent virus. It can quietly damage the liver over many years without making the person feel sick right away. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is septicemia?

options.A: Presence of multiplying bacteria in the bloodstream
options.B: Inflammation limited to the outer layer of skin
options.C: A localized collection of pus in a single muscle
options.D: Sudden paralysis caused by a damaged nerve

explanation: Septicemia happens when bacteria get past local defenses and start multiplying in the general blood circulation, making the patient very ill all over. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h4)

question: A patient comes back three days after an injection with a hot, swollen, throbbing lump at the site. What is this most likely?

options.A: A localized muscle abscess
options.B: Systemic blood poisoning
options.C: Chronic hepatitis C infection
options.D: An acute HIV seroconversion illness

explanation: That classic combo of throbbing pain, heat, swelling, and a lump usually points to a bacterial abscess from an unsterile injection that may need draining. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which nerve is most at risk when a gluteal (buttock) injection is given with poor technique?

options.A: Femoral nerve
options.B: Median nerve
options.C: Sciatic nerve
options.D: Radial nerve

explanation: Great nursing knowledge! The sciatic nerve runs deep in the lower buttock, so injections must be placed carefully in the upper outer quadrant to avoid it. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why should nurses rotate injection sites for patients who need frequent medications?

options.A: It ensures the medication reaches the bloodstream much faster
options.B: It stops bacteria from multiplying on the surface of the skin
options.C: It gives previous tissue time to heal instead of forming hard scar tissue
options.D: It prevents the needle from becoming dull during the procedure

explanation: Sticking the exact same spot over and over causes fibrous scar knots, which hurt the patient and make drug absorption difficult. Rotating sites keeps tissue healthy! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why is it important to ask patients if they have visited patent medicine vendors when taking their history?

options.A: Hospital records automatically track all purchases made in private shops
options.B: Many informal vendors administer unsterile injections that patients forget to mention
options.C: Patent medicine vendors are legally required to report side effects
options.D: Patients only get infections when visiting registered general hospitals

explanation: Patients often think of informal drug purchases as casual and might forget to mention them. Asking directly helps us catch hidden risks like unsterile shots! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h6)

question: A patient has a red, swollen, tender gluteal injection site. What extra sign would tell you the sciatic nerve might be involved?

options.A: Bleeding from the puncture hole on the skin surface
options.B: Numbness, tingling, or weakness radiating down the leg
options.C: High fever and generalized body shivering
options.D: Yellowish discoloration of the eyes and skin

explanation: When a nerve is irritated or hit, it sends warning signs down its pathway—like pins and needles, burning pain, or weakness in the leg. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h6)

question: What is the main goal of giving post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) right after an accidental needle stick?

options.A: To cure a chronic bacterial skin infection
options.B: To prevent the establishment of a viral infection
options.C: To numb the skin and prevent local tissue scarring
options.D: To relieve muscle spasms around the injury site

explanation: PEP uses quick antiviral meds to stop a virus from taking hold and multiplying after an accidental exposure. Every minute counts! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h7)

question: How is a painful muscle abscess caused by an unsterile injection usually managed?

options.A: Apply tight bandages to squeeze the trapped fluid out through the skin
options.B: Massage the lump firmly to help disperse the pus into surrounding tissue
options.C: Assist with surgical incision and drainage while maintaining sterile dressings
options.D: Advise the patient to ignore the lump until it dissolves on its own

explanation: Trapped pus has to come out! An abscess requires sterile incision and drainage, followed by proper wound care and antibiotics to help the patient heal. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h7)

question: Why is it a bad safety practice for healthcare workers to recap used needles?

options.A: It is the leading cause of accidental needlestick injuries
options.B: It makes the needle too dull for future use
options.C: It contaminates the plastic barrel with air bubbles
options.D: It violates hospital rules regarding medication labeling

explanation: Trying to guide a used needle back into its tiny cap is the easiest way to slip and prick your own finger. Safety first—never recap! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h8)

question: Where should a used injection needle go immediately after you give an injection?

options.A: Inside your pocket until you reach the utility room
options.B: Directly into a puncture-resistant safety box
options.C: Back into the original plastic wrapper on the desk
options.D: On top of the medication tray for later sorting

explanation: Always drop sharps straight into a designated safety box kept right beside you. Never carry them around or leave them on trays! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T4#GNS122_U3_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of injection safety practices?

options.A: To make medication administration faster in busy wards
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing new needles
options.C: To ensure patients experience no pain during injections
options.D: To prevent harm and infections for everyone involved

explanation: Injection safety focuses on protecting patients, health workers, and communities from preventable injuries and infections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why are certain populations classified as high-risk groups for unsafe injections?

options.A: They metabolize injectable drugs much slower than other people
options.B: They always refuse standard vaccination programs in rural clinics
options.C: They have higher exposure to contaminated needles or biological fluids
options.D: They lack basic knowledge about oral medication administration

explanation: High-risk groups face a greater chance of harm because their daily routines or health conditions put them near contaminated equipment. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which pathogen is most commonly transmitted through an accidental needle-stick injury?

options.A: Tetanus spore
options.B: Malaria parasite
options.C: Streptococcus bacteria
options.D: Hepatitis B virus

explanation: Hepatitis B is highly infectious through blood and remains a major occupational risk for health workers experiencing needle pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h2)

question: When do accidental needle-stick injuries most frequently occur in clinical settings?

options.A: When storing unopened boxes of sterile syringes in the pharmacy
options.B: During the physical assessment of a newly admitted patient
options.C: While washing hands with soap and water before a procedure
options.D: While recapping used needles after giving an injection

explanation: Trying to put the cap back onto a used needle is a leading cause of accidental punctures in nursing practice. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h2)

question: The main danger of reusing a single-use syringe across different patients is:

options.A: Destroying the active chemical drug
options.B: Causing severe muscle atrophy
options.C: Transmission of blood-borne infections
options.D: Causing immediate allergic skin reactions

explanation: Reusing syringes transfers microscopic amounts of blood and pathogens directly into the next recipient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h3)

question: A clinic patient insists on receiving an injectable vitamin instead of tablets for a mild fatigue complaint. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Administer the injection immediately to satisfy the patient's demand
options.B: Tell the patient injections are completely risk-free in modern clinics
options.C: Explain the risks of unnecessary injections and discuss oral options
options.D: Use a larger needle to ensure the vitamin absorbs faster

explanation: Nurses must protect patients from unnecessary invasive procedures by promoting safer, effective oral alternatives. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h3)

question: Why are waste handlers considered a high-risk group for unsafe injection practices?

options.A: They frequently handle poorly disposed sharp medical waste
options.B: They process expired oral medications in the pharmacy
options.C: They administer injections to community members at home
options.D: They clean hospital floors without wearing heavy boots

explanation: Waste handlers often encounter stray needles thrown into regular trash instead of puncture-proof safety boxes. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a safe way to manage community medical waste?

options.A: Ensuring sharps containers are sealed before final disposal
options.B: Using puncture-resistant safety boxes for all used needles
options.C: Incinerating medical waste under controlled high temperatures
options.D: Throwing used syringes into ordinary household plastic garbage bags

explanation: Household bags easily puncture, exposing trash collectors and the public to contaminated needles. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is the recommended method for handling a needle if a safety device is unavailable?

options.A: Ask a nearby colleague to hold the cap in place
options.B: Leave the needle uncapped on the procedure tray
options.C: Use a one-hand scoop technique to guide the cap on
options.D: Hold the cap firmly with both hands while sliding the needle

explanation: The one-handed scoop method prevents the fingers of the non-dominant hand from being accidentally poked. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h5)

question: Where is the best place to locate a sharps disposal container in a patient care area?

options.A: Inside the nurse manager's private office desk
options.B: Underneath the clean supply storage cupboard
options.C: Locked inside the main utility room down the hall
options.D: Right at the point of use within arm's reach

explanation: Putting sharps boxes close by stops staff from walking around with exposed needles, reducing injury risks. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the immediate first-aid step after sustaining an accidental needle-stick injury?

options.A: Squeeze the puncture wound hard to force blood out
options.B: Soak the affected finger in undiluted bleach
options.C: Wash the site thoroughly with soap and running water
options.D: Apply a strong iodine solution and cover it tightly

explanation: Washing with soap and water immediately helps remove contaminants before they enter the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why is rapid reporting of a needle-stick injury essential for a healthcare worker?

options.A: To ensure the hospital avoids paying workers compensation claims
options.B: To document who broke the medication administration protocol
options.C: To allow quick assessment and timely start of preventive medications
options.D: To replace the lost syringe in the daily inventory count

explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis works best when started very soon after the potential exposure to blood-borne viruses. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is another name for a hospital-acquired infection?

options.A: Congenital disease
options.B: Chronic ailment
options.C: Idiopathic condition
options.D: Nosocomial infection

explanation: Infections caught while receiving medical care in a hospital or clinic are formally called nosocomial infections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is breaking any single link in the chain of infection effective?

options.A: It boosts the patient's natural red blood cell count
options.B: It stops the infectious cycle from continuing
options.C: It permanently destroys all bacteria in the room
options.D: It cures the underlying primary disease immediately

explanation: Because the chain relies on every link connecting, removing or blocking just one link halts the spread of germs. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h1)

question: How many times can a single sterile syringe and needle be used safely?

options.A: For multiple injections on the same patient
options.B: As many times as needed until the needle bends
options.C: For up to three patients if wiped with alcohol
options.D: For exactly one injection on one patient

explanation: Syringes and needles are single-use medical devices meant for one patient and one procedure only. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h2)

question: A nurse finishes drawing up an emergency medication from a single-dose vial. What should be done with the remaining liquid in the vial?

options.A: Save it in the pocket for the next patient
options.B: Put it back into the main supply drawer
options.C: Discard the leftover portion immediately
options.D: Leave the syringe attached for later use

explanation: Single-dose vials do not contain preservatives, so any leftover medication must be thrown away to prevent microbial growth. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is considered the single most important measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Taking daily antibiotics
options.B: Wearing heavy gloves
options.C: Proper hand hygiene
options.D: Changing bed sheets daily

explanation: Cleaning hands correctly removes transient microorganisms acquired from patients and environmental surfaces. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h3)

question: When is it strictly necessary for a nurse to use soap and water instead of an alcohol hand rub?

options.A: Only when starting a surgical procedure in the theater
options.B: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.C: Whenever the alcohol dispenser is empty for the day
options.D: Every time a nurse enters a new hospital ward

explanation: Alcohol rubs cannot remove physical dirt or certain tough bacterial spores as effectively as physical washing with soap and water. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h3)

question: What must a nurse do immediately after wiping a medication vial rubber top with an alcohol swab?

options.A: Allow the alcohol to dry completely before piercing
options.B: Blow on the rubber top to dry it fast
options.C: Insert the needle immediately while it is wet
options.D: Rinse the top with sterile tap water

explanation: Giving the alcohol time to air dry ensures proper disinfection of the rubber stopper surface. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h4)

question: Which part of a sterile syringe must a nurse avoid touching to maintain proper aseptic technique?

options.A: The inner barrel and the plunger shaft
options.B: The outer colored flange of the syringe
options.C: The paper packaging before it is opened
options.D: The outside plastic wall of the barrel

explanation: Touching parts of the syringe that will contact medication or enter the sterile pathway introduces germs directly into the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h4)

question: At what fill level should a clinical sharps container be securely closed and replaced?

options.A: Whenever a new nurse starts a shift
options.B: Only at the end of every working week
options.C: When it reaches three-quarters full
options.D: When it is completely packed to the top brim

explanation: Stopping at the three-quarters mark prevents accidental pokes from overflowing needles when dropping items in. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why is two-handed needle recapping strongly discouraged in clinical practice?

options.A: It dramatically increases the risk of an accidental finger puncture
options.B: It makes the plastic syringe barrel crack under pressure
options.C: It violates basic hospital waste management laws for paper
options.D: It causes the medication inside the needle to evaporate

explanation: Holding the cap with one hand and guiding the sharp needle toward it with the other hand frequently leads to missed caps and deep finger injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h5)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take after sustaining an accidental needle-stick injury?

options.A: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water
options.B: Fill out an incident report form for the manager
options.C: Squeeze the finger tightly to push out old blood
options.D: Apply an antiseptic iodine ointment and a bandage

explanation: Immediate washing reduces the viral or bacterial load introduced at the puncture site before it enters the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid aggressively squeezing a needle-stick wound?

options.A: It causes permanent paralysis of the affected finger
options.B: It neutralizes the effect of any washing soap used
options.C: It damages local tissue and can increase pathogen entry
options.D: It makes the bleeding stop too fast for testing

explanation: Squeezing or milking the puncture site tears delicate capillaries, creating a larger pathway for infectious agents to enter circulation. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is a common patient misconception regarding injections that nurses should actively address?

options.A: Expecting nurses to reuse needles to save money for the clinic
options.B: Assuming all vaccines contain active live viruses that cause severe disease
options.C: Thinking that single-use syringes can be washed at home with hot water
options.D: Believing injections are always superior or faster than oral drugs for any illness

explanation: Many patients demand injections unnecessarily, unaware that safe oral medications are often just as effective and carry fewer risks. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h7)

question: A patient asks a student nurse why a new sterile syringe is being opened for every single dose. How should the student best respond?

options.A: Because hospital policy says old plastic gets too brittle to use
options.B: So that the pharmaceutical companies can sell more plastic items
options.C: To make the medication taste better when it enters the body
options.D: To prevent passing infections and germs between different patients

explanation: Explaining that sterile single-use devices stop the transfer of bloodborne germs reassures the patient and reinforces safety standards. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T6#GNS122_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why do we study occupational health risks in nursing?

options.A: To help nurses stay safe and maintain a healthy career
options.B: To reduce the financial expenses of the hospital management
options.C: To eliminate all physical tasks from daily nursing duties
options.D: To ensure patients recover faster from their illnesses

explanation: Spotting workplace hazards early helps you protect your own health so you can enjoy a long, injury-free nursing journey. You matter too! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why must a nurse pay attention to workplace hazards even if they currently feel strong and healthy?

options.A: Because infectious diseases disappear once they are identified
options.B: Because patients expect nurses to know about building safety
options.C: Because early awareness prevents future injury and chronic illness
options.D: Because hospital laws require passing a test every month

explanation: Many workplace risks cause slow, quiet damage over years of practice. Knowing the dangers now keeps you protected down the road. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which disease is most commonly caught through accidental needle stick injuries in the clinic?

options.A: Malaria
options.B: Cholera
options.C: Typhoid fever
options.D: Hepatitis B

explanation: Hepatitis B is very easily spread through contaminated sharps in the hospital. This is why safety with needles is a huge deal for every nurse! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h2)

question: How do airborne germs mainly travel from one person to another?

options.A: Through direct contact with contaminated wound dressings
options.B: Through drinking unboiled water from hospital taps
options.C: Through tiny respiratory droplets suspended in the air
options.D: Through sharing unwashed eating utensils at the nurses station

explanation: Airborne pathogens hitch a ride on microscopic moisture droplets that float in the air and can be breathed in by anyone nearby. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h2)

question: Why are chemotherapy drugs considered dangerous for the nurses who handle them?

options.A: They always emit a poisonous gas that fills the entire hospital ward
options.B: They are designed to kill cells and can harm the nurse's cellular health
options.C: They cause immediate fainting if the nurse smells them
options.D: They instantly burn through standard hospital uniforms and skin

explanation: Chemo drugs work by destroying cells. That makes them powerful treatments for patients, but it also means nurses must handle them with extreme care to avoid toxic exposure. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is a common cause of latex allergies among healthcare workers?

options.A: Drinking contaminated water from hospital supply pipes
options.B: Touching metal instruments sterilized in chemical baths
options.C: Repeated skin exposure to natural rubber proteins in gloves
options.D: Inhaling powder from standard surgical face masks

explanation: Wearing rubber gloves all day exposes your skin to natural proteins over and over, which can sensitize your immune system and trigger allergies over time. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is the leading cause of ongoing back pain and injuries among nursing staff?

options.A: Writing patient reports while sitting on unadjusted chairs
options.B: Walking across slippery hospital floors in soft shoes
options.C: Lifting and moving heavy patients without proper mechanical assistance
options.D: Standing still at the nursing station during long night shifts

explanation: Pulling or lifting heavy patients manually puts massive strain on your lower back. Always use proper leverage, help, or lifting devices! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h4)

question: You need to move a heavy patient from a stretcher to a bed. What is the safest move?

options.A: Ask the patient to jump across while you hold their hands
options.B: Use a mechanical lift and ask another colleague to help
options.C: Pull the patient quickly using your arm muscles alone
options.D: Bend your back completely straight to gain extra lifting power

explanation: Teamwork and mechanical aids save your back! Never try to lift a heavy patient all by yourself. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h4)

question: Which protective gear is a must-have when working near an active X-ray machine?

options.A: Thick rubber industrial gloves
options.B: Lead apron and thyroid collar
options.C: N95 respiratory face mask
options.D: Waterproof plastic shoe covers

explanation: Lead aprons and thyroid shields act like a block, stopping harmful radiation from reaching your sensitive organs and tissues. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why is little-by-little exposure to radiation dangerous for healthcare workers over time?

options.A: It makes the nurse feel dizzy immediately after entering the room
options.B: It can cause gradual tissue damage and cellular mutations over years
options.C: It weakens the bones within a few minutes of standing nearby
options.D: It instantly heats up the skin and causes severe third-degree burns

explanation: Radiation adds up in the body over your career. That's why wearing your lead shield every single time is so important. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h5)

question: What do we call the emotional exhaustion and loss of care caused by long-term stress at work?

options.A: Hypothermia
options.B: Hysteria
options.C: Burnout
options.D: Hyperglycemia

explanation: Burnout is real in demanding fields like nursing. It's that feeling of complete mental and emotional tiredness from too much stress. Take care of your mental health! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT the right way to handle workplace violence in a hospital?

options.A: Using de-escalation techniques to calm an agitated patient
options.B: Ensuring an easy exit route is available during a patient interview
options.C: Accepting physical abuse quietly because it is part of the job
options.D: Reporting all threatening incidents to hospital security and management

explanation: Violence is never part of the job description. If someone threatens or abuses you, report it and use your hospital's security protocols immediately. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h6)

question: When should standard precautions be used in clinical practice?

options.A: Only when blood or body fluid is visibly staining the bedsheets
options.B: To every patient, regardless of their diagnosis or infection status
options.C: Strictly during surgical procedures in the main operating theatre
options.D: Only when caring for patients with known infectious diseases

explanation: Treat every patient as potentially infectious. Standard precautions keep you and everyone around you safe from hidden germs. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h7)

question: Why are nurses strongly advised NOT to recap used needles?

options.A: It violates hospital rules regarding plastic waste recycling
options.B: It drastically increases the risk of accidental needle stick injuries
options.C: It damages the sharp tip making it useless for the next patient
options.D: It wastes valuable nursing time during busy medication rounds

explanation: Trying to guide a tiny cap back onto a used needle is one of the quickest ways to accidentally poke yourself. Drop it straight into the safety box instead! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of wearing Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)?

options.A: To create a physical barrier between the nurse and infectious hazards
options.B: To hide the nurse's facial expressions from anxious family members
options.C: To comply with fashion trends established by hospital management
options.D: To keep the nurse's personal clothing clean from everyday dust

explanation: PPE acts like your personal shield, stopping germs, chemicals, and fluids from touching your skin or clothes. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h8)

question: Why is taking off your PPE in the correct, specific order so important?

options.A: To ensure the equipment can be washed and reused for the next shift
options.B: To prevent transferring trapped pathogens from the gear onto your skin
options.C: To prevent the plastic straps from snapping during disposal
options.D: To speed up the process so you can leave the isolation room faster

explanation: The outside of your PPE is covered in germs. If you take it off carelessly, you'll end up wiping those germs right onto your face or hands! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h8)

question: Who has the primary legal duty to provide a safe working environment in a hospital?

options.A: The pharmaceutical companies supplying hospital medications
options.B: The individual nursing students on clinical placement
options.C: The patients admitted to the medical and surgical wards
options.D: The hospital management and institutional administration

explanation: Management is legally required to give you safe facilities, working gear, and proper protection so you can do your job without undue risk. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h9)

question: What is your responsibility as a nurse regarding hospital safety rules?

options.A: To follow protocols, report hazards, and participate in safety training
options.B: To rewrite hospital rulebooks whenever a new patient is admitted
options.C: To purchase safety equipment using personal financial funds
options.D: To inspect all electrical wiring in the building every weekend

explanation: Safety is a team effort! Following guidelines and speaking up when something is broken helps keep both you and your patients out of harm's way. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T7#GNS122_U3_T7_h9)

question: What is the primary goal of patient safety measures in a hospital?

options.A: To reduce the likelihood of harmful adverse events
options.B: To decrease the documentation workload for nurses
options.C: To speed up the hospital discharge process
options.D: To lower the overall cost of medical equipment

explanation: Safety measures are specifically designed to protect patients from preventable harm and unexpected injuries while they receive care. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why is spotting patient risks early considered a protective action?

options.A: It guarantees the patient will never experience an infection
options.B: It allows nurses to build barriers against potential hazards
options.C: It removes all clinical responsibilities from the doctor
options.D: It stops patients from moving around the ward

explanation: Spotting risks beforehand lets you put preventative steps in place before an accident or complication actually happens. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which of these is an example of an intrinsic (internal) risk factor for a patient?

options.A: An improperly calibrated infusion pump
options.B: Muscle weakness from advanced age
options.C: A wet floor in the hallway
options.D: Poor lighting in the patient room

explanation: Intrinsic risks come from inside the patient's own body, like age-related muscle weakness, rather than from things around the ward. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h2)

question: How does confusion or memory loss directly increase a patient's safety risk?

options.A: It causes the ward floors to become slippery
options.B: It makes it hard for the patient to understand safety instructions
options.C: It directly lowers the patient's blood pressure
options.D: It prevents medications from being absorbed properly

explanation: Patients with memory or thinking problems often forget their limits (like needing help to walk), which can lead to falls. Always good to keep an extra eye on them! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h2)

question: In nursing, what does the term 'polypharmacy' mean?

options.A: Using a machine to deliver intravenous fluids
options.B: Taking multiple medications at the same time
options.C: Receiving treatment in a private hospital room
options.D: Having a severe allergy to common antibiotics

explanation: Polypharmacy simply means taking many drugs at once. This often increases the risk of side effects and drug clashes, so nurses have to monitor these patients closely. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h3)

question: A patient who struggles to walk is put in a room where a bedside table blocks the path to the toilet. What kind of risk is this blocked path?

options.A: Metabolic risk
options.B: Intrinsic risk
options.C: Extrinsic risk
options.D: Genetic risk

explanation: Extrinsic risks are environmental hazards outside the patient's body, like a blocked pathway in the room. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h3)

question: Why does severe anemia put a patient at high risk of fainting?

options.A: It blocks the patient from hearing safety alarms
options.B: Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery to the brain
options.C: It makes the hospital floors slippery and dangerous
options.D: It causes high blood sugar levels after meals

explanation: Red blood cells carry oxygen around the body. When hemoglobin is low, the brain gets less oxygen, causing dizziness and fainting. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h4)

question: What do we call a sudden, severe change in mental state where a patient becomes very confused and restless?

options.A: Chronic anemia
options.B: Stable hypertension
options.C: Mild osteoarthritis
options.D: Acute delirium

explanation: Delirium is a sudden, temporary state of confusion often seen in hospitalised patients. It puts them at risk of pulling out their IV lines or climbing out of bed unassisted. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the main use of the Braden Scale in the ward?

options.A: To predict the risk of pressure injury development
options.B: To calculate the correct dose of intravenous fluids
options.C: To measure the severity of patient chest pain
options.D: To assess the likelihood of a patient having a seizure

explanation: The Braden Scale checks things like skin moisture, movement, and nutrition to help you spot patients who are likely to develop bedsores. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why do nurses use standard scoring tools instead of just guessing a patient's risk level?

options.A: To ensure doctors do not have to write care plans
options.B: To obtain an objective score that guides consistent care planning
options.C: To replace the need for physical assessments on the ward
options.D: To speed up the patient discharge paperwork process

explanation: Standard tools take away personal guesswork and give the whole nursing team a clear, reliable picture of what care the patient needs. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h5)

question: A patient is assessed as a high fall risk. Which nursing action is best to keep them safe?

options.A: Remove all pillows from the bed to reduce soft surface risks
options.B: Ensure the bed is in the lowest position with the call bell close by
options.C: Keep the room lights completely off to encourage deep sleep
options.D: Encourage the patient to walk alone to the bathroom frequently

explanation: Keeping the bed low reduces injury if they fall, and keeping the call bell close means they can easily ask for your help before trying to get up! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h6)

question: How often should a bedbound patient usually be turned to prevent bedsores?

options.A: Every thirty minutes
options.B: Every two hours
options.C: Once every shift
options.D: Only when they complain of pain

explanation: Turning a patient at least every two hours takes pressure off bony areas and protects their skin from breaking down. Great routine to master for clinicals! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is your very first priority as a nurse right after an incident or accident happens on the ward?

options.A: Complete the online incident report form
options.B: Assess and stabilize the patient
options.C: Interview witnesses on the ward
options.D: Notify the hospital legal department

explanation: Patient care and safety always come first before you worry about filling out forms or doing paperwork. Clinical care is king! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is the true purpose of writing a hospital incident report?

options.A: It is used for quality improvement and learning from system flaws
options.B: It serves as a formal legal tool to discipline negligent nurses
options.C: It is placed permanently in the patient's bedside clinical chart
options.D: It is required by insurance companies to calculate hospital bills

explanation: Incident reports are confidential tools meant to help the hospital figure out what went wrong in the system so safety can be improved for everyone. It's about fixing the system, not witch-hunting! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T8#GNS122_U3_T8_h7)

question: What exactly is a community health risk?

options.A: The total cost of running a primary health care clinic
options.B: Any factor increasing the chance of illness or injury for a group
options.C: A personal medical diagnosis given inside a hospital ward
options.D: A genetic disease passed down through generations in a family

explanation: Think of community health risks as collective dangers that affect many people together, rather than just one person's isolated sickness. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h1)

question: How does community health nursing differ from bedside nursing in the hospital?

options.A: It ignores individual patient histories completely
options.B: It requires advanced surgical training for field emergencies
options.C: It deals strictly with paperwork and government health budgets
options.D: It focuses on the collective environment and health of populations

explanation: While bedside nursing cares for one patient at a time, community nursing zooms out to look at whole neighborhoods, environments, and populations! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h1)

question: Which environmental issue is a major breeding ground for malaria mosquitoes in local neighborhoods?

options.A: Thick concrete flooring inside residential buildings
options.B: Blocked drainage channels and stagnant water pools
options.C: Dry sandy soil found in northern farming regions
options.D: Solar panels installed on health center roofs

explanation: Mosquitoes love standing water! Blocked drains and puddles give them a safe place to lay eggs, which drives up malaria rates. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h2)

question: A nurse notices women suffering from regular coughs and eye irritation because they cook daily with firewood in closed kitchens. What is the main culprit here?

options.A: A contagious bacterial lung infection spreading through handshakes
options.B: Indoor air pollution from inadequate ventilation and smoke
options.C: Severe vitamin deficiency caused by poor farming output
options.D: Direct allergic reaction to new insecticides used outdoors

explanation: Cooking with firewood in rooms without good windows traps heavy smoke inside, irritating the eyes and lungs over time. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h2)

question: Which of these does NOT help cause a disease outbreak?

options.A: High routine immunization coverage in children
options.B: Inadequate waste management systems
options.C: Poor access to safe, clean drinking water
options.D: Overcrowded housing and living quarters

explanation: Vaccines are our shield! High immunization rates protect a community and stop outbreaks, unlike bad water or crowded living spaces which spread disease. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h3)

question: A sudden outbreak of watery diarrhea hits a village. As a community nurse, what is your very first step?

options.A: Report the cluster promptly and investigate potential water sources
options.B: Prescribe strong antibiotics to every single person in the village
options.C: Advise villagers to stop drinking all liquids for several days
options.D: Wait patiently until the local hospital requests formal assistance

explanation: Spotting the pattern, reporting it quickly, and hunting down the water source stops cholera and similar outbreaks in their tracks! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h3)

question: What do we mean by 'socioeconomic determinants of health'?

options.A: Blood pressure readings taken at annual checkups
options.B: Income level, education, and living conditions
options.C: The specific surgical tools used in major hospitals
options.D: Genetic mutations inherited from biological parents

explanation: These are the social and money-related factors—like how much money you make, where you live, and your education—that heavily shape your health. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why must a nurse be culturally sensitive when talking about traditional health practices in a rural area?

options.A: It proves that traditional beliefs are always scientifically accurate
options.B: It builds trust and encourages the community to accept safer health practices
options.C: It ensures the nurse receives financial grants from foreign donors
options.D: It prevents the government from closing down the local health post

explanation: Respect opens doors! When you honor people's culture, they trust you enough to listen when you introduce safer health habits. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h4)

question: Which group is generally most at risk for malnutrition and vaccine-preventable infections?

options.A: Retired civil servants receiving regular pensions
options.B: University students living in private hostels
options.C: Employed adult males aged thirty to forty
options.D: Children under five years of age

explanation: Under-fives are still building their immune systems and need plenty of nutrients, making them the most vulnerable group. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h5)

question: Your clinic gets a donation of mosquito nets and supplements. Who should you give priority to?

options.A: Healthy young men in the local football club
options.B: Local political leaders and chiefs
options.C: Pregnant women and young children
options.D: Wealthy traders in the central market

explanation: Pregnant mums and young kids face the deadliest risks from malaria and poor nutrition, so they always come first. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is a 'windshield survey' in community nursing?

options.A: Checking vehicle exhaust fumes to measure air pollution levels
options.B: Observing a community firsthand by walking or driving through it
options.C: Testing the driving vision of commercial vehicle drivers
options.D: Administering a written questionnaire to hospital patients

explanation: Imagine driving or walking slowly through a neighborhood just observing houses, trash disposal, and daily life. That's a windshield survey! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h6)

question: Why do a community health assessment before starting a new health project?

options.A: It proves that the community has no existing health problems
options.B: It ensures interventions address the actual, specific needs of the population
options.C: It eliminates the need to ever speak with traditional leaders
options.D: It is a legal requirement that guarantees government funding approval

explanation: You don't want to guess what people need! Assessing first makes sure you are solving their real, everyday struggles. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the main aim of disaster preparedness in a community?

options.A: To prevent natural weather events from ever occurring
options.B: To relocate all community residents to permanent urban centers
options.C: To ensure hospitals make a profit during unexpected crises
options.D: To minimize injury, loss of life, and disruption during an emergency

explanation: While we can't stop storms or floods, good planning helps keep people safe and cuts down the damage when disaster hits. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h7)

question: A village floods every rainy season. What is the best proactive nursing action to prepare?

options.A: Focusing solely on treating broken bones after the flood recedes
options.B: Telling families to abandon their ancestral land permanently
options.C: Waiting until the floodwaters rise before requesting relief materials
options.D: Educating residents on evacuation routes and establishing early warning systems

explanation: Preparation means teaching escape routes and setting up warnings *before* the water starts rising. Great job working through these! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T9#GNS122_U3_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of injection safety in clinical practice?

options.A: To speed up the administration of intravenous medications
options.B: To prevent harm to patients, health workers, and the community
options.C: To eliminate the need for wearing gloves during procedures
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing medical syringes

explanation: Injection safety encompasses measures that protect the patient receiving the injection, the nurse administering it, and the surrounding community from hazardous waste. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is proper injection safety so important for nurses?

options.A: Injections are rare procedures that need special certification
options.B: Injections are done daily and can spread serious infections if mishandled
options.C: Hospital management uses injection logs to grade nursing speed
options.D: Patients expect disposable equipment for financial reasons

explanation: You'll give lots of injections! Because they happen so often, even a tiny slip in safety can quickly pass an infection to many people. Staying sharp keeps everyone safe. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which of these best describes an unsafe injection practice?

options.A: Giving an intramuscular shot without asking the patient's age first
options.B: Any injection action that puts patients or staff at risk of preventable harm
options.C: Using a plastic syringe instead of a glass one
options.D: Giving an injection past normal visiting hours

explanation: If it puts anyone at risk of harm through contamination, reuse, or bad handling, it's unsafe. Trust your gut—if it feels risky, it probably is! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is a clear example of an unsafe injection habit?

options.A: Using a contaminated needle to enter a single-dose medication vial
options.B: Using a fresh, sterile needle and syringe for every single patient
options.C: Dropping a used syringe straight into a safety box
options.D: Cleaning the skin with an alcohol swab before the poke

explanation: Never use a needle that has touched a surface or a patient to draw more medicine. It contaminates the whole vial and puts the next person in danger. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT a safe way to handle used needles?

options.A: Putting sharps containers right next to where you work
options.B: Avoiding bending needles before throwing them away
options.C: Dropping the whole syringe and needle into a safety box
options.D: Recapping needles using both hands right after use

explanation: Using both hands to recap is a top way nurses accidentally stick themselves. Always avoid it! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h3)

question: You need to give medications to two patients in your ward. What should you do with your equipment?

options.A: Rinse the syringe with hot water between patients
options.B: Change only the needle and keep the same syringe barrel
options.C: Use the same syringe if the drug is prescribed for both
options.D: Use a fresh, sterile syringe and needle for each patient

explanation: Syringes and needles are strictly single-use. Never share them between patients—ever! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h3)

question: What is a major reason why unsafe injections happen in low-resource clinics?

options.A: Having too many nurses on duty at night
options.B: Having way too many sterile water supplies
options.C: Shortages of disposable syringes and safety boxes
options.D: Too many mandatory infection control classes

explanation: When basic supplies run low, healthcare workers are put in tough spots. Advocating for proper supplies is a big part of nursing advocacy. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h4)

question: How can a severe shortage of nurses lead to unsafe injections?

options.A: It gives nurses extra time to clean equipment
options.B: It automatically gets rid of multi-dose vials
options.C: It causes rushed procedures where safety steps get skipped
options.D: It forces patients to inject themselves

explanation: When you're overworked and tired, it's easy to rush. Staying aware helps us protect our patients even on busy shifts. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which infections are most commonly spread through unsafe injections?

options.A: Respiratory viruses like the common cold
options.B: Parasites spread by mosquito bites
options.C: Blood-borne viruses like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV
options.D: Intestinal worms like hookworm

explanation: Injections go straight past the skin barrier into tissues and blood vessels, making it easy for blood-borne viruses to travel if gear isn't sterile. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why are accidental needlestick injuries so scary for healthcare workers?

options.A: They stop the worker from ever touching medical tools again
options.B: They instantly paralyze the hand
options.C: They instantly trigger severe allergies to latex
options.D: They can push infected blood straight into the nurse's bloodstream

explanation: A hollow needle often carries leftover blood from a patient. That's why safe disposal isn't just about the patient—it protects YOU too! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is a major cause of unsafe injection risks in informal healthcare settings?

options.A: Mandatory training for birth attendants
options.B: Too much government checking of pharmacies
options.C: An oversupply of safety boxes
options.D: Not enough clean, single-use equipment available

explanation: When places lack a steady supply of cheap, disposable syringes, dangerous reuse habits can creep in. Community health education helps fix this! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why is teaching community members about injection safety so important in Nigeria?

options.A: To cut down the cost of running clinics
options.B: To replace nursing school training
options.C: To help patients understand they don't always need an injection
options.D: To teach patients to give themselves IV drugs at home

explanation: Many people believe injections work faster than tablets, leading to a huge demand for unnecessary shots. Educating the public keeps everyone safer. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h6)

question: Where is the best place to keep your sharps disposal box during an injection?

options.A: In the nurse's station for later
options.B: Locked in a store room down the hall
options.C: On the floor right under the patient's bed
options.D: Right within arm's reach of your workspace

explanation: Keep your safety box close! Walking around with an open, used needle just asks for an accidental poke. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is the big advantage of using single-dose medication vials?

options.A: They let nurses reuse syringes safely
options.B: They make the medicine taste sweeter
options.C: They completely stop the risk of contaminating shared medicine bottles
options.D: They mean fewer patients will need shots

explanation: Single-dose vials are used once and thrown away. No sharing means no chance of passing germs into the next dose! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is a key professional duty of every nurse when it comes to injection safety?

options.A: Hiding unsafe practices to protect the hospital's image
options.B: Refusing unsafe practices and speaking up for proper supplies
options.C: Reusing needles when the hospital budget is tight
options.D: Leaving all injections to untrained volunteers

explanation: As a nurse, your primary loyalty is to safety. You have an ethical duty to speak up against dangerous shortcuts and shortages. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h8)

question: You see a senior nurse recapping a needle with both hands. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Kindly remind them of the risk and suggest a safer way
options.B: Report them to the police right away
options.C: Ignore it because they have more experience
options.D: Copy them so you can finish your work faster

explanation: Be polite and respectful, but speak up! Friendly peer reminders build a safer, more supportive workplace for everyone. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h8)

question: What is the main goal of injection safety in your daily clinical practice?

options.A: Administering medication without causing harm to patients or yourself
options.B: Using only intravenous routes for fluid replacement
options.C: Ensuring every patient gets at least one daily injection
options.D: Disposing of all used syringes in household trash bins

explanation: You've got this! Injection safety is all about protecting everyone—patients, healthcare workers, and the community—from any harm related to injections. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why are nurses so important when it comes to keeping injection safety protocols working?

options.A: Nurses are the only staff legally allowed to handle medical waste
options.B: Nurses write the hospital policies regarding medication purchases
options.C: Nurses manufacture all disposable syringes used in hospitals
options.D: Nurses administer the majority of clinical injections daily

explanation: Spot on! Since you and your fellow nurses give most of the injections, your daily habits directly keep safety standards alive on the ward. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which viral infection is most commonly linked globally to unsafe injections?

options.A: Hepatitis B Virus
options.B: Influenza Virus
options.C: Varicella Zoster
options.D: Rhinovirus

explanation: Well done! Along with Hepatitis C and HIV, Hepatitis B is one of the main bloodborne pathogens spread when injection safety rules are broken. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the main reason developing countries experience more complications from unsafe injections?

options.A: A complete lack of trained nurses in regional clinics
options.B: Patients refusing oral medications in favor of injections
options.C: The natural resistance of tropical germs to standard soap
options.D: Supply shortages and poor waste management systems

explanation: Exactly. When clinics struggle with equipment shortages, it can unfortunately lead to dangerous workarounds like reusing syringes. You're building great clinical awareness! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the dangerous practice of using the same syringe barrel for more than one patient called?

options.A: Syringe reuse
options.B: Z-track administration
options.C: Aseptic transfer
options.D: Vial reconstitution

explanation: You nailed it! Reusing syringes—even if you change the needle—transfers microscopic amounts of blood and fluids between patients, spreading serious infections. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h3)

question: In a busy clinic, how does a multi-dose medication vial usually get contaminated?

options.A: Using a previously used needle or syringe to enter the vial
options.B: Cleaning the rubber stopper with alcohol before every puncture
options.C: Storing the medicine bottle inside a warm medication refrigerator
options.D: Failing to shake the suspension liquid before drawing a dose

explanation: That's right! If a needle has touched a patient, using it to enter a shared multi-dose vial contaminates the whole bottle for everyone else. Always use a fresh, sterile needle and syringe! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which bloodborne virus is known to survive on environmental surfaces for several days?

options.A: Ebola Virus
options.B: Rabies Virus
options.C: Hepatitis B Virus
options.D: Human Immunodeficiency Virus

explanation: Good job! Hepatitis B is remarkably hardy and can stay infectious on surfaces outside the body for quite a while, which is why strict disinfection matters so much. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h4)

question: What creates the direct pathway for spreading disease during an unsafe injection?

options.A: Inhaling medication droplets while prepping a syringe
options.B: A contaminated needle breaking the skin and entering circulation
options.C: Swallowing oral tablets without enough water
options.D: Touching a sealed medication package with bare hands

explanation: Spot on! Injections bypass your skin's natural defense barrier, meaning any germs on a dirty needle go straight into the patient's tissues and bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is a major community-wide effect when a clinic suffers an outbreak of healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Loss of public trust in the healthcare system
options.B: Lower costs for public health insurance programs
options.C: An immediate surplus of available hospital beds
options.D: Increased willingness of patients to receive injections

explanation: Exactly. When a clinic spreads disease instead of healing, people lose faith and may stop seeking care when they truly need it. Safe nursing builds community trust! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h5)

question: If a patient catches Hepatitis C from a poorly sterilized procedure, what long-term organ damage are they most at risk for?

options.A: Progressive hearing loss and blindness
options.B: Chronic liver damage and cirrhosis
options.C: Chronic respiratory failure and asthma
options.D: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs

explanation: You got it! Hepatitis C attacks the liver, often causing long-term inflammation and scarring over time. Protecting patients from bloodborne infections is a huge part of our job. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is one of the most common workplace hazards for nurses during medication rounds?

options.A: Airborne tuberculosis transmission
options.B: Accidental needle-stick injuries
options.C: Developing chronic bone fractures
options.D: Sudden chemical skin burns

explanation: Spot on! Needle-stick injuries are a constant hazard on the ward, which is why practicing safe handling techniques every single day is so crucial for your own safety. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h6)

question: Besides the risk of physical infection, what immediate emotional impact does a needle-stick injury often have on a nurse?

options.A: Complete temporary paralysis of the affected hand
options.B: Immediate dismissal from their nursing position
options.C: Automatic immunity to all future bloodborne viruses
options.D: Severe psychological stress and anxiety while waiting for test results

explanation: So true. Waiting for screening results after a needle poke can cause a lot of worry and sleepless nights. That's why prevention is always your best friend! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h6)

question: If you absolutely must recap a used needle, what is the safest technique to use?

options.A: The one-handed scoop technique
options.B: Holding the cap tightly in the palm of your hand
options.C: Pushing the needle directly into the cap using both hands
options.D: Asking a colleague to hold the cap while you insert the needle

explanation: Brilliant! The one-handed scoop method keeps your free hand safely away from the sharp tip so you don't accidentally poke yourself. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h7)

question: Why are single-dose medication vials much better for infection control than multi-dose vials?

options.A: They completely eliminate the risk of cross-contamination between patients
options.B: They contain larger volumes of liquid for multiple shifts
options.C: They are always cheaper for hospital procurement to buy
options.D: They never require alcohol swabbing of the rubber top

explanation: You got it! Since single-dose vials are used for just one patient, there's zero chance of a contaminated needle transferring germs to the next dose. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h7)

question: Where is the best place to set up a sharps disposal container in a patient care area?

options.A: On the floor underneath the nurse's station desk
options.B: Inside the central facility storage warehouse
options.C: Inside the clean utility supply cupboard
options.D: As close as possible to where the injection is given

explanation: Spot on! Keeping sharps bins right at the point of use means you never have to walk across the room carrying an exposed needle. Safety first! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h8)

question: What major hazard happens when sharps disposal boxes are allowed to become overfilled?

options.A: Rapid evaporation of liquid medications stored inside
options.B: Chemical reactions that dissolve the plastic bin
options.C: Foul odors spreading throughout the hospital ward
options.D: Higher risk of accidental needle pricks for staff and waste handlers

explanation: Exactly! When bins are stuffed too full, needles start poking out and endangering everyone nearby. Always swap out sharps bins before they hit the fill line! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h8)

question: How can you, as a bedside nurse, help improve injection safety standards in your clinic?

options.A: By buying new safety syringes with your own personal money
options.B: By reporting unsafe practices and joining safety audits
options.C: By handling all medical waste disposal completely alone
options.D: By refusing to give any injections during night shifts

explanation: Well done! Speaking up about risks and taking part in safety checks helps fix system flaws and protects everyone. You're thinking like a professional nurse! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h9)

question: You notice your clinic frequently runs out of single-use syringes, causing staff to reuse equipment. What is your best professional action?

options.A: Keep quiet so you don't upset the clinic manager during a busy shift
options.B: Buy plastic syringes from a local pharmacy using your own money
options.C: Stop giving all prescribed medications until the hospital closes
options.D: Report the shortage through official channels and advocate for safer supplies

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you have a duty to advocate for your patients and push for proper resources when safety is on the line. Great clinical leadership! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T2#GNS122_U4_T2_h9)

question: What is the main goal of injection safety in nursing?

options.A: To prevent harm to the patient, nurse, and community
options.B: To ensure medications dissolve faster in the bloodstream
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital supplies
options.D: To speed up the delivery of emergency medications

explanation: You got this! Injection safety is all about protecting everyone from accidental injury or infection. Keeping patients, ourselves, and our communities safe always comes first. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why do very busy hospital wards sometimes lead to unsafe injection practices?

options.A: High patient loads and supply limits tempt staff to rush or cut corners
options.B: New nursing graduates are rarely taught basic injection techniques
options.C: Modern equipment requires electricity that is often unstable
options.D: Patients demand faster injections when waiting rooms are crowded

explanation: True story in many clinics: when resources are tight and too many patients are waiting, pressure mounts. But remember, we must never let stress push us into dangerous shortcuts like reusing gear. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h1)

question: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) define a safe injection?

options.A: One that does not harm the recipient, provider, or community
options.B: One that uses only glass syringes and metal needles
options.C: One that is administered exclusively by registered nurses
options.D: One that costs less than standard oral medications

explanation: Think of the WHO definition as a circle of safety: it covers the patient getting the drug, the nurse giving it, and the public handling the waste. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h2)

question: A nurse uses a single-dose medication vial for three different patients to save time. How would you classify this action?

options.A: An acceptable resource-saving method
options.B: An evidence-based nursing intervention
options.C: A standard emergency protocol
options.D: An unsafe injection practice

explanation: Even when trying to save time or materials, single-dose vials are strictly for one patient only. Sharing them easily spreads blood and germs between patients! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT a safe injection practice?

options.A: Reusing a disposable syringe after washing it with warm water
options.B: Disposing of used needles immediately into a puncture-proof box
options.C: Using a brand new, sterile syringe for every single patient
options.D: Wiping the rubber top of a medication vial with an alcohol swab

explanation: Never wash and reuse disposable syringes! Washing doesn't kill microscopic germs. Every patient deserves a fresh, sterile syringe. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h3)

question: What happens if a nurse dips a needle that has already touched a patient back into a multi-dose medication vial?

options.A: The remaining fluid becomes completely neutralized
options.B: Pathogens from the patient can contaminate the entire remaining medicine
options.C: The medication instantly changes color to signal contamination
options.D: The pressure inside the glass vial drops to zero

explanation: That used needle carries tiny traces of blood and germs right into the shared bottle, turning the rest of the medication into a breeding ground for infection. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why are injections uniquely risky when it comes to spreading diseases?

options.A: It increases the normal body temperature of the recipient
options.B: It destroys all white blood cells found near the injection site
options.C: It forces medications to travel too quickly through the digestive tract
options.D: It bypasses the skin, creating a direct pathway into the body's tissues

explanation: Our skin is an amazing shield against germs. A needle breaks that shield, making injections a super-highway straight into the body if we aren't careful. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which group of viruses is most commonly spread through contaminated injection equipment?

options.A: Respiratory viruses like Influenza and the common cold
options.B: Fungal spores that cause superficial skin rashes
options.C: Intestinal parasites spread through contaminated water
options.D: Blood-borne pathogens like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV

explanation: Because unsafe injections often transfer tiny amounts of blood between people, blood-borne viruses are our biggest concern in clinical safety. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h4)

question: A patient develops a painful, swollen, pus-filled lump at an injection site a few days after treatment. What is this likely a sign of?

options.A: A mild allergic reaction to clean cotton wool
options.B: An expected systemic reaction to vitamin supplements
options.C: A local bacterial infection and abscess formation
options.D: The normal healing process of deep muscle tissue

explanation: Ouch! When unsterile equipment or poor technique introduces bacteria into the tissue, it causes localized inflammation and can form a nasty abscess. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is a major long-term health problem linked to chronic Hepatitis C caught from unsafe injections?

options.A: Rapid weakening of the leg muscles
options.B: Permanent loss of hearing and balance
options.C: Chronic respiratory failure and asthma
options.D: Cirrhosis and severe liver damage

explanation: Hepatitis C quietly attacks the liver over many years, leading to scarring (cirrhosis) and raising the risk of liver cancer. This is why our injection technique matters so much! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the main reason doctors order blood screening tests for a patient exposed to unsafe injections?

options.A: To measure the exact amount of muscle mass in the limbs
options.B: To test for common food allergies and dietary sensitivities
options.C: To determine how quickly the patient's kidneys filter water
options.D: To check for the presence of blood-borne viral infections

explanation: Serological screening helps us catch antibodies or antigens for viruses like HIV or Hepatitis early, so the patient can get timely support. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h6)

question: A patient with a history of getting injections from an unlicensed vendor arrives showing signs of jaundice (yellow eyes/skin). What tests should the nurse expect first?

options.A: Fasting blood sugar and lipid profile test
options.B: Complete blood count and routine urinalysis
options.C: Stool microscopy and electrolyte panel
options.D: Liver function tests and viral hepatitis serology

explanation: Jaundice is a classic red flag for liver stress. Checking liver enzymes and running hepatitis screens are our top priorities here. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h6)

question: If a needle absolutely must be recapped in an emergency, what is the safest way to do it?

options.A: Holding the cap in your mouth while positioning the syringe
options.B: Using both hands to snap the cap back on firmly
options.C: The one-handed scoop technique
options.D: Asking an untrained assistant to hold the cap for you

explanation: Always use the one-handed scoop method! It keeps your free hand safely out of the way, preventing accidental needle pricks. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h7)

question: Why do we keep hard, puncture-proof sharps containers right at medication stations?

options.A: To collect expired medication vials for proper pharmacy return
options.B: To safely contain used needles and prevent staff injuries
options.C: To store extra syringes for emergency night shifts
options.D: To keep cotton swabs clean before giving an injection

explanation: Sharps containers are specially designed so needles can't poke through, protecting nurses, cleaners, and patients from accidental injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T3#GNS122_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the main goal of injection safety protocols in nursing?

options.A: To prevent harm to patients and protect healthcare workers
options.B: To ensure medications are absorbed faster by the body
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing new syringes
options.D: To speed up medication administration during busy shifts

explanation: Injection safety is all about keeping both sides safe—protecting the patient receiving the injection and keeping you, the nurse, safe from injuries and infections! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is practicing injection safety a core professional duty for every nurse?

options.A: Because patients will refuse treatment if nurses lack safety gear
options.B: Because drug manufacturers mandate strict handling instructions
options.C: Because hospital management requires paperwork for every needle used
options.D: Because handling needles always carries a potential window for exposure and infection

explanation: You handle sharps every single day on the ward. Knowing safety rules protects your own health just as much as it protects your patients! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h1)

question: What is a very common cause of accidental needle-stick injuries among nurses?

options.A: Disinfecting rubber seals on vials
options.B: Manually recapping used needles
options.C: Using single-dose medication vials
options.D: Dropping plastic syringe barrels

explanation: Try to avoid recapping used needles whenever possible! Missing the cap is the easiest way to accidentally poke your own finger. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h2)

question: A nurse needs to draw medication from a multidose vial for another patient. Which of these actions is unsafe?

options.A: Swabbing the rubber top of the vial with an alcohol wipe before piercing
options.B: Using a brand new, sterile syringe and needle for drawing up the dose
options.C: Checking the expiration date printed on the label of the vial
options.D: Leaving a previously used dispensing needle inserted in the vial rubber septum

explanation: Never leave a needle stuck inside a multidose vial! It acts like an open door for bacteria to crawl inside and contaminate the medicine for the next patient. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which blood-borne infection has the highest statistical risk of transmission after a single accidental needle-stick?

options.A: Hepatitis C virus
options.B: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.C: Hepatitis B virus
options.D: Cytomegalovirus

explanation: Hepatitis B is remarkably hardy and infectious. That is why getting your Hep B vaccine and safety training early in nursing school is so important! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h3)

question: Apart from physical illness, what is a major hidden toll of a needle-stick injury on a nurse?

options.A: Automatic financial compensation from the hospital
options.B: Severe psychological distress and anxiety while awaiting test results
options.C: Permanent inability to administer oral medications
options.D: Immediate loss of nursing license and mandatory demotion

explanation: The emotional weight of waiting weeks for blood test results can be really heavy. Taking precautions protects your peace of mind as well as your body. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h3)

question: Why do hospital system issues often lead nurses to break safety rules?

options.A: Supply shortages and heavy workloads force staff into dangerous workarounds
options.B: Modern medical equipment is intentionally designed to be difficult to use
options.C: Hospital policies explicitly instruct nurses to reuse needles to save money
options.D: Healthcare workers prefer taking risks to finish their shifts early

explanation: When the ward is short-staffed and lacking basic supplies, tired nurses may be tempted to cut corners just to get through the shift. Good systems protect staff from having to make those choices. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is a common management failure that lets unsafe injection habits keep happening?

options.A: Failing to provide safety training and discouraging near-miss reporting
options.B: Requiring doctors to supervise every single routine intramuscular injection
options.C: Enforcing strict handwashing rules during morning shift handovers
options.D: Providing too many sharps disposal containers in medication rooms

explanation: When hospitals punish people for speaking up or ignore close calls, hidden dangers stay on the ward waiting to cause actual harm. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is considered the single most effective way to stop the spread of infections in a hospital?

options.A: Wearing heavy utility gloves all day
options.B: Frequent and proper hand hygiene
options.C: Administering prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Changing bed linens every morning

explanation: Never underestimate the power of clean hands! Good hand hygiene washes away transient germs before they can travel from patient to patient. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h5)

question: How do non-sterile gloves affect your hand hygiene routine during medication rounds?

options.A: Gloves make skin completely impervious to all bacterial transfer
options.B: Hand rubs should only be applied directly over dirty gloves
options.C: Gloves do not replace the need for proper hand hygiene
options.D: Wearing gloves eliminates the requirement for washing hands

explanation: Gloves can have tiny invisible tears, and your hands can easily pick up germs while taking them off. Always wash your hands before and after wearing gloves! [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you accidentally prick yourself with a used needle?

options.A: Wash the puncture wound immediately with soap and running water
options.B: Squeeze the wound forcefully to bleed out all contaminated fluid
options.C: Wait until the end of the shift to report the incident to management
options.D: Apply a tight tourniquet above the injury site to trap the virus

explanation: Act fast! Wash the spot right away with soap and running water to help rinse away germs before heading to report the incident. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T4#GNS122_U4_T4_h6)

question: You notice that the sharps box in the treatment room is filled right past the max line. What should you do?

options.A: Transfer some of the used needles into a regular plastic trash bin
options.B: Push the protruding syringes down firmly with a gloved hand to create more room
options.C: Close and seal the container safely for disposal, then replace it with a new one
options.D: Leave the container open until the end of the week to save on plastic bags
