question: When would a nurse most likely need to insert a flatus tube?

options.A: Chronic diarrhea lasting longer than three days
options.B: Severe postoperative gaseous abdominal distention
options.C: A suspected complete mechanical bowel obstruction
options.D: Active and profuse upper gastrointestinal bleeding

explanation: Flatus tubes are super helpful when gas builds up painfully after surgery because the bowels are temporarily slow. Spot on! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h2)

question: Why is recent rectal surgery considered a strict contraindication for a flatus tube?

options.A: It disrupts healing surgical suture lines and causes injury
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from producing urine
options.C: It permanently damages the anal sphincter muscles
options.D: It causes severe respiratory depression

explanation: Inserting a tube into a freshly operated rectum can tear fragile sutures, cause severe hemorrhage, and damage healing tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the best position for a patient receiving a flatus tube?

options.A: High Fowler's sitting position
options.B: Left lateral Sims' position
options.C: Prone position flat on the stomach
options.D: Supine position with legs flat

explanation: The left Sims' position naturally follows the curve of the lower bowel, making the procedure much smoother and easier. Well done! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is clear communication important before starting this procedure?

options.A: It speeds up the process of digestion in the stomach
options.B: It replaces the need for using water-soluble lubricant
options.C: It relaxes the patient and reduces anxiety about privacy
options.D: It ensures the patient's blood pressure remains high

explanation: Rectal procedures can cause embarrassment and tension; explaining the steps helps the patient relax their muscles and cooperate fully. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h3)

question: What type of lubricant should always be used on a flatus tube before insertion?

options.A: Water-soluble lubricant
options.B: Sterile cooking oil
options.C: Petroleum-based jelly
options.D: Alcohol-based gel

explanation: Water-soluble lubricant is safe for mucous membranes and prevents trauma, unlike petroleum-based products which are harder to clear and can damage tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h4)

question: What should the nurse do immediately if resistance is felt while advancing the flatus tube?

options.A: Inject warm tap water through the lumen
options.B: Push harder to bypass the blockage
options.C: Rotate the tube rapidly in a circle
options.D: Stop advancing and remove the tube immediately

explanation: Forcing a tube against resistance can cause severe trauma or perforation to the delicate rectal wall; the procedure must be halted. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why is a flatus tube generally left in place for only a short period, such as 20 to 30 minutes?

options.A: To ensure the tube does not dissolve inside the bowel
options.B: To prevent the kidneys from stopping urine output
options.C: To prevent pressure damage to the delicate rectal lining
options.D: To stop the patient from drinking too much water

explanation: Prolonged pressure from an indwelling tube can compromise blood flow to the rectal mucosa, leading to irritation, ulceration, or necrosis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h5)

question: What nursing action should be performed immediately after removing the flatus tube?

options.A: Check the patient's blood pressure
options.B: Insert a new tube into the urethra
options.C: Clean and dry the perianal area
options.D: Administer a strong oral laxative

explanation: Cleaning the perianal area removes any residual lubricant or discharge, ensuring skin integrity and patient comfort. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h5)

question: Which of the following is a potential complication of prolonged flatus tube placement?

options.A: Abnormal stiffening of the knee joints
options.B: Sudden enlargement of the thyroid gland
options.C: Permanent hearing loss in both ears
options.D: Pressure necrosis of the rectal mucosa

explanation: Leaving a tube in the rectum too long puts constant pressure on the tissue, cutting off blood supply and causing tissue death. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h6)

question: Which detail is most important to include in the nursing documentation after the procedure?

options.A: The color of the bedsheets on the patient's bed
options.B: The names of all visiting family members present
options.C: The amount and character of gas or stool expelled
options.D: The exact brand name of the lubricant used

explanation: Documenting what was expelled helps the healthcare team evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention in relieving abdominal distention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T11#GNS212_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a gastric lavage on a patient?

options.A: To measure daily digestive enzyme production in the pancreas
options.B: To provide long-term nutritional support for unconscious patients
options.C: To relieve chronic constipation by clearing the lower bowels
options.D: To remove ingested poisons from the stomach before they are absorbed

explanation: Gastric lavage acts as an emergency washing technique specifically targeted at flushing out harmful substances from the upper gastrointestinal tract before systemic absorption takes place. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is the timing of gastric lavage crucial after a toxic ingestion?

options.A: Nurse fatigue prevents safe tube insertion after the first hour
options.B: Substances leave the stomach quickly and enter the intestines within hours
options.C: The stomach lining becomes permanently closed off after two hours
options.D: Lavage fluid reacts dangerously with most drugs if delayed too long

explanation: Once toxins pass through the pylorus into the small intestine, washing out the stomach no longer retrieves the substance because absorption happens rapidly in the intestines. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for gastric lavage?

options.A: Consuming a small amount of liquid plant fertilizer
options.B: Ingestion of strong corrosive alkali acids
options.C: A mild overdose of over-the-counter paracetamol
options.D: Swallowing a non-toxic household plastic toy

explanation: Corrosive substances severely damage tissue, meaning the mechanical friction of a lavage tube can easily cause an esophageal or gastric perforation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h2)

question: A patient arrives in the emergency ward after drinking kerosene. What is the main danger if a nurse performs gastric lavage?

options.A: Instant calcification of stomach contents
options.B: Chemical pneumonia from aspiration into the lungs
options.C: Complete blockage of the large intestine
options.D: Severe permanent staining of the tooth enamel

explanation: Hydrocarbons have very low viscosity and easily slip into the respiratory tract during lavage, causing severe, life-threatening lung inflammation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h2)

question: Why is a large-bore tube used for gastric lavage instead of a standard small feeding tube?

options.A: To make it easier for the nurse to push fluid deep into the small intestines
options.B: To ensure the fluid goes directly into the respiratory airway for safety
options.C: To allow pill fragments and food pieces to pass out without blocking the tube
options.D: To prevent the patient from experiencing any gag reflex during insertion

explanation: Small tubes easily clog with partially digested food or pill debris, rendering the wash ineffective; large-bore tubes provide a clear channel for thick debris to escape. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h3)

question: What is the primary reason for keeping a functioning suction apparatus nearby during a gastric lavage setup?

options.A: To suck out blood from the esophagus before the tube goes in
options.B: To clear the airway immediately if the patient vomits or aspirates
options.C: To pump air into the stomach and inflate it for better viewing
options.D: To clean the outside of the rubber tube after the procedure ends

explanation: Vomiting is a common reflex during lavage, and immediate suction is critical to keep the airway clear and prevent aspiration pneumonia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why must an endotracheal tube with an inflated cuff be placed in an unconscious patient before gastric lavage?

options.A: To keep the patient's mouth open wide during tube insertion
options.B: To measure the exact temperature of the lavage fluid
options.C: To deliver extra oxygen straight to the stomach lining
options.D: To protect the airway and stop fluid from entering the lungs

explanation: Unconscious patients lose their protective swallowing and gag reflexes, so a cuffed airway tube creates a physical barrier against aspiration of stomach washings. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h4)

question: What baseline assessment is most critical to perform and record before starting a gastric lavage?

options.A: Abdominal skin turgor and color tone
options.B: Recent dietary history for the past week
options.C: Vital signs and neurological status
options.D: Detailed psychological background history

explanation: Recording baseline vitals and mental status allows the nurse to monitor for rapid changes caused by toxin absorption or procedural complications like vagal stimulation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h4)

question: In which position should a patient be placed during a gastric lavage to reduce safety risks?

options.A: Left lateral position with the head lowered slightly
options.B: Flat on the back with legs raised high in the air
options.C: Sitting completely upright straight in a hard chair
options.D: Right lateral position with the head elevated high

explanation: The left lateral Trendelenburg position keeps the stomach contents pooled away from the pylorus and promotes safe drainage away from the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h5)

question: When should the nurse stop the repeating cycles of fluid instillation and drainage during a gastric lavage?

options.A: When the collection bucket is half filled with fluid
options.B: When exactly one hour has passed on the clock
options.C: When the returned lavage fluid runs completely clear
options.D: When the patient asks for a glass of cold water

explanation: The wash cycles continue until the fluid coming back out is completely clear of toxins, pills, or debris, indicating the stomach is empty. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why is activated charcoal often instilled right before the lavage tube is removed?

options.A: To lubricate the tube so it slips out of the throat without friction
options.B: To stimulate normal bowel movements and speed up total digestion
options.C: To neutralize any acidic cleaning fluids remaining in the stomach wall
options.D: To catch and bind any remaining toxin particles left behind in the gut

explanation: Charcoal binds tightly to residual toxins that escaped the physical washing process, preventing them from entering the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which nursing documentation detail is essential after finishing a gastric lavage session?

options.A: The brand name and factory serial number of the lavage tube
options.B: Total amounts of fluid put in and taken out of the stomach
options.C: The exact weight of the patient measured in kilograms
options.D: The name of the family member who gave consent for care

explanation: Recording fluid balance prevents water intoxication or electrolyte imbalances, confirming that the nurse recovered roughly what was instilled. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h6)

question: During a gastric lavage, a patient suddenly turns cyanotic, coughs hard, and has a drop in oxygen saturation. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Ask the patient to take deep breaths through their nose
options.B: Stop the procedure immediately and suction the airway
options.C: Instill more wash fluid to clear out any remaining blockages
options.D: Remove the protective endotracheal tube right away

explanation: These signs point to fluid aspiration into the lungs, requiring an immediate halt to fluid instillation and clearing of the airway to restore breathing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h7)

question: What complication can happen if large amounts of plain tap water are used for lavage in young children?

options.A: Instant calcification of leftover food particles inside the gut
options.B: Dangerous drops in blood sodium levels known as hyponatremia
options.C: Sudden spikes in blood pressure throughout the body
options.D: Permanent hardening of the muscular walls of the stomach

explanation: Plain water lacks electrolytes, and when absorbed in large volumes across the stomach lining, it dilutes blood sodium and causes dangerous water intoxication. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the main goal of a rectal washout?

options.A: To measure the exact core body temperature
options.B: To administer liquid nutrition directly to the colon
options.C: To permanently cure chronic lower back pain
options.D: To completely cleanse the lower bowel using fluid cycles

explanation: Think of a rectal washout as a thorough internal clean. It uses repeated cycles of fluid to wash out stubborn stool and debris from the lower colon. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h1)

question: How does a rectal washout mostly differ from a regular cleansing enema?

options.A: It uses larger fluid volumes and cycles to thoroughly wash the lower colon
options.B: It is used exclusively to treat severe upper respiratory infections
options.C: It is only performed by surgeons in the operating theatre
options.D: It relies entirely on oral medications rather than rectal tubes

explanation: While a normal enema gives a quick flush, a rectal washout uses back-and-forth filling and draining cycles for a much deeper clean. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h1)

question: Which children's condition often needs rectal washouts before surgery?

options.A: Hirschsprung's disease
options.B: Acute appendicitis
options.C: Congenital heart failure
options.D: Infantile jaundice

explanation: In Hirschsprung's disease, a part of the baby's bowel lacks the nerves to push stool out. Washouts are safely used to clear things out before surgery! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h2)

question: A patient has a stubborn, hard mass of stool that normal enemas can't shift. What procedure is best here?

options.A: A rectal washout
options.B: An intravenous fluid bolus
options.C: A nasogastric tube insertion
options.D: An oral laxative challenge

explanation: When standard enemas aren't strong enough to break up severe blockages, a rectal washout provides the extra mechanical help needed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h2)

question: When should you definitely NOT perform a rectal washout?

options.A: A stable history of controlled high blood pressure
options.B: Temporary loss of appetite for two days
options.C: Recent bowel surgery with an active anastomosis
options.D: Mild chronic constipation in an elderly adult

explanation: Never force fluid into a fresh surgical connection (anastomosis)! The pressure could cause it to break open, leading to dangerous leaks. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h3)

question: What is a major risk when using large amounts of plain tap water for a washout?

options.A: Permanent damage to the upper respiratory tract
options.B: Water intoxication and severe hyponatremia
options.C: Sudden spikes in systemic blood pressure
options.D: Rapid development of iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Plain water can pass through the bowel wall into the bloodstream, diluting vital body salts and causing a dangerous drop in sodium levels. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which fluid is normally used for a washout to keep body salts balanced?

options.A: Hypertonic glucose
options.B: Plain tap water
options.C: Undiluted hydrogen peroxide
options.D: Normal saline

explanation: Normal saline is isotonic, meaning it matches body fluids and prevents dangerous shifts of water and salt across the bowel wall. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why do we position the patient in the left lateral Sims' position for a rectal washout?

options.A: It follows the natural anatomical curve of the lower colon
options.B: It prevents the patient from falling asleep during the task
options.C: It completely stops normal peristaltic movement in the gut
options.D: It keeps the patient's head elevated above the heart level

explanation: The lower part of the colon curves down toward the left side, making the left lateral position the smoothest and easiest way to insert the tube. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why should the fluid bag be kept at a low height during a washout?

options.A: To ensure a gentle, low-pressure gravity flow into the bowel
options.B: To speed up the chemical reaction of the irrigating fluid
options.C: To prevent the fluid inside the container from evaporating
options.D: To allow the nurse to check the temperature of the solution

explanation: Keeping the bag low prevents high pressure, protecting the delicate walls of the patient's intestine from accidental injury. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h5)

question: What should you do right away if your patient feels sharp belly cramps while you are running the fluid?

options.A: Stop the flow immediately until the cramp passes
options.B: Ignore the symptom as a normal expected reaction
options.C: Raise the fluid container higher to finish quickly
options.D: Push the rectal tube deeper into the sigmoid colon

explanation: Cramping means the bowel is filling up too fast! Always pause the flow and let the patient relax before starting again. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h5)

question: What is a common sign of vagal nerve irritation during rectal procedures?

options.A: Uncontrollable muscle spasms in the legs
options.B: Rapid spikes in body temperature
options.C: Sudden loss of visual acuity
options.D: Sudden bradycardia and dizziness

explanation: The rectum is very close to the vagus nerve. If it gets irritated, it can cause the heart rate and blood pressure to drop suddenly, making the patient dizzy. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h6)

question: Why is checking the net fluid balance important after a rectal washout?

options.A: To calculate the exact caloric intake of the patient
options.B: To make sure the patient is not retaining excessive fluid
options.C: To verify the total operating room expenses for the day
options.D: To determine how much medication to give orally

explanation: Comparing how much fluid went in versus how much came out helps you make sure the patient isn't holding onto too much water. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the most crucial detail to write in your nursing notes after a washout?

options.A: The favorite food of the patient's family
options.B: The volume and appearance of the fluid returned
options.C: The weather conditions outside the hospital
options.D: The exact brand name of the lubricant used

explanation: Always document what came out! Recording the amount and look of the return proves that the procedure worked and was safe. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h7)

question: What should you do if you notice fresh, bright red bleeding from the rectum after a washout?

options.A: Report the finding to the physician immediately
options.B: Document it as a completely normal expected result
options.C: Administer a stronger oral laxative dose to the patient
options.D: Wait twenty-four hours to see if it stops on its own

explanation: Bright red blood means there might be a small injury or tear in the lining. Always let the doctor know right away so it can be checked. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is the name for the surgical opening of the large intestine onto the belly wall?

options.A: A catheter
options.B: A stoma
options.C: An incision
options.D: A fistula

explanation: Great job! A stoma is simply the surgically created opening of the bowel onto the tummy surface where waste leaves the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why do doctors most commonly perform a colostomy?

options.A: To permanently cure long-term constipation without changing diet
options.B: To bypass or remove a diseased or damaged part of the bowel
options.C: To allow direct medicine administration into the bloodstream
options.D: To increase the length of the small intestine for better food absorption

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like severe infection, injury, or cancer mean we need to safely divert waste away from a sick section of the large intestine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which type of colostomy usually gives the most firm and solid stool?

options.A: Transverse colostomy
options.B: Sigmoid colostomy
options.C: Loop colostomy
options.D: Ascending colostomy

explanation: You got it! Because a sigmoid colostomy sits near the very end of the colon, the body has absorbed lots of water, leaving solid stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h2)

question: What decides how thick or watery a colostomy stool will be?

options.A: The anatomical location of the stoma along the large intestine
options.B: The amount of physical exercise the patient does every day
options.C: The time of day the patient eats their main meal
options.D: The exact brand of the appliance pouch the patient wears

explanation: Exactly! Stool gets thicker the longer it travels through the colon because more water is absorbed along the way. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is the normal, healthy look of a newly made intestinal stoma?

options.A: Pink to brick-red
options.B: Bright yellow or green
options.C: Dark purple to black
options.D: Pale white or gray

explanation: Correct! A healthy stoma is packed with tiny blood vessels, which gives it a nice moist, pink to brick-red color. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h3)

question: During a routine check, what does a pale, dusky, or blue-purple stoma tell you?

options.A: Inadequate blood supply to the stoma tissue
options.B: Normal healing after belly surgery
options.C: Too much fluid intake by the patient
options.D: A properly sealed ostomy appliance

explanation: Spot on. Color changes like blue, purple, or paleness mean blood flow is blocked or low—this is a true surgical emergency! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h3)

question: Why must the hole on the skin barrier be measured to fit just a tiny bit larger than the stoma?

options.A: To allow for the natural shrinking of the stoma over many years
options.B: To prevent the barrier from rubbing against and injuring the stoma tissue
options.C: To give extra space for air to circulate under the pouch
options.D: To make it easier to empty liquid waste from the bottom

explanation: You nailed it! Cutting the opening slightly larger protects the delicate stoma tissue from painful friction while keeping the skin safe. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h4)

question: You are getting ready to put a new colostomy bag on a patient. What is the right first step for the skin?

options.A: Rub a thick layer of oily moisturizing lotion to soften the skin
options.B: Scrub the area hard with an alcohol-based antiseptic
options.C: Dust the moist skin heavily with a scented powder
options.D: Clean the skin gently with warm water and pat it completely dry

explanation: Correct! The skin needs to be clean and totally dry so the adhesive barrier can stick securely without leaking. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which foods are most likely to cause a blockage in a patient with a colostomy?

options.A: Corn, nuts, and popcorn
options.B: Cooked carrots and soft pumpkin
options.C: Applesauce and plain yogurt
options.D: Plain rice and boiled potatoes

explanation: Spot on! Foods with tough hulls, skins, or hard fibrous bits don't digest easily and can get stuck right inside the stoma. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which of these foods should a patient expect to cause extra gas and strong odor?

options.A: Plain steamed rice
options.B: Boiled white chicken
options.C: Beans and onions
options.D: White toast and butter

explanation: You got it! Certain sulfur-rich or fermentable foods naturally lead to more tummy gas and stronger stoma smells. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h5)

question: What do we call a colostomy problem where the bowel telescopes out and the stoma becomes way too long?

options.A: Retraction
options.B: Hernia
options.C: Necrosis
options.D: Prolapse

explanation: Correct! A prolapse happens when extra bowel pushes out through the stoma site, making it stick out much further than normal. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is a parastomal hernia in a patient with a colostomy?

options.A: Total loss of blood flow leading to dark, dead tissue at the stoma tip
options.B: Chemical skin burns caused by leaked digestive juices
options.C: Complete blockage of the bowel by tough food particles
options.D: A loop of intestine pushing through a weakened belly wall muscle near the stoma

explanation: Spot on! A parastomal hernia is a weak spot in the muscle around the stoma that lets tummy contents bulge out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h6)

question: Why do we encourage a new colostomy patient to start practicing bag changes early?

options.A: To prove the patient doesn't need emotional counseling anymore
options.B: To make the surgical belly cut heal much faster
options.C: To help the hospital nurses finish their heavy daily chores
options.D: To build self-confidence and lower worry about caring for themselves at home

explanation: You nailed it! Practicing with a nurse nearby helps patients beat their fears and master the skills they need to be independent. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h7)

question: What emotional feeling do patients adjusting to a new stoma most commonly experience?

options.A: Complete indifference to physical changes
options.B: Immediate excitement to rush back to work
options.C: Angry behavior toward medical staff
options.D: Body image disturbance and anxiety

explanation: Spot on. Adjusting to a changed body appearance and worrying about leaks or smells can easily cause stress and emotional upset. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is the main job of the nephrons in the kidneys?

options.A: Transporting urine directly to the urethra
options.B: Storing urine until it leaves the body
options.C: Pumping blood through the lower back
options.D: Filtering the blood to form urine

explanation: You've got this! Nephrons are the tiny working units inside your kidneys that clean your blood and make urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h1)

question: What is the main difference between the ureters and the urethra?

options.A: Ureters store urine, while the urethra filters waste products from the bloodstream
options.B: Ureters and urethra perform the exact same task on opposite sides of the pelvis
options.C: Ureters carry urine from kidneys to the bladder, while the urethra carries urine outside the body
options.D: Ureters pump urine out of the body, while the urethra connects the kidneys directly to the outside

explanation: Think of ureters as the pipes coming down from the kidneys to the bladder, and the urethra as the final exit tube to the outside world! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h1)

question: What do we call pain or a burning feeling when passing urine?

options.A: Retention
options.B: Dysuria
options.C: Incontinence
options.D: Hematuria

explanation: Dysuria is just the medical word for painful or burning urination. Great term to keep in your clinical vocabulary bag! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h2)

question: A patient suddenly feels a strong need to pee and leaks a little before reaching the toilet. What is this called?

options.A: Urinary incontinence
options.B: Hematuria
options.C: Renal failure
options.D: Urinary retention

explanation: Incontinence simply means losing control of urine flow. You will see this a lot in clinical rotations! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h2)

question: When checking for urinary retention, what does a nurse feel for in the lower belly?

options.A: A firm, rounded bladder above the pubic bone
options.B: Soft, empty folds of skin near the belly button
options.C: Warm fluid moving freely inside the intestines
options.D: A hard, pulsing mass on the left side

explanation: When urine gets trapped (retention), the bladder fills up and feels like a firm dome right above the pubic bone. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h3)

question: Why do doctors order a urine culture after a test shows an infection?

options.A: To find the exact type of bacteria and the best antibiotic to treat it
options.B: To check if the kidneys are filtering red blood cells properly
options.C: To measure the exact total volume of urine produced in twenty-four hours
options.D: To scan the bladder walls for structural tears or tumors

explanation: A regular test tells us there's an infection, but a culture helps us pick the exact right drug to knock it out! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h3)

question: Tracking a patient's fluid intake and output mainly helps you evaluate what?

options.A: Lung capacity and oxygen levels
options.B: Muscle strength in the lower limbs
options.C: Kidney function and hydration status
options.D: The patient's daily calorie intake

explanation: Checking what goes in versus what comes out is a brilliant way to see if the kidneys are doing their job and if the patient is well-hydrated. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h4)

question: A patient on a bedpan is struggling to urinate while lying flat. What should you try first?

options.A: Assist the patient into a more natural, upright sitting position
options.B: Restrict all fluid intake for the rest of the day
options.C: Insert an indwelling catheter immediately without further delay
options.D: Administer a strong diuretic medication by mouth

explanation: Gravity and a normal sitting posture help relax the muscles, making it much easier to pass urine naturally. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h4)

question: Where should a urinary drainage bag always hang relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Below the level of the bladder
options.B: Flat on the floor next to the bed
options.C: Above the level of the bladder
options.D: Level with the patient's chest

explanation: Always keep it lower than the bladder! Gravity keeps the urine flowing away from the body and stops nasty germs from creeping back up. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h5)

question: Which of these is unsafe when caring for a patient with an indwelling catheter?

options.A: Keeping the drainage bag below the level of the bladder
options.B: Cleaning the perineal area and catheter tubing daily
options.C: Disconnecting the tubing frequently to let the patient walk easier
options.D: Removing the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed

explanation: Never break that closed system! Opening the tubing lets bacteria waltz right into the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the main goal of teaching Kegel exercises to someone with urinary incontinence?

options.A: To strengthen the pelvic floor muscles supporting the bladder
options.B: To relax the abdominal wall during a physical exam
options.C: To stretch the ureters and widen the urinary tract
options.D: To increase total daily urine production in the kidneys

explanation: Kegels tone up those pelvic floor muscles, giving the patient much better control over when they go. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h6)

question: How does bladder retraining help a patient with urge incontinence?

options.A: It numbs the bladder nerves permanently using special exercises
options.B: It trains the bladder to hold increasing amounts of urine by voiding on a set timetable
options.C: It empties the bladder continuously so the patient never feels any sensation
options.D: It stops the kidneys from producing urine during the night hours

explanation: Following a set bathroom schedule helps calm the bladder down and slowly helps it hold more urine over time. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h6)

question: What is the main sign of acute urinary retention?

options.A: Slow, painless loss of small amounts of urine all day
options.B: Sudden and painful inability to pass urine
options.C: Total absence of urine production by the kidneys
options.D: Constant burning pain while urinating frequently

explanation: Acute retention happens quickly and hurts a lot because the bladder fills up fast and cannot empty. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h1)

question: How is chronic urinary retention different from acute urinary retention?

options.A: It involves painful spasms of the ureters.
options.B: It causes complete kidney shutdown right away.
options.C: It develops slowly and is often painless.
options.D: It only happens to younger female patients.

explanation: Because chronic retention builds up gradually, the bladder stretches out slowly over time, so the patient usually doesn't feel severe, sudden pain. Great job thinking it through! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h1)

question: Which common condition causes physical blockage and urinary retention in older men?

options.A: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.B: Glomerular nephritis
options.C: Chronic kidney failure
options.D: Urinary tract infection

explanation: An enlarged prostate gland squeezes the pipe (urethra), making it physically hard for urine to flow out of the bladder. Keep up the great practice! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h2)

question: A patient taking a strong muscle relaxant suddenly cannot pee. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The medication dissolved the bladder lining.
options.B: The patient drank too much water too quickly.
options.C: The drug caused a sudden kidney infection.
options.D: The medication weakened the bladder muscle contraction.

explanation: Certain drugs can make the bladder muscle too weak to squeeze hard enough for you to empty it. Don't worry, pharmacology gets easier with practice! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h2)

question: What does 'overflow incontinence' mean when talking about urinary retention?

options.A: Passing large amounts of clear urine every hour
options.B: Total loss of bladder control due to a spinal injury
options.C: Leaking small amounts of urine because the bladder is too full
options.D: Involuntary loss of urine only during physical exercise

explanation: When a full bladder is stretched to the max, small amounts just leak past the tight valve simply because the pressure is too high. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h3)

question: Which physical finding shows a patient has a very full, distended bladder?

options.A: A firm, rounded swelling above the pubic bone that sounds dull when tapped
options.B: Severe swelling and redness around the external genitalia
options.C: A soft, sunken abdomen that is completely silent to stethoscope listening
options.D: Sharp pain radiating from the flank down to the groin area

explanation: A full bladder feels like a firm bump just above the pubic bone, and fluid makes a dull sound when you tap on it. Assessment skills unlocked! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h3)

question: What is the main reason nurses use a portable bladder scanner at the bedside?

options.A: To measure the exact blood flow to the bladder wall
options.B: To estimate the volume of urine left inside the bladder
options.C: To check the chemical composition of the urine
options.D: To look for physical stones inside the kidneys

explanation: A bladder scanner uses harmless sound waves to check how much urine is trapped inside without sticking anything in. Super handy clinical tool! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h4)

question: Why do doctors order a serum creatinine test for a patient with long-term urine retention?

options.A: To determine if the patient has a urinary tract infection
options.B: To evaluate how well the liver is producing proteins
options.C: To check if urine backup is damaging kidney function
options.D: To measure the level of sugar in the circulating blood

explanation: When urine cannot get out, the pressure travels backward up to the kidneys, which can slow down their filtering work. Checking creatinine helps us catch kidney stress early! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h4)

question: What is the immediate first step to help a patient with acute urinary retention?

options.A: Administering a potent diuretic to stop urine production
options.B: Sending the patient home with oral muscle relaxants
options.C: Starting strong intravenous antibiotics for infection
options.D: Inserting a urinary catheter to drain the bladder

explanation: The urgent goal is to relieve that dangerous pressure right away by passing a catheter to empty the bladder. Spot on! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h5)

question: Why might a nurse need to drain a huge, overfilled bladder in stages instead of all at once?

options.A: To ensure the drainage bag does not overflow onto the floor
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling a sudden surge of happiness
options.C: To give the laboratory technicians enough time to test the urine
options.D: To prevent rapid decompression injury and bleeding inside the bladder

explanation: Draining a massive amount of urine too fast can cause the blood vessels inside the bladder wall to burst and bleed. Slow and steady is safer here! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h5)

question: Which nursing action is most important when putting in a urinary catheter?

options.A: Inflating the retention balloon before inserting the tube
options.B: Lubricating only the very tip of the drainage collection bag
options.C: Applying heavy pressure to the lower abdomen while pushing
options.D: Maintaining strict sterile technique throughout the procedure

explanation: Keeping everything super sterile stops nasty germs from hitching a ride up into the bladder and causing a painful infection. Safety first in clinicals! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h6)

question: What is 'post-obstructive diuresis' after getting a catheter?

options.A: A sudden total stop in urine production caused by kidney failure
options.B: An infection caused by bacteria entering the open urinary tract
options.C: A painful spasm of the bladder muscles around the catheter
options.D: A temporary phase where the kidneys produce a massive amount of urine

explanation: Once the blockage is gone, the kidneys can overcompensate for a bit and flush out lots of fluid. You're learning real hospital scenarios! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h6)

question: What complication happens most easily when urine stays stuck in the bladder for too long?

options.A: High blood pressure in the arms
options.B: Severe stomach ulcers
options.C: Urinary tract infection
options.D: Lower limb bone fractures

explanation: Stagnant urine is like a breeding ground where bacteria love to multiply in the warm bladder environment. Regular emptying keeps infections away! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h7)

question: Which of these instructions is WRONG for a patient going home with a catheter?

options.A: Wash your hands thoroughly before touching the tubing or drainage bag
options.B: Secure the catheter tubing to your thigh to prevent pulling
options.C: Keep the drainage bag higher than the level of your bladder at all times
options.D: Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day unless restricted

explanation: The bag must ALWAYS stay below the bladder! If it's higher, gravity will make the urine flow right back inside the patient. Great catch! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the basic medical definition of urinary incontinence?

options.A: The involuntary loss of urine
options.B: An infection in the urinary tract
options.C: Painful and burning urination
options.D: The complete inability to produce urine

explanation: Urinary incontinence specifically refers to the accidental or involuntary leaking of urine from the bladder. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why is it risky to think of urine leaking as just a normal part of getting older?

options.A: It causes severe skin rashes in all elderly people
options.B: It stops patients from seeking helpful treatment
options.C: It automatically leads to kidney failure
options.D: It means the bladder has completely stopped working

explanation: When patients or their families think leaking is just normal aging, they keep quiet and miss out on treatments that could really help them feel better. Great insight for a nurse! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h1)

question: What is the primary name of the smooth muscle that forms the wall of the urinary bladder?

options.A: Detrusor muscle
options.B: Sphincter muscle
options.C: Urethral muscle
options.D: Pelvic floor muscle

explanation: The detrusor muscle makes up the main muscular wall of the bladder and contracts to push urine out during urination. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h2)

question: What must the urinary sphincters do so that normal urination can happen?

options.A: They must contract tightly
options.B: They must relax
options.C: They must spasm
options.D: They must thicken

explanation: For urine to flow out smoothly, the urinary sphincters need to open up (relax) at the same time the bladder muscle squeezes. Teamwork! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h2)

question: Which type of incontinence happens when a person leaks urine while coughing, sneezing, or lifting heavy objects?

options.A: Stress urinary incontinence
options.B: Functional urinary incontinence
options.C: Urge urinary incontinence
options.D: Overflow urinary incontinence

explanation: Stress incontinence is triggered by physical movements that suddenly push down on the bladder when pelvic support is weak. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h3)

question: A patient with severe arthritis cannot walk to the bathroom or manage clothing buttons fast enough, resulting in accidental urine loss. What type of incontinence is this?

options.A: Overflow incontinence
options.B: Urge incontinence
options.C: Functional incontinence
options.D: Stress incontinence

explanation: Functional incontinence occurs when the urinary tract is fine, but physical or environmental barriers stop the person from reaching the toilet. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h3)

question: Which of these is a very common cause of weakened pelvic floor muscles in women?

options.A: Vaginal childbirth
options.B: Regular aerobic exercise
options.C: Eating high-fiber foods
options.D: Drinking too much water

explanation: The stretching and hard work of vaginal delivery can tire out or stretch the pelvic floor support structures, making leaks more likely later on. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h4)

question: How do conditions like a stroke often lead to urinary incontinence?

options.A: They cause the kidneys to produce excessive amounts of urine
options.B: They permanently shrink the overall size of the bladder
options.C: They destroy the lining of the urinary tract
options.D: They disrupt nerve signals between the brain and the bladder

explanation: Our brain and spinal cord need to talk to the bladder to control peeing. When a stroke damages those pathways, that communication gets mixed up. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is the main reason for having a patient keep a bladder diary?

options.A: To record fluid intake, leakage episodes, and voiding patterns
options.B: To list all daily medications and food allergies
options.C: To track blood pressure changes throughout the day
options.D: To measure daily weight fluctuations and calorie consumption

explanation: A bladder diary gives you a clear, real-life picture of when the patient drinks, when they leak, and how often they go. Super helpful for planning care! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why do nurses routinely check a urine sample (urinalysis) when evaluating new urine leaks?

options.A: To check for a urinary tract infection
options.B: To determine the patient's blood type
options.C: To screen for prostate cancer markers
options.D: To measure exact kidney filtration rates

explanation: Infections can irritate the bladder and cause sudden leaks. Ruling out an infection is always a smart first step in nursing assessment. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the common name for exercises designed to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles?

options.A: Aerobic exercises
options.B: Range of motion drills
options.C: Kegel exercises
options.D: Isometric stretches

explanation: Kegel exercises involve repeatedly contracting and relaxing the pelvic floor muscles to improve structural support and urinary control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: A patient with urge incontinence is starting a bladder retraining program. What is the right instruction to give them?

options.A: Stop doing pelvic floor exercises completely
options.B: Hold urine for as long as possible until severe pain occurs
options.C: Drink large amounts of water only right before bedtime
options.D: Urinate on a strict schedule, slowly increasing the time between trips

explanation: Bladder retraining uses a set schedule that slowly stretches out the time between bathroom breaks, helping the bladder hold more without sudden spasms. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: Which type of medication is often given to calm down an overactive bladder?

options.A: Anticholinergics
options.B: Antibiotics
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Diuretics

explanation: Anticholinergic drugs block the nerve signals that tell the bladder muscle to squeeze too often. It helps the bladder relax! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the main goal of sling surgery done for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: To provide physical support under the urethra
options.B: To increase the total urine production rate
options.C: To shrink an enlarged prostate gland
options.D: To relax the overactive detrusor muscle

explanation: A sling creates a tiny hammock of mesh or tissue to lift and support the urethra so it stays shut when abdominal pressure spikes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is a very common skin problem caused by unmanaged urine leaks over time?

options.A: Incontinence-associated dermatitis
options.B: Chronic skin pigmentation loss
options.C: Diffuse bacterial cellulitis of the face
options.D: Severe subcutaneous fat necrosis

explanation: When urine sits on the skin, it breaks down the natural skin barrier, causing painful redness and irritation called incontinence-associated dermatitis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h8)

question: Why does ongoing urinary incontinence put a patient at higher risk for urinary tract infections?

options.A: Skin breakdown allows bacteria to travel directly into the bloodstream
options.B: Frequent urination washes away all the normal protective cells
options.C: Moisture and residual urine create an environment where bacteria multiply easily
options.D: Absorbent pads permanently stop the kidneys from filtering waste

explanation: Sticking around in lingering moisture gives bacteria a cozy place to grow and easily find their way into the urinary tract. Good skin care and hygiene prevent this! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h8)

question: What main event causes urine to leak out in stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Complete blockage of the urethra
options.B: An overactive detrusor muscle spasm
options.C: A sudden urinary tract infection
options.D: Sudden physical pressure on the bladder

explanation: You've got this! Stress incontinence happens when sudden physical pressure—like coughing, laughing, or lifting—pushes urine out because the bladder pressure beats the urethra's grip. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h1)

question: Why do people often get confused by the word 'stress' in stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: They believe it is caused by mental exhaustion
options.B: They assume it only happens during high-intensity sports
options.C: They confuse it with neurological distress
options.D: They think it relates to emotional anxiety rather than physical pressure

explanation: It's an easy mix-up! In this case, 'stress' means physical force or pressure on your organs, not emotional stress or worry. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which muscle group acts like a supportive hammock at the bottom of the pelvis?

options.A: Rectus abdominis muscles
options.B: Detrusor muscle group
options.C: Levator ani muscle group
options.D: Abdominal wall muscles

explanation: Think of the levator ani as a strong sling or hammock holding all your pelvic organs neatly in place. Great job! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the main job of the urethral sphincter in normal bladder control?

options.A: To sense when the bladder is completely full
options.B: To push urine out of the bladder during voiding
options.C: To stay contracted and maintain a tight seal against urine leakage
options.D: To stretch when the bladder fills with urine

explanation: The urethral sphincter acts like a tight valve, staying closed to keep urine inside until you're ready to use the bathroom. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h2)

question: What happens to the bladder and urethra during 'urethral hypermobility' when a patient coughs?

options.A: The bladder instantly shrinks in size
options.B: The urethral sphincter locks tightly shut to block flow
options.C: The detrusor muscle contracts with too much force
options.D: The bladder and urethra drop downward due to weak support

explanation: When the pelvic tissues are a bit weak, coughing causes the bladder and urethra to sag downward instead of staying firmly in place. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: What does 'intrinsic sphincter deficiency' mean?

options.A: Blockage of urine flow by the prostate gland
options.B: Damage or weakness of the urethral sphincter muscle itself
options.C: A temporary infection lining the urinary tract
options.D: Overactivity of the main bladder muscle

explanation: Simply put, the valve muscle itself has lost some of its strength and can no longer seal tightly on its own. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: A patient with long-term severe bronchitis has a higher risk for which type of urine leakage?

options.A: Overflow incontinence due to a blocked prostate
options.B: Stress incontinence due to repeated pressure from coughing
options.C: Urge incontinence due to bladder muscle irritation
options.D: Functional incontinence due to immobility

explanation: Constant coughing creates repeated downward pressure on the pelvic floor, which can wear down its support over time. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a common risk factor for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Obesity and excess body weight
options.B: Menopause and decreased estrogen levels
options.C: Frequent high-fluid intake throughout the day
options.D: Vaginal childbirth and multiple pregnancies

explanation: Drinking plenty of water is healthy! The real risk factors involve things that weaken pelvic support, like childbirth, hormonal shifts, or heavy pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h4)

question: Why is a urinalysis always done when checking for stress incontinence?

options.A: To check kidney function and filtration rates
options.B: To measure the exact amount of residual urine left in the bladder
options.C: To test the patient for diabetes and high blood sugar levels
options.D: To rule out a urinary tract infection that can cause similar symptoms

explanation: Infections can mimic incontinence by irritating the bladder, so checking the urine first helps doctors make a clear diagnosis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: What is the purpose of a cough stress test during a physical checkup?

options.A: To check if coughing triggers a bladder spasm
options.B: To test the strength of the patient's respiratory muscles
options.C: To measure lung capacity while the patient lies flat
options.D: To observe if physical pressure causes immediate urine leakage

explanation: By asking the patient to cough, the clinician can watch directly to see if pressure causes any accidental leakage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: A nurse is teaching a patient how to do Kegel exercises correctly. What is the key instruction?

options.A: Contract the pelvic floor muscles as if trying to stop the flow of urine
options.B: Squeeze the abdominal and thigh muscles tightly while holding your breath
options.C: Push down gently as if having a bowel movement
options.D: Flex the buttocks and hips until your pelvis rises off the bed

explanation: Spot on! Kegels are all about squeezing those pelvic floor muscles—just like you're pausing your urine stream mid-flow, without squeezing your tummy or thighs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which lifestyle change helps the most in managing stress incontinence?

options.A: Drinking less than two cups of fluid per day
options.B: Achieving and maintaining a healthy body weight
options.C: Eliminating all forms of physical exercise completely
options.D: Increasing daily intake of carbonated beverages

explanation: Shedding extra pounds takes a huge amount of constant pressure off the pelvic floor muscles. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is the main surgical option used to treat severe stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Widening the urethral opening with a stent
options.B: Placing a supportive sling under the urethra
options.C: Implanting an artificial kidney to filter urine
options.D: Removing the lower portion of the bladder

explanation: A surgical sling acts like a little hammock or seatbelt underneath the urethra to keep it from dropping when you move. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h7)

question: Why are pills and medications rarely the main treatment for stress incontinence?

options.A: Surgical options and pelvic therapy target the mechanical cause much more effectively
options.B: Medications for stress incontinence always cause permanent kidney damage
options.C: Pills are unable to dissolve inside the human digestive tract
options.D: Doctors prefer lifestyle changes because drugs are illegal for this use

explanation: Since stress incontinence is a physical, mechanical problem of loose support, fixing it requires physical strengthening or surgery rather than drugs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h7)

question: What is a very common emotional or social challenge for patients with chronic stress incontinence?

options.A: False belief that they are pregnant
options.B: Uncontrolled aggressive behavior toward caregivers
options.C: Severe memory loss and cognitive decline
options.D: Social isolation and anxiety about public leaks

explanation: The fear of leaking in public can make patients feel embarrassed, causing them to stay home and miss out on social life. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h8)

question: Which skin problem happens most often when urinary incontinence is left untreated?

options.A: Deep pressure ulcers over the shoulder blades
options.B: Dry, scaly skin patches across the upper arms
options.C: Perineal dermatitis and breakdown from moisture
options.D: Fungal rashes spreading across the face and chest

explanation: When skin stays in contact with urine too long, the moisture breaks down the skin barrier and causes painful irritation or rashes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h8)

question: What is the main job of a medical bougie?

options.A: To deliver high-flow oxygen therapy
options.B: To monitor internal body temperature
options.C: To navigate or explore narrow passages
options.D: To permanently remove tissue masses

explanation: Think of a bougie as a flexible guide. It's a slender tool used mainly to safely guide instruments or explore tight, narrow areas in the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h1)

question: How is a dilator different from a regular feeding tube?

options.A: A dilator is specifically designed to stretch tight strictures.
options.B: A dilator is only used for temporary fluid drainage.
options.C: A feeding tube contains a built-in cutting blade.
options.D: A feeding tube is rigid while dilators are always soft.

explanation: While feeding tubes are for giving food, dilators are specially sized and shaped to gently stretch out narrowed tubes in the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which type of bougie uses heavy mercury or tungsten fillings so gravity helps it slide down?

options.A: Rigid urethral sounds
options.B: Eder-Puestow metal springs
options.C: Hurst or Maloney bougies
options.D: Pneumatic balloon dilators

explanation: Hurst and Maloney bougies have heavy tips filled with things like mercury or tungsten. This extra weight lets gravity help guide them smoothly down the esophagus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h2)

question: When would a doctor choose a balloon dilator instead of a solid bougie?

options.A: When radial, controlled pressure is needed under direct visualization
options.B: When the patient is completely unconscious in the emergency room
options.C: When the stricture requires heavy metal weight to force it open
options.D: When direct tactile feedback through the hands is the only goal

explanation: Balloon dilators use air or fluid to expand outward evenly in all directions, and doctors usually place them using an endoscope so they can see what they're doing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h2)

question: What is a very common cause of esophageal strictures (narrowing) that need dilation?

options.A: Chronic acid reflux disease
options.B: Benign gastric hypersecretion
options.C: Excessive dietary fiber intake
options.D: Congenital throat widening

explanation: When stomach acid keeps splashing up into the esophagus over a long time, it irritates the tissue, causes scarring, and makes the passage narrow. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h3)

question: A patient comes to the clinic struggling with a weak urine stream after a past pelvic injury. What procedure are they most likely getting ready for?

options.A: Gastric tube insertion
options.B: Urethral dilation
options.C: Endotracheal intubation
options.D: Esophageal manometry

explanation: Pelvic trauma can cause scarring in the urethra (the urine passage), leading to a tight spot or stricture that needs to be gently stretched out to restore normal flow. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h3)

question: Why is it important to check blood clotting lab results before a dilation procedure?

options.A: To assess the risk of bleeding from potential mucosal tears
options.B: To check if the patient has an active systemic infection
options.C: To calculate the exact dosage of local anesthetic required
options.D: To determine the correct size of the dilator to be used

explanation: Stretching tight tissues can sometimes cause minor scratches or tears. If a patient has poor blood clotting, those little tears could turn into heavy bleeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h4)

question: What is a key nursing duty right before an upper GI (throat and esophagus) dilation?

options.A: Administering a heavy oral laxative to clear the esophagus
options.B: Ensuring removable dental appliances are taken out
options.C: Instructing the patient to drink large volumes of water
options.D: Placing a heavy weighted blanket over the patient's chest

explanation: False teeth or removable dental plates can easily pop loose and block the airway during throat procedures, so they must always be taken out first. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h4)

question: During a sedated dilation procedure, what are the most critical vital signs for the nurse to keep watching?

options.A: Oxygen saturation and heart rate
options.B: Peripheral skin temperature
options.C: Capillary refill time
options.D: Bowel sound frequency

explanation: Because the patient is sedated and instruments are working near their airway or GI tract, monitoring their breathing (oxygen) and heart rate is top priority for safety. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why does the nurse need to keep track of the exact sizes of the dilators used during the procedure?

options.A: To determine how long the patient must stay NPO afterward
options.B: To prevent the doctor from using metal instruments twice
options.C: To monitor the progressive widening of the stricture safely
options.D: To bill the hospital pharmacy for disposable plastic items

explanation: Doctors stretch the tissue step-by-step, going up in size very gradually. Tracking the sizes helps the team avoid jumping up in diameter too fast, which protects the patient from tearing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h5)

question: What is the most serious and dangerous complication that can happen after a gastrointestinal dilation?

options.A: Mild throat irritation
options.B: Temporary hiccups
options.C: Visceral perforation
options.D: Dry mouth sensation

explanation: Perforation means a tear or hole gets poked through the wall of the esophagus or bowel. It's a medical emergency that happens if the tissue tears during stretching. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: Which sign should immediately make a nurse suspect a post-procedure perforation after an esophageal dilation?

options.A: A slight drop in blood pressure after resting
options.B: Sudden severe chest pain and rising heart rate
options.C: Mild sore throat when swallowing saliva
options.D: Low-grade nausea from mild residual sedation

explanation: If a patient suddenly gets severe, worsening chest pain and a fast heart rate (tachycardia), it's a huge red flag that there might be a tear leaking into the chest cavity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: What warning signs should you teach a patient to report right away after going home from a dilation?

options.A: Mild scratchy throat sensation
options.B: Slight fatigue from the sedation
options.C: Temporary change in voice pitch
options.D: Fever and severe worsening pain

explanation: A little throat scratchiness is totally normal after having tools passed down. But fever and severe, getting-worse pain mean infection or a tear, which need immediate care. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the best diet to start a patient on right after they go home from an esophageal dilation?

options.A: Consume only dry cracker products for the first three days
options.B: Maintain strict total parenteral nutrition for one full week
options.C: Resume regular heavy solid meals immediately to test the stretch
options.D: Start with clear liquids and slowly advance to soft foods

explanation: The lining of the esophagus needs a little time to calm down. Starting with clear liquids gives it a break before slowly moving up to soft, easy-to-swallow foods. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a nasogastric tube?

options.A: To provide continuous oxygen to the lungs
options.B: To deliver liquid nutrients directly into the stomach
options.C: To drain excess urine from the bladder
options.D: To remove harmful toxins from the bloodstream

explanation: A nasogastric tube is passed through the nose into the stomach to supply food and medications when a patient cannot swallow safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do we prefer feeding through a stomach tube rather than an IV drip when the patient's digestive system is working?

options.A: It keeps the gut healthy and stops bad bacteria from moving around
options.B: It is completely painless and requires no monitoring
options.C: It completely eliminates the risk of aspiration
options.D: It takes only a few minutes to set up every morning

explanation: Using the normal digestive tract keeps the gut lining strong and stops dangerous bacteria from escaping into the bloodstream. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: What position should your patient be in when you are inserting a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Lying on the left side (Sims position)
options.B: Sitting upright in high Fowler's position
options.C: Head tilted downward (Trendelenburg)
options.D: Flat on the back (supine)

explanation: Sitting the patient straight up aligns their throat nicely, making it much easier and safer to slide the tube down. Great job! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: A patient needs a nasogastric tube but has a history of a severe skull fracture at the base of the head. What should you do?

options.A: Perform the insertion quickly while the patient is asleep
options.B: Proceed with normal insertion using extra lubrication
options.C: Consult the doctor because putting a tube through the nose is risky here
options.D: Insert the tube through the mouth instead without checking

explanation: A basilar skull fracture means the bone near the brain is damaged, so passing a tube through the nose could accidentally enter the brain. Always check with your senior or doctor! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: What kind of lubricant should you put on a nasogastric tube before sliding it in?

options.A: Sterile mineral oil
options.B: Antiseptic surgical gel
options.C: Water-soluble lubricant
options.D: Petroleum jelly ointment

explanation: We use a water-soluble jelly so that if a tiny bit accidentally goes into the lungs, the body absorbs it safely without causing pneumonia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why do nurses use a pH testing strip when checking a newly placed nasogastric tube?

options.A: To test how acidic the fluid pulled from the tube is
options.B: To check the expiry date of the food formula
options.C: To check if the patient has a stomach ulcer
options.D: To measure the sugar level in the feed

explanation: Stomach acid is very sour! Testing the pH of fluid from the tube helps us confirm the tip is safely inside the acidic stomach, not the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h3)

question: When measuring for a nasogastric tube using the NEX method, what does the letter 'E' stand for?

options.A: Earlobe
options.B: Epiglottis
options.C: Esophagus
options.D: Eyebrow

explanation: NEX stands for Nose to Earlobe to Xiphoid process. It's the classic bedside trick to guess how far the tube needs to go! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: What should you do immediately if your patient starts coughing violently and turning blue while you are passing a tube?

options.A: Ask the patient to take a deep breath and swallow
options.B: Push the tube down faster to clear the way
options.C: Stop pushing and pull the tube right back out
options.D: Inject water to wash it down

explanation: Coughing and turning blue (cyanosis) means the tube has mistakenly slipped into the windpipe instead of the food pipe. Pull it back out immediately and let them catch their breath! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is considered the absolute best (gold standard) way to confirm a nasogastric tube is in the right spot?

options.A: Measuring the length of tubing left outside the nose
options.B: Listening for air sounds over the belly with a stethoscope
options.C: Checking for water drops inside the clear plastic tube
options.D: Abdominal X-ray

explanation: An X-ray gives us clear visual proof that the tip is sitting comfortably in the stomach before we start any feeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which pH test result tells you that the nasogastric tube is successfully resting in the stomach?

options.A: A high reading of 9.0
options.B: An alkaline reading of 8.5
options.C: A reading of 4.0
options.D: A neutral reading of 7.0

explanation: Stomach contents are acidic, so a low pH (like 4.0 or lower) is a strong sign that your tube is in the right place. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: How much water is normally used to flush a nasogastric tube before and after giving feeds?

options.A: 200 milliliters
options.B: 30 milliliters
options.C: 5 milliliters
options.D: 500 milliliters

explanation: A quick flush of about 30 mL of clean water keeps the tube clear of leftover formula and prevents blocks without flooding the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why must the head of the bed stay raised for at least 30 minutes after a tube feeding?

options.A: To let gravity keep the food down and prevent it from flowing into the lungs
options.B: To help the stomach absorb food much faster
options.C: To keep the patient awake and chatty
options.D: To ensure the nurse can easily check the vital signs

explanation: Keeping the bed elevated uses gravity to stop the food from flowing back up into the throat and causing aspiration pneumonia. Safety first! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the best way to stop a nasogastric tube from getting blocked?

options.A: Changing the tube to a smaller size every week
options.B: Adding cooking oil to every feed
options.C: Flushing it with warm water before and after feeds and drugs
options.D: Blowing air down the tube twice a shift

explanation: Regular water flushes wash away sticky food and medicine residue before they can dry up and clog your tube. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: A patient on continuous tube feeding has a red, sore spot right on the edge of their nostril. What should you do?

options.A: Clean the skin, apply a protective cream, and tape the tube to a slightly different spot
options.B: Put thick gauze padding under the tube
options.C: Leave the tape loose so the tube rubs freely
options.D: Pull the tube out permanently and stop feeding

explanation: Protecting the skin and shifting the pressure point gives the sore spot a chance to heal while keeping the patient fed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: What instruction should you give your patient right before you pull out a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Cough gently to clear the throat
options.B: Swallow hard several times
options.C: Blow air out forcefully through the mouth
options.D: Take a deep breath and hold it

explanation: Holding the breath closes the windpipe, keeping the lungs safe from breathing in any leftover fluid as the tube slides out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h8)

question: Why should you always look closely at the tip of the nasogastric tube right after removing it?

options.A: To measure the patient's stomach length
options.B: To check how much stomach acid is left on it
options.C: To make sure the whole tube came out in one piece and nothing broke off inside
options.D: To check if the patient chewed on the plastic

explanation: Checking the removed tube ensures no broken bits were left behind in the patient's stomach or food pipe. A quick glance saves a lot of trouble! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of a urinary catheter?

options.A: To deliver fluids directly into the kidneys
options.B: To prevent the formation of kidney stones
options.C: To drain urine from the bladder
options.D: To measure the capacity of the ureters

explanation: A catheter is a flexible tube inserted through the urethra specifically to allow urine to drain out of the bladder when a patient cannot do so naturally. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why do nurses try to avoid using a urinary catheter unless it's truly necessary?

options.A: It brings a high risk of introducing bacteria into the urinary tract
options.B: It is extremely painful for every patient who receives one
options.C: It requires surgical removal by a urologist
options.D: It permanently weakens the bladder muscles within hours

explanation: You got it! Because catheters bypass the body's natural defenses, they easily let germs in, making infections a big risk. That's why we only use them when we really have to. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Which body feature makes female patients more likely to get a catheter-related urinary tract infection?

options.A: A wider urethral opening
options.B: A larger bladder capacity than males
options.C: An absence of a muscular sphincter
options.D: A shorter urethra close to the anal opening

explanation: Spot on! The female urethra is quite short and sits very close to the anus, giving bacteria a short and easy path straight into the bladder. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h2)

question: How is putting a catheter into a male patient different from a female patient?

options.A: It lacks a sphincter muscle, making insertion completely effortless
options.B: It opens directly into the abdominal cavity
options.C: It is longer and has natural curves that require careful maneuvering
options.D: It is wider, requiring much larger catheter sizes

explanation: Exactly! The male urethra is longer and travels through the prostate, so you have to gently navigate a few natural bends during the procedure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h2)

question: What keeps a Foley catheter securely in place inside the bladder?

options.A: A flexible wire attached to the belly wall
options.B: External adhesive tape on the thigh
options.C: Natural suction created by the drainage bag
options.D: A water-filled balloon at the tip

explanation: Correct! Once the catheter is inside the bladder, sterile water fills a tiny balloon at the end, acting like an anchor so it doesn't slip out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h3)

question: When would you choose a simple straight catheter instead of a permanent Foley catheter?

options.A: When the patient is unconscious in the intensive care unit
options.B: When a patient needs periodic bladder emptying without a permanent bag
options.C: When the patient has a severe urethral blockage
options.D: When long-term continuous monitoring of hourly urine output is required

explanation: You nailed it! Straight catheters are popped in to drain the bladder and taken right back out, which lowers the risk of infection compared to leaving a tube in all day. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h3)

question: Which of these is a valid medical reason to put in an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: General urinary incontinence with no skin breakdown
options.B: To make things easier for nursing staff during busy night shifts
options.C: Accurate hourly urine output measurement in a critically ill patient
options.D: The patient prefers not to get up to use the toilet at night

explanation: Spot on! We only use indwelling catheters when there is a strong medical need, like closely tracking kidney function in very sick patients. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h4)

question: A patient with an enlarged prostate hasn't peed in eight hours and has severe lower belly pain. What should you do first?

options.A: Encourage the patient to drink more water to flush the system
options.B: Administer a mild oral water pill (diuretic)
options.C: Prepare equipment for urinary catheterisation as ordered
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the lower back and wait two hours

explanation: Great thinking! When urine gets trapped because of an enlarged prostate, getting it out with a catheter right away relieves the painful pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h4)

question: What common allergy must you always check for before using a standard urinary catheter?

options.A: Sulfonamides
options.B: Aspirin
options.C: Penicillin
options.D: Latex

explanation: You got it! Many standard catheters contain latex, which can cause severe allergic reactions. Always check your patient's history and grab a silicone one if they are allergic! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h5)

question: Why is it helpful to feel (palpate) the patient's lower belly before doing a catheterisation?

options.A: To stimulate the urethral sphincter to open
options.B: To check if the kidneys are infected
options.C: To measure the exact length of the urethra
options.D: To confirm the presence of a full, distended bladder

explanation: Spot on! Feeling the lower belly (suprapubic area) lets you check if urine is actually backed up and trapped in the bladder, confirming you really need to catheterize. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h5)

question: In what direction should you clean a female patient's perineal area before putting in a catheter?

options.A: From back to front
options.B: From side to side vigorously
options.C: From front to back
options.D: In a circular outward motion

explanation: Correct! Always wipe from front to back (toward the back passage) so you don't drag any germs from the anus toward the urethral opening. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h6)

question: In male patients, why must you push the catheter a bit further in even after urine first starts to flow?

options.A: To clear any leftover bacteria sitting in the outer urethra
options.B: To make the drainage bag fill up much faster
options.C: To stretch the urethral muscle and reduce future spasms
options.D: To ensure the retention balloon is completely inside the bladder before inflating it

explanation: Spot on! If you inflate the balloon while it's still stuck in the narrow urethra instead of the open bladder, it causes terrible pain and injury. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h6)

question: Where must the urine drainage bag be placed at all times?

options.A: Level with the patient's hips
options.B: Resting directly on the patient's chest
options.C: Hanging from the top of the bed frame
options.D: Below the level of the bladder

explanation: You got it! Gravity is our friend here. Keeping the bag lower than the bladder keeps urine flowing smoothly downward and stops dirty urine from washing back up. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h7)

question: What is the main danger of disconnecting the catheter tubing from the drainage bag?

options.A: It breaks the closed system and lets bacteria enter
options.B: It triggers severe allergic reactions to the plastic
options.C: It causes immediate permanent damage to the urethral sphincter
options.D: It creates high pressure that bursts the balloon
