explanation: CPR acts as an artificial pump to circulate remaining oxygen in the blood to the brain and heart until advanced help arrives. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is early initiation of CPR critical during a cardiac arrest?

options.A: It prevents permanent brain damage by maintaining minimal perfusion
options.B: It eliminates the need for any medications or defibrillation later
options.C: It completely cures the underlying heart disease causing the arrest
options.D: It guarantees the immediate return of spontaneous heartbeat

explanation: Brain cells begin to die within minutes without oxygen, so starting compressions quickly buys vital time. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h1)

question: What is the very first link in the adult chain of survival?

options.A: Early recognition and call for help
options.B: Immediate high-quality chest compressions
options.C: Rapid use of an automated external defibrillator
options.D: Advanced life support by paramedics

explanation: Recognizing an emergency and activating the emergency response system quickly starts the entire rescue process. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which link in the chain of survival specifically addresses restoring a shockable heart rhythm?

options.A: Post-cardiac arrest care
options.B: Rapid defibrillation
options.C: Early recognition and prevention
options.D: Advanced life support medication

explanation: Defibrillation delivers an electric shock to treat life-threatening rhythms like ventricular fibrillation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the very first step a nurse must take before starting CPR on a fallen person?

options.A: Attach the automated external defibrillator
options.B: Ensure the surrounding scene is safe
options.C: Open the airway with a head-tilt maneuver
options.D: Check the patient for a pulse

explanation: Rescuers must check for hazards like fire, live wires, or traffic so they do not become victims themselves. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient collapses in the hospital ward. What should the nurse do right after confirming the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally?

options.A: Leave the patient to find a doctor
options.B: Call for help and activate the emergency response
options.C: Administer rescue breaths through a mask
options.D: Start chest compressions immediately

explanation: Activating the emergency team immediately ensures that extra hands and equipment like an AED are on the way. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which maneuver is standardly used to open the airway of an unresponsive patient without a neck injury?

options.A: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
options.B: Jaw-thrust maneuver
options.C: Chest compression sweep
options.D: Recovery position roll

explanation: The head-tilt, chin-lift lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat to clear the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why should a nurse avoid pressing heavily on the soft tissue under the chin during the chin-lift maneuver?

options.A: it triggers an automatic reflex to vomit
options.B: It can push the tongue backward and block the airway
options.C: It forces stomach contents up into the mouth
options.D: It can cause permanent damage to the patient's jawbone

explanation: Pressing on the soft neck tissue collapses the airway instead of opening it, preventing proper breathing assessment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is the recommended compression rate per minute for performing adult CPR?

options.A: 80 to 100 compressions
options.B: 140 to 160 compressions
options.C: 60 to 80 compressions
options.D: 100 to 120 compressions

explanation: A rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute mimics an effective heart rate and maximizes blood flow. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why is complete chest recoil important between individual chest compressions?

options.A: It keeps the patient's lungs inflated with fresh air
options.B: It gives the rescuer's tired arm muscles a chance to rest
options.C: It prevents the ribs from fracturing during compressions
options.D: It lets the heart chambers fill back up with blood

explanation: If the chest does not recoil fully, the heart cannot refill properly, making the next compression useless. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h5)

question: What must all rescuers do immediately before an AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Clear the patient and ensure nobody is touching them
options.B: Check the patient's carotid pulse
options.C: Perform two quick rescue breaths
options.D: Turn the device power switch off

explanation: Rescuers must step away so the shock affects only the patient and does not injure anyone else nearby. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h6)

question: An AED has just been brought to the side of an adult patient in cardiac arrest. What is the very first thing the nurse should do with it?

options.A: Press the shock button
options.B: Apply the electrode pads
options.C: Check the battery level
options.D: Turn the AED on

explanation: Turning the device on activates the audio and visual prompts that guide the rest of the rescue steps. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid performing blind finger sweeps when clearing an airway obstruction?

options.A: It causes severe bleeding inside the oral cavity
options.B: It can push the foreign object deeper into the airway
options.C: It breaks the patient's lower teeth and gums
options.D: It triggers an irreversible spasm of the vocal cords

explanation: Blind finger sweeps risk jamming a loose object further down the throat, making the blockage worse. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h7)

question: Which of the following is a common physical complication of performing high-quality chest compressions?

options.A: Severe internal bleeding
options.B: Rupture of the liver
options.C: Puncture of both lungs
options.D: Rib or sternal fractures

explanation: Compressing the chest hard enough to circulate blood frequently causes fractured ribs, which is an accepted risk. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h7)

question: When is it appropriate for a nurse to stop performing CPR?

options.A: When trained medical help arrives and takes over care
options.B: When family members ask the team to take a break
options.C: As soon as the nurse feels physically tired and sweaty
options.D: After five minutes of continuous compressions without a pulse

explanation: CPR continues until the patient recovers, professionals take over, or clear signs of death appear. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h8)

question: Why is accurate timing and documentation following a cardiac arrest event so crucial?

options.A: It replaces the need for a verbal handover to the intensive care unit
options.B: It guarantees insurance payment for hospital equipment used
options.C: It is required only if the resuscitation attempt was completely successful
options.D: It provides a clear legal and clinical record of the emergency timeline

explanation: Detailed notes record the exact interventions and timing, which helps evaluate patient outcomes and guide future care. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h8)

question: What is the main use of an oxygen tent in children's wards?

options.A: Administering aerosolized chemotherapy drugs
options.B: Providing mechanical ventilation for adult trauma
options.C: Delivering controlled oxygen in pediatric care
options.D: Treating severe burn wounds in sterile isolation

explanation: Oxygen tents are super helpful in pediatric wards! They let us give steady oxygen to toddlers and young kids who might keep pulling off a standard face mask. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why do nurses tuck the edges of an oxygen tent firmly under the mattress?

options.A: To anchor the heavy metal frame securely to the bed
options.B: To prevent the loss of the enriched oxygen atmosphere
options.C: To completely block all ambient light from the room
options.D: To keep the pediatric patient from crawling out of bed

explanation: Tucking the plastic sides under the mattress creates a nice seal so the oxygen stays inside with the child instead of leaking out into the room. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which young patient is most likely to need an oxygen tent?

options.A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in an adult
options.B: Severe diabetic ketoacidosis
options.C: Decompensated heart failure with fluid overload
options.D: Acute bronchiolitis in a toddler

explanation: Spot on! Respiratory infections like bronchiolitis make it hard for little ones to breathe, making an oxygen tent a great choice to help them recover. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h2)

question: Why is an oxygen tent not the best choice when a patient needs very high oxygen levels?

options.A: The plastic material is chemically unable to hold high pressure
options.B: Opening the canopy to care for the patient causes the oxygen level to drop
options.C: Adults consume too much oxygen for the tent motor to handle
options.D: High oxygen levels melt the seals of the canopy frame

explanation: Every time you unzip or open the tent to check on the child or feed them, the trapped oxygen escapes quickly into the room air. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h2)

question: What is the job of the cooling unit attached to an oxygen tent?

options.A: Filtering bacteria out of the room air supply
options.B: Preventing the inside of the tent from becoming too hot
options.C: Increasing the pressure of oxygen inside the canopy
options.D: Freezing the oxygen gas into liquid form for storage

explanation: Because plastic tents trap body heat and humidity, the cooling unit is essential to keep the little patient comfortable and cool. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h3)

question: Which piece of equipment attaches to the oxygen source to control gas flow into the tent?

options.A: Pulse oximeter
options.B: Flowmeter
options.C: Infusion pump
options.D: Suction canister

explanation: The flowmeter is your best friend for regulating the exact liters per minute of oxygen going into the tent system. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why do we use high flow rates when running an oxygen tent?

options.A: To create positive pressure that forces fluid out of the lungs
options.B: To dry out excess moisture accumulating on the plastic
options.C: To speed up the cooling unit's internal fan blades
options.D: To flush out exhaled carbon dioxide and maintain oxygen levels

explanation: High gas flow keeps fresh oxygen coming in while pushing out the carbon dioxide the child breathes out, keeping the air safe inside. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h4)

question: What happens to the oxygen inside the tent right after a nurse opens the canopy?

options.A: It spikes to one hundred percent
options.B: It drops significantly
options.C: It converts into carbon dioxide
options.D: It remains completely unchanged

explanation: Opening the tent lets the oxygen rush out into the wider room, causing a temporary drop in concentration until you seal it back up. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h4)

question: A nurse finds a toddler in an oxygen tent with damp clothes and cool skin. What should you do first?

options.A: Change the damp clothing and check the tent cooling settings
options.B: Administer an antipyretic medication for potential fever
options.C: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the wall flowmeter
options.D: Remove the child from the tent and place a nasal cannula

explanation: Moisture inside the tent can get clothes wet, which makes the child cold fast. Dressing them in dry clothes keeps them cozy and safe! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which assessment is most important to keep checking for a patient in an oxygen tent?

options.A: Respiratory rate and work of breathing
options.B: Bowel sounds and abdominal circumference
options.C: Daily weight and fluid intake volume
options.D: Neurological reflex response scores

explanation: Since oxygen tents treat breathing problems, always keep a close eye on how hard the child is working to breathe and their breathing rate. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why are electrical toys not allowed inside or near an oxygen tent?

options.A: They interfere with the digital pulse oximeter readings
options.B: They can create small sparks that ignite the oxygen-rich air
options.C: They consume too much electricity from the hospital wall outlet
options.D: They make too much noise and frighten the pediatric patient

explanation: Oxygen feeds fire! Even a tiny spark from a toy motor can cause a serious fire hazard in an oxygen-rich space. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which of these items is NOT safe to use inside an oxygen tent?

options.A: Silicone pacifiers used to soothe an infant
options.B: Plastic washable containers for holding water
options.C: Woolen blankets that generate static electricity
options.D: Cotton hospital gowns worn by the young patient

explanation: Woolen blankets create static sparks from friction, which is a major danger around high oxygen levels. Stick to cotton or safe materials instead! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is a very common result of high humidity inside an oxygen tent?

options.A: Water condensation building up on the inner plastic walls
options.B: Sudden dropping of the room's overall humidity level
options.C: Freezing of the oxygen gas into solid ice crystals
options.D: Complete drying out of the patient's nasal passages

explanation: All that moisture in the enclosed space naturally turns into water droplets on the cooler plastic walls of the tent. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h7)

question: How can a nurse best stop a child in an oxygen tent from getting chilled by moisture?

options.A: Frequently dry the child's skin and change damp linens
options.B: Turn off the humidifier completely during the night shift
options.C: Apply petroleum jelly over the child's entire body
options.D: Open the canopy wide for one hour every morning

explanation: Regularly swapping out damp clothes and blankets prevents the moisture from chilling the child's body. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h7)

question: What should you check first if the oxygen level inside the tent suddenly goes down?

options.A: The hospital's central pharmacy inventory
options.B: The expiration date of the plastic canopy
options.C: Tubing connections and canopy edge seals
options.D: The patient's blood pressure and heart rate

explanation: Always check your basics first! Loose tubing or edges that popped out from under the mattress are usually why oxygen is leaking out. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h8)

question: What should you do right away if the tent's cooling motor stops working during your shift?

options.A: Notify maintenance, monitor temperature closely, and provide temporary ventilation
options.B: Wrap the child in extra heavy blankets to prevent shivering
options.C: Increase the oxygen flow rate to maximum to cool the air down
options.D: Disconnect the oxygen entirely and move the child to a regular chair

explanation: A broken cooler will cause heat to build up inside. Call maintenance right away, keep an eye on the temperature, and fan or ventilate carefully to keep the child safe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the main goal of giving oxygen therapy with a face mask?

options.A: Permanently cure chronic respiratory diseases
options.B: Lower the patient's baseline body temperature
options.C: Maintain safe arterial oxygen saturation levels
options.D: Increase the patient's total body weight

explanation: You give extra oxygen mainly to keep the patient's blood oxygen in a safe range and stop their tissues from lacking air. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h1)

question: When would you choose a face mask instead of a nasal cannula for oxygen delivery?

options.A: When the patient only requires a very low flow rate of oxygen
options.B: When the patient refuses to have anything touching their face
options.C: When the patient is completely free of any respiratory distress
options.D: When the patient needs higher and more precise oxygen concentrations

explanation: Face masks cover both the nose and mouth, making them the go-to choice when a patient in distress needs a stronger, concentrated flow of oxygen. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why is a Venturi mask often chosen for patients with COPD?

options.A: It pumps high-pressure air directly into the stomach.
options.B: It allows the patient to eat and drink without removing it.
options.C: It delivers a precise and controlled concentration of oxygen.
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any humidification.

explanation: Venturi masks use clever color-coded adapters to give an exact percentage of oxygen, keeping vulnerable COPD patients safe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the purpose of attaching a humidifier bottle filled with sterile water to the oxygen setup?

options.A: Add pleasant artificial fragrances to the oxygen flow
options.B: Moisten dry medical gas to prevent mucous membrane irritation
options.C: Filter out all bacteria from the room air
options.D: Measure the exact blood pressure of the patient

explanation: Medical oxygen is very dry. Adding moisture protects the delicate lining of your patient's nose and throat from drying out and cracking. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h3)

question: Which piece of equipment do you need to safely connect an oxygen mask to a hospital wall supply?

options.A: Sphygmomanometer
options.B: Suction canister
options.C: Flowmeter
options.D: Glucometer strip

explanation: The flowmeter plugs into the wall outlet so you can easily control and measure the liters per minute flowing to the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h3)

question: What is a major safety rule you must enforce when a patient is receiving oxygen therapy?

options.A: Keep all open flames and smoking materials away from the area
options.B: Remove all metal objects from the entire hospital floor
options.C: Turn off all room lights to keep the oxygen cool
options.D: Keep the patient lying completely flat on their back at all times

explanation: Oxygen makes fires catch faster and burn much hotter! Always make sure sparks, matches, and cigarettes stay far away. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h4)

question: You are about to put an oxygen mask on an anxious patient. What is your best first nursing action?

options.A: Explain the procedure simply to reduce anxiety and calm the patient
options.B: Tie the mask straps as tightly as possible to prevent removal
options.C: Leave the room immediately and let the patient put the mask on alone
options.D: Administer a strong sedative drug without a doctor's order

explanation: Talking calmly to your patient builds trust, eases their panic, and helps them breathe much easier during the setup. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h4)

question: Why should you mold the metal strip of a face mask over the patient's nose bridge?

options.A: To increase the structural weight of the plastic device
options.B: To stop the patient from speaking to the nursing staff
options.C: To lock the patient's jaw in a closed position during sleep
options.D: To prevent oxygen from leaking upward into the patient's eyes

explanation: Molding the nose piece stops air from blowing into the eyes and drying them out, while ensuring the patient gets their full dose. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h5)

question: How often should you check the skin where an oxygen mask and its straps rest?

options.A: Only when the patient complains of severe bleeding
options.B: Regularly during routine shifts and care checks
options.C: Only once a week before the patient is discharged
options.D: Never, because oxygen masks do not touch the skin

explanation: Checking the skin often helps you catch early redness and prevents pressure sores from the plastic edges and elastic bands. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h6)

question: A patient on face mask oxygen suddenly drops in saturation and the tubing feels warm and static. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Normal adjustment of the lungs to high flow rates
options.B: A kink or blockage in the oxygen delivery tubing
options.C: The humidifier bottle being completely overfilled
options.D: An increase in the patient's physical activity level

explanation: If the tubing gets twisted or blocked, the oxygen stops flowing, causing saturation levels to drop fast. Always check the lines first! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h6)

question: What is a major danger of giving high-flow oxygen to a patient who retains carbon dioxide?

options.A: Rapid increase in the patient's daily fluid retention
options.B: Loss of the hypoxic drive, leading to respiratory depression
options.C: Sudden development of severe skin allergies on the face
options.D: Permanent discoloration of the nose and cheek tissues

explanation: Some chronic lung patients breathe because their oxygen is low. Giving too much oxygen can make their brain say 'we don't need to breathe anymore,' which is dangerous. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h7)

question: Which nursing action helps prevent skin breakdown caused by oxygen mask straps?

options.A: Apply strong medical adhesive tape directly to the forehead
options.B: Remove the mask permanently and stop all oxygen therapy
options.C: Place protective padding under pressure points and check skin often
options.D: Pull the elastic straps tighter so the mask never shifts

explanation: Padding shares the load evenly across the skin, and checking frequently lets you spot irritation before it turns into a wound. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T11#GNS212_U2_T11_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of tracheobronchial suctioning?

options.A: Removing secretions to keep the airway clear
options.B: Expanding collapsed lung alveoli directly
options.C: Measuring the exact lung capacity
options.D: Delivering high concentrations of oxygen

explanation: Suctioning is primarily performed to clear trapped mucus and fluids when a patient cannot cough them out independently. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why is suction applied intermittently rather than continuously during airway clearance?

options.A: To allow the suction machine time to build up mechanical pressure
options.B: To make sure the sterile catheter stays clean on the inside
options.C: To prevent severe damage to the airway lining and low oxygen levels
options.D: To give the nurse enough time to measure the suction gauge

explanation: Continuous suctioning pulls too much air out of the lungs and aggressively grips the delicate tissue inside the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: A patient with an endotracheal tube needs suctioning when which sign appears?

options.A: Warm, dry skin with pink nail beds
options.B: Audible or visible secretions in the airway tube
options.C: Deep, quiet breathing sounds in all lung fields
options.D: A normal, steady heart rate and blood pressure

explanation: Seeing or hearing mucus rattling in the tube tells the nurse the airway is partially blocked and needs clearing. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which condition is a clear contraindication for routine nasotracheal suctioning?

options.A: Severe bleeding disorders or severe nasal trauma
options.B: Needing a routine check of vital signs every four hours
options.C: A mild low-grade fever without respiratory changes
options.D: Being sleepy but easily waking up when spoken to

explanation: Passing a catheter through a damaged or bleeding nose can cause dangerous hemorrhage and further trauma. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the typical safe suction pressure range for an adult patient?

options.A: 500 to 600 mmHg
options.B: 10 to 20 mmHg
options.C: 80 to 120 mmHg
options.D: 200 to 300 mmHg

explanation: Pressures between 80 and 120 mmHg are strong enough to remove thick mucus without causing excessive trauma to the airway lining. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: You are preparing a suction catheter for an adult patient with an artificial airway. What is the rule of thumb for selecting the catheter size?

options.A: It must be the largest possible size that fits through the opening
options.B: It should always be a uniform size 14 French regardless of the tube
options.C: It should fill the entire inside of the tube to grab all the mucus
options.D: It should take up no more than half the inner diameter of the airway

explanation: Leaving enough open space around the catheter prevents a vacuum from forming inside the lungs, which would dangerously drop oxygen levels. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: Why is a patient hyperoxygenated right before undergoing tracheobronchial suctioning?

options.A: To force thick mucus plugs to dissolve and loosen up inside the lungs
options.B: To build up an oxygen reserve and prevent dangerous drops during the procedure
options.C: To test if the oxygen tank and flowmeter are working properly
options.D: To help the patient fall into a deep sleep so they feel no discomfort

explanation: Because the suction catheter temporarily removes air from the airway, extra oxygen beforehand protects the patient from sudden hypoxia. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is an important step when preparing a conscious patient for suctioning?

options.A: Explaining what will happen to reduce anxiety and fear
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill before starting
options.C: Telling them not to cough under any circumstances
options.D: Asking them to hold their breath until the procedure ends

explanation: Clear communication helps calm the patient, ensuring better cooperation and less panic during a vulnerable moment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the maximum recommended time for a single suction pass?

options.A: 3 to 5 minutes
options.B: 1 to 2 minutes
options.C: 30 to 45 seconds
options.D: 10 to 15 seconds

explanation: Limiting passes to 10 to 15 seconds prevents the patient from running out of oxygen and developing dangerous heart rhythms. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h5)

question: When should suction be applied as you insert the catheter into the artificial airway?

options.A: Never apply suction while inserting the catheter
options.B: Apply continuous suction the entire time you push it in
options.C: Apply suction only when the catheter hits the back of the throat
options.D: Apply suction in short bursts on the way down

explanation: Applying suction during insertion damages the delicate lining of the airway and removes helpful air; suction is only applied while withdrawing. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why might a patient experience a sudden dangerous drop in heart rate during suctioning?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood pressure from anxiety
options.B: Too much clean air rushing into the stomach
options.C: Stimulation of the vagus nerve in the airway
options.D: An allergic reaction to the sterile glove powder

explanation: The vagus nerve runs close to the airway and triggers a slowing of the heart rate when irritated by the suction catheter. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h6)

question: During suctioning, your patient's oxygen saturation drops rapidly and their heart rate becomes irregular. What is your very first action?

options.A: Document the normal finding and check the patient again in one hour
options.B: Quickly insert the catheter deeper to grab the remaining thick mucus
options.C: Turn up the wall suction pressure to finish the procedure faster
options.D: Stop suctioning immediately and provide oxygen via manual resuscitator

explanation: Safety comes first: stop the trauma, remove the negative pressure, and give the patient oxygen to recover. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which detail is essential to include when charting after suctioning a patient?

options.A: Color, consistency, and amount of the removed secretions
options.B: The exact brand name of the sterile gloves used
options.C: The name of the company that manufactured the suction machine
options.D: The room temperature at the moment of the procedure

explanation: Recording the characteristics of mucus gives vital clues about infection, hydration status, and overall lung health. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the best way to evaluate if the suctioning procedure was successful?

options.A: Ask the doctor to review the nursing notes at the end of the shift
options.B: Measure the weight of the empty suction canister on a scale
options.C: Listen to the patient's lung sounds and check oxygen levels
options.D: Confirm that the patient has fallen asleep comfortably

explanation: Checking lung sounds and oxygen saturation directly shows whether airway clearance improved breathing function. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the main job of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) during a cardiac arrest?

options.A: Provide mechanical chest compressions at a steady rate
options.B: Pump oxygen directly into the lungs of the patient
options.C: Measure the exact blood pressure of an unresponsive person
options.D: Deliver an electrical shock to reset an abnormal heart rhythm

explanation: Think of an AED as a smart device that checks the heart rhythm and gives a quick shock only when needed to get the heart beating right again. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is using an AED as quickly as possible so important during cardiac arrest?

options.A: It automatically contacts the local police department for help
options.B: It permanently cures any underlying heart disease causing the arrest
options.C: It replaces the need to ever perform chest compressions
options.D: Survival rates drop significantly with every minute that defibrillation is delayed

explanation: Every single minute counts! Without blood flow, the brain quickly loses oxygen, so acting fast truly saves lives. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which patient sign means you should grab and attach an AED right away?

options.A: Severe chest pain and heavy sweating
options.B: Confusion and mild shortness of breath
options.C: High fever and a rapid pulse rate
options.D: Unresponsiveness and no normal breathing

explanation: An AED is meant for sudden cardiac arrest. We look for someone who has collapsed, doesn't respond, and isn't breathing normally. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h2)

question: What happens if an AED is accidentally used on someone whose heart is beating normally?

options.A: The heart will instantly stop due to the excess electrical current
options.B: The device will analyze the rhythm and refuse to deliver a shock
options.C: The machine will automatically start delivering CPR compressions
options.D: The internal battery of the device will permanently burn out

explanation: Don't worry, AEDs are very smart! They scan the heart first and will block any shock if the heart rhythm is normal. They won't harm a healthy beat. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the job of the sticky adhesive pads that come with an AED?

options.A: Secure the patient firmly to the flat floor surface
options.B: Deliver a continuous supply of medical oxygen to the lungs
options.C: Transmit electrical current from the machine to the patient's heart
options.D: Measure the exact body temperature of the victim

explanation: The pads act as the bridge. They stick to the skin to read the heart rhythm and deliver the life-saving shock safely. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why should you regularly check the status indicator light on an AED machine?

options.A: To calibrate the internal thermometer for accurate skin readings
options.B: To measure how many shocks are left in the main computer processor
options.C: To ensure the voice volume is loud enough for a noisy room
options.D: To confirm that the internal battery and system components are operational

explanation: Routine checks make sure the machine is ready to work the exact second an emergency happens. Good nursing practice! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h3)

question: Where should you place the two AED pads on an adult patient's bare chest?

options.A: Center of the chest and middle of the back
options.B: Left side of the ribs and right side of the abdomen
options.C: Both shoulders near the neck collarbones
options.D: Upper right chest and lower left ribcage

explanation: Placing one pad on the upper right and the other on the lower left lets the electrical current flow diagonally right through the heart muscle. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is the very next thing you must do after the AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Check the carotid pulse for at least one full minute
options.B: Turn the machine off and wait for the ambulance crew
options.C: Remove the sticky pads and wipe the skin with alcohol
options.D: Resume chest compressions and CPR for two minutes

explanation: Right after a shock, don't wait—jump right back into CPR starting with chest compressions to keep blood moving! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h4)

question: How should you handle an implanted pacemaker lump when placing an AED pad?

options.A: Refuse to use the AED because pacemakers block all shocks
options.B: Place the pad at least one inch away from the device lump
options.C: Place the pad directly over the lump to boost the shock
options.D: Cut out the pacemaker wires before attaching the sticky pads

explanation: Keep the pad about an inch away from a pacemaker lump so the machine's energy goes into the heart instead of damaging the device. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h5)

question: What safety step is required if a patient experiencing cardiac arrest is lying in a puddle of water?

options.A: Turn off all nearby electrical appliances in the room
options.B: Double the number of chest compressions you deliver
options.C: Move the patient to a dry area and dry the chest
options.D: Place rubber mats under your own shoes while working

explanation: Water conducts electricity. Moving the patient to dry ground and wiping their chest ensures the shock goes through the heart, not out into the water. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h5)

question: What usually causes an AED to flash a 'Check Pads' error message?

options.A: The patient's heart rate is too fast for the machine to read
options.B: The rescuer is pressing the shock button at the wrong time
options.C: Loose cable connections or moisture on the patient's skin
options.D: The battery inside the computer unit is completely dead

explanation: If pads aren't sticking well or the skin is wet, the machine can't get a good connection. A quick dry and press usually fixes it! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h6)

question: What must you do immediately when the AED announces 'Movement Detected'?

options.A: Shake the patient harder to restart the heart rhythm
options.B: Unplug the machine and replace both electrode pads
options.C: Stop chest compressions and ensure everyone steps back
options.D: Increase the speed of rescue breaths being delivered

explanation: Movement—even from CPR—can trick the AED into reading the wrong thing. Always step back and stay clear while it analyzes. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h6)

question: What should you do with the AED pads if the patient suddenly wakes up and starts breathing?

options.A: Move both pads to the patient's back to keep the skin warm
options.B: Peel them off immediately and throw them in the trash
options.C: Leave the pads attached to the chest in case arrest recurs
options.D: Wipe them down with bleach and pack them in the box

explanation: Leave the pads on! A recovered patient can still slip back into cardiac arrest very quickly, and you want the AED ready to go. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why is placing an unconscious, breathing patient into the recovery position so important?

options.A: It keeps the airway clear and prevents aspiration of fluids
options.B: It stops involuntary muscle spasms in the arms and legs
options.C: It makes it easier to reapply the AED pads if needed
options.D: It lowers the patient's elevated blood pressure quickly

explanation: The recovery position uses gravity to keep the tongue and saliva from blocking the airway of someone who is knocked out. Safety first! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h7)

question: What is the main goal of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT)?

options.A: To calculate the correct medication dosage for the child
options.B: To perform a rapid, hands-off visual evaluation from the doorway
options.C: To measure the exact blood pressure and temperature
options.D: To listen carefully to heart murmurs with a stethoscope

explanation: You don't even need to touch the child right away! The PAT is a quick, visual tool you can use from the doorway to size up how sick a little one is. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: A child comes in with chest retractions, nasal flaring, and breathing very fast. Which part of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle does this show?

options.A: Circulation to the skin
options.B: Work of breathing
options.C: Appearance
options.D: Neurological status

explanation: Spotting retractions and nasal flaring tells you right away how hard the child is working to pull air in. That's all about their work of breathing! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is a slow heart rate (bradycardia) in a sick baby or child such a red flag?

options.A: It is a normal response to mild fever
options.B: It means the heart muscle is exceptionally strong
options.C: It proves the child is well-conditioned
options.D: It usually indicates impending cardiac arrest

explanation: Unlike adults who might have a slow heart rate because they are fit athletes, sick kids drop their heart rate when their body is failing and running out of oxygen. It's a serious warning sign! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What makes an infant's upper airway much easier to block compared to an adult's?

options.A: A larger tongue relative to the oral cavity
options.B: A much wider trachea and larynx
options.C: Complete rigidity of the upper airway cartilage
options.D: An absence of mucus glands in the pharynx

explanation: Babies have surprisingly large tongues for their little mouths! If their head isn't positioned quite right, that tongue can easily slide back and block their airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: When two rescuers are doing CPR on a child, what is the compression-to-ventilation ratio?

options.A: 5 compressions to 1 breath
options.B: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
options.C: 100 compressions to 5 breaths
options.D: 15 compressions to 2 breaths

explanation: When you have two people working together on a pediatric patient, you use a 15:2 ratio to get more rescue breaths into the child. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why is letting the chest spring all the way back up between compressions so important during CPR?

options.A: It gives the rescuer time to rest their arms
options.B: It lowers the child's body temperature
options.C: It prevents the ribs from fracturing
options.D: It allows blood to refill the heart chambers

explanation: Think of the heart like a sponge. When you push down, you squeeze blood out; when you let the chest recoil, it refills with fresh blood for the next push! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is a major danger of giving a child too many breaths during resuscitation?

options.A: Causing immediate permanent brain damage from too much oxygen
options.B: Lowering the child's heart rate into normal ranges
options.C: Preventing the lungs from ever collapsing
options.D: Increasing intrathoracic pressure and reducing blood return to the heart

explanation: If you bag a child too fast or too hard, you trap too much pressure inside their chest. That extra pressure actually blocks blood from flowing back to the heart. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why should you avoid tilting an infant's head too far back when opening their airway?

options.A: It completely stops spontaneous breathing
options.B: It always causes immediate cervical spine fractures
options.C: The flexible trachea can kink and cause an obstruction
options.D: It makes it impossible to check the pulse

explanation: An infant's windpipe is soft and flexible. If you tilt their head back too far (hyperextension), the airway actually kinks shut like a bent garden hose! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which sign tells you that a child's breathing problem is getting worse and turning into respiratory failure?

options.A: Slow, irregular breathing and cyanosis
options.B: An increase in spontaneous talking
options.C: Loud, powerful crying and high energy
options.D: Rapid, deep breathing with normal skin color

explanation: At first, a struggling child breathes super fast. But once their muscles get too tired, they slow down, breathe irregularly, and turn blue (cyanosis). That's a true emergency! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: A toddler arrives at the emergency unit suddenly drooling, making high-pitched breathing sounds (stridor), and very restless, but has no cough. What should you do first?

options.A: Keep the child calm and avoid invasive examinations
options.B: Immediately force the child to lie flat for an X-ray
options.C: Attempt to visualize the vocal cords with a tongue depressor
options.D: Administer oral fluids immediately to soothe the throat

explanation: This sounds like epiglottitis! If you upset or cry the child, their swollen airway can snap shut completely. Keep them calm in their mother's arms and don't force anything into their mouth. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: If a seriously ill child has a completely normal blood pressure reading, does that mean they are out of danger?

options.A: Fluid resuscitation is definitely not needed
options.B: The child is completely free from danger
options.C: Cardiac output is at its absolute maximum
options.D: The child may still be in compensated shock

explanation: Kids are amazing at squeezing their blood vessels tight to keep their blood pressure looking normal, even when they are crashing. A normal BP doesn't mean they aren't in shock! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard type of shock seen in children?

options.A: Cardiogenic shock
options.B: Distributive shock
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Metabolic shock

explanation: You'll hear about hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock in pediatrics—'metabolic shock' isn't one of the classic categories. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the most common heart rhythm seen when a child goes into cardiac arrest?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation with rapid response
options.B: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
options.C: Ventricular fibrillation
options.D: Asystole or pulseless electrical activity

explanation: Unlike adults who often arrest with a shockable rhythm like VF, children usually arrest after a long period of low oxygen, leading straight to asystole or PEA. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: During a pediatric resuscitation, how often should epinephrine be given?

options.A: Only after five defibrillation shocks
options.B: Every 3 to 5 minutes
options.C: Once every hour
options.D: Every 30 seconds

explanation: Epinephrine is a trusty emergency medication given every 3 to 5 minutes during a code to help keep blood flowing to the heart and brain. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is a major focus of care right after a child's heartbeat and breathing return (after ROSC)?

options.A: Discontinuing all cardiac and respiratory monitoring
options.B: Minimizing secondary brain injury and multi-organ damage
options.C: Withholding all fluids to prevent fluid overload
options.D: Allowing the child's body temperature to rise unchecked

explanation: Getting their pulse back is a huge win, but the job isn't done! Now we have to protect their organs—especially the brain—from further stress and damage. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)

question: Why is developing a fever especially dangerous for a child right after they recover from cardiac arrest?

options.A: It stops all medications from working
options.B: It automatically triggers another cardiac arrest
options.C: It increases the metabolic demand of the injured brain
options.D: It proves the resuscitation attempt failed entirely

explanation: When a child's brain is recovering from lack of oxygen, a fever forces it to work much harder and use up oxygen it simply doesn't have to spare. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)

question: Where does the actual exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide take place in the lungs?

options.A: Within the upper pharynx
options.B: Inside the main trachea
options.C: In the tiny alveoli
options.D: Through the vocal cords

explanation: Alveoli are surrounded by tiny blood vessels where oxygen and carbon dioxide easily pass back and forth. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h1)

question: What happens inside the chest cavity when the diaphragm muscle contracts during inhalation?

options.A: Chest volume increases and air is pulled inward
options.B: The lungs collapse due to increased internal pressure
options.C: Chest volume decreases and air is pushed outward
options.D: Air pressure inside the lungs becomes higher than outside

explanation: Contracting the diaphragm flattens it out, making the chest cavity bigger and creating a vacuum that draws air into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h1)

question: What is the normal resting breathing rate for a healthy adult in breaths per minute?

options.A: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
options.B: 25 to 35 breaths per minute
options.C: 5 to 10 breaths per minute
options.D: 40 to 50 breaths per minute

explanation: A healthy adult at rest normally breathes between 12 and 20 times every minute. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h2)

question: A patient is using their neck and shoulder muscles heavily to take every breath. What does this sign indicate?

options.A: The patient has a normal, healthy breathing pattern
options.B: The patient's lungs are expanding with minimal effort
options.C: The patient is in a deeply relaxed sleeping state
options.D: The patient is experiencing increased respiratory effort and distress

explanation: Using accessory muscles means the main breathing muscles need extra help because breathing has become difficult. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why might a patient with low oxygen levels first appear restless and confused?

options.A: Restlessness is a side effect of normal breathing
options.B: The patient's stomach is empty during the assessment
options.C: The patient is reacting to cold hospital room temperatures
options.D: The brain is sensitive to a shortage of oxygen

explanation: Brain tissue needs a constant, heavy supply of oxygen, so even mild shortages quickly cause mental changes like confusion or anxiety. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which of the following is considered a late sign of low oxygen levels in the body?

options.A: Mild restlessness and anxiety
options.B: Leaning forward in a tripod position
options.C: Cyanosis or bluish skin discoloration
options.D: An increased breathing rate

explanation: Skin turning blue usually happens only after oxygen levels have dropped severely for some time. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which bed position is best for instantly helping an out-of-breath patient expand their lungs?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: High-Fowler's position
options.C: Prone lying position
options.D: Flat supine position

explanation: Sitting upright in High-Fowler's position uses gravity to push abdominal organs downward, giving the lungs more room to fill with air. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h4)

question: A patient with thick mucus cannot clear their throat and shows signs of airway blockage. What immediate nursing action is required?

options.A: Asking the patient to hold their breath for one minute
options.B: Placing the patient flat on their back to rest
options.C: Suctioning the airway to remove the trapped secretions
options.D: Administering a dose of blood pressure medication

explanation: When a patient cannot cough up mucus blocking their airway, suctioning physically clears the passage so air can flow. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which oxygen delivery device is best for providing an exact, controlled percentage of oxygen to a patient?

options.A: Non-rebreather bag
options.B: Standard nasal cannula
options.C: Venturi mask
options.D: Simple face mask

explanation: The Venturi mask uses special adapter barrels to mix room air and oxygen precisely, delivering a specific, reliable oxygen percentage. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why must petroleum jelly and open flames be strictly avoided around active oxygen delivery equipment?

options.A: Grease stops the oxygen machine from making a buzzing sound
options.B: Oxygen strongly supports and quickens combustion and fire
options.C: Petroleum products block the tiny holes in the nasal cannula
options.D: Flames cause the oxygen tank to instantly fill with water

explanation: Oxygen makes fires burn much hotter and faster, so any spark or flame near an oxygen source creates an extreme fire hazard. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of pursed-lip breathing for a patient with chronic breathing difficulties?

options.A: It stops the heart from beating too fast during movement
options.B: It keeps airways open longer by creating gentle back-pressure during exhalation
options.C: It forces all the air out of the lungs in a single quick second
options.D: It pumps extra water vapor directly into the stomach lining

explanation: Breathing out through pursed lips creates small back-pressure that stops fragile airways from collapsing too early during exhalation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of having a surgical patient use an incentive spirometer?

options.A: To pump liquid medicine directly into the throat
options.B: To check the patient's blood pressure levels
options.C: To measure how loudly the patient can talk
options.D: To encourage deep breathing and prevent lung collapse

explanation: Incentive spirometry makes patients take deep, deliberate breaths, keeping their alveoli open and preventing postoperative atelectasis. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which factor can cause a pulse oximeter sensor to give an inaccurate reading on a patient's finger?

options.A: Cold fingers and poor peripheral circulation
options.B: Speaking in a normal tone of voice during the test
options.C: Drinking a glass of cold water before testing
options.D: A high room temperature on the hospital ward

explanation: Pulse oximeters rely on good blood flow through the finger; if circulation is sluggish or cold, the machine cannot read the pulse well. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which nursing action helps thin thick respiratory secretions so they are easier for the patient to cough up?

options.A: Lying the patient flat on their back
options.B: Keeping the room air completely dry
options.C: Encouraging adequate daily fluid intake
options.D: Restricting all drinking water after meals

explanation: Drinking enough water keeps body fluids thin, which naturally loosens thick mucus in the respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of inhalation therapy?

options.A: To deliver medication directly to the respiratory tract
options.B: To remove excess fluid directly from the pleural space
options.C: To bypass the digestive system completely for nutrition
options.D: To increase blood pressure through systemic absorption

explanation: Inhalation therapy deposits drugs straight into the airways and lungs for a localized effect. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is inhalation therapy often preferred over oral medications for lung conditions?

options.A: It guarantees 100 percent absorption into the bloodstream
options.B: It works faster locally and reduces widespread side effects
options.C: It is completely free of any potential complications
options.D: It never requires patient coordination or special training

explanation: Targeting the lungs directly means smaller doses can treat the problem without affecting the rest of the body as heavily. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which part of the respiratory tract filters out large particles before they reach the lungs?

options.A: The upper airway and nose
options.B: The pulmonary alveoli
options.C: The terminal bronchioles
options.D: The visceral pleura

explanation: The nasal passages and upper airway warm, humidify, and filter incoming air, catching larger debris and particles. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: What particle size is generally needed for medication to reach the deep lower airways and alveoli?

options.A: Between 50 and 100 micrometers
options.B: Greater than 20 micrometers
options.C: Between 1 and 5 micrometers
options.D: Any visible dust particle size

explanation: Fine particles measuring 1 to 5 micrometers are small enough to bypass the upper airway and settle deep in the bronchioles and alveoli. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which inhalation device requires the patient to take a fast, forceful breath to activate medication delivery?

options.A: Dry Powder Inhaler
options.B: Metered-dose inhaler with spacer
options.C: Simple nasal cannula
options.D: Standard nebulizer machine

explanation: Dry Powder Inhalers rely entirely on the patient's own inhalation effort to pull the powder out of the device and into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h3)

question: When is a nebulizer most commonly chosen over a metered-dose inhaler?

options.A: When the patient needs a device that fits easily in a small shirt pocket
options.B: When treatment must be completed in less than five seconds
options.C: When the patient cannot coordinate deep breathing with a handheld inhaler
options.D: When the healthcare provider wants to avoid using any electricity or gas

explanation: Nebulizers produce a continuous mist over several minutes, making them great for young children, the elderly, or acutely breathless patients. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary condition treated using emergency inhaled bronchodilators?

options.A: Acute bronchospasm
options.B: Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Chronic bacterial skin infection
options.D: Severe iron-deficiency anemia

explanation: Bronchodilators relax tightened airway muscles, making them the primary treatment for sudden breathing constriction or asthma attacks. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h4)

question: A patient with thick, sticky mucus blocking their airways is most likely to be prescribed which type of inhalable medication?

options.A: Beta-blockers
options.B: Anticoagulants
options.C: Vasopressors
options.D: Mucolytics

explanation: Mucolytics are specifically designed to break down and thin thick respiratory secretions so they can be cleared more easily. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the best body position for a patient receiving inhalation therapy?

options.A: Flat on the back with a low pillow
options.B: Lying flat on the left side
options.C: Pronated face down on the bed
options.D: Upright sitting or high Fowler's position

explanation: Sitting upright allows the diaphragm to move freely and promotes maximum lung expansion during medication delivery. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why must a nurse assess a patient's breathing technique and coordination before handing them an inhaler?

options.A: Assessment ensures the patient will never experience any drug side effects
options.B: All inhalation devices function identically regardless of the patient's skill
options.C: Patients are legally required to pass a written test before treatment
options.D: Different devices require specific breathing maneuvers for the drug to work

explanation: An MDI requires slow, deep breaths with a spacer, while a DPI requires a sharp inhalation, so matching technique is critical. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h5)

question: How long should a patient typically hold their breath after inhaling a dose of medication from an inhaler?

options.A: Until they feel dizzy
options.B: No more than one second
options.C: Exactly one minute
options.D: About 10 seconds

explanation: Holding the breath for about 10 seconds allows the tiny medication particles time to settle deep into the lung tissue instead of being exhaled right away. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h6)

question: What should the nurse instruct the patient to do immediately before actuating a metered-dose inhaler?

options.A: Inhale as fast as possible through the nose
options.B: Hyperventilate for thirty seconds
options.C: Exhale completely to empty the lungs
options.D: Take a quick swallow of cold water

explanation: Exhaling fully clears space in the lungs so the subsequent slow, deep inhalation can pull maximum medication into the airways. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which complication can occur if a patient fails to rinse their mouth after using an inhaled corticosteroid?

options.A: Sudden closure of the vocal cords
options.B: Severe inflammation of the esophagus
options.C: Oral fungal infection or thrush
options.D: Permanent discoloration of the teeth

explanation: Residual steroid powder left in the oral cavity alters normal flora, frequently causing fungal overgrowth known as oral thrush. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why might a patient experience a fast heartbeat (tachycardia) and hand tremors after using a rescue inhaler?

options.A: The inhaler device was shaken upside down before use
options.B: The patient drank cold water right before taking the medication
options.C: The medication has a systemic stimulant effect on beta receptors
options.D: The patient held their breath for too long during administration

explanation: Rescue inhalers often contain beta-agonists which, when absorbed into the bloodstream, stimulate the heart and nervous system. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h7)

question: When a patient is prescribed both a bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid, which one should they generally use first?

options.A: Whichever medication is closer to hand
options.B: The corticosteroid to coat the throat
options.C: The bronchodilator to open the airways
options.D: Neither, they must be mixed together first

explanation: Using the bronchodilator first opens up the air passages, allowing the subsequent corticosteroid to penetrate much deeper into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h8)

question: A home care nurse is reviewing proper maintenance with a client who uses a metered-dose inhaler. What instruction should the nurse include?

options.A: Never clean the plastic mouthpiece housing to preserve the internal valve
options.B: Store the active inhaler device inside a humid bathroom cabinet
options.C: Check the built-in dose counter regularly to avoid running out of medication
options.D: Wash the pressurized metal canister inside a dishwasher once every week

explanation: Monitoring the dose counter ensures patients know when their medication is running low or empty before an emergency arises. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h8)

question: What main substance does a Nelson inhaler deliver to help a patient breathe better?

options.A: Dry chemical powder
options.B: Medicated steam
options.C: Oxygen gas
options.D: Sterile saline mist

explanation: Spot on! The Nelson inhaler is a classic bedside tool used to vaporize hot water and soothing drugs so the patient breathes in warm, comforting medicated steam. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why is moist heat therapy so helpful for a patient dealing with chest and airway congestion?

options.A: It expands the lung tissue to increase total capacity
options.B: It loosens thick mucus and soothes irritated airways
options.C: It kills all bacterial infections in the chest instantly
options.D: It cools down body temperature during a high fever

explanation: You got it! Warm moisture works like magic to thin out sticky, thick mucus in the upper airway, making it much easier to cough up while calming down raw, irritated throat linings. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the job of the air inlet on a Nelson inhaler?

options.A: It locks the cork lid tightly into the ceramic jar
options.B: It lets the nurse pour medicine in while treating
options.C: It acts as a drain for extra water collection
options.D: It allows fresh air to mix with the rising steam

explanation: Exactly! The air inlet lets a bit of cooler room air mix with the vapor. This keeps the steam from being too scorching hot for the patient's mouth and throat. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h2)

question: What purpose does the cork bung serve when using a Nelson inhaler?

options.A: It filters out dust particles before the patient breathes the vapor
options.B: It seals the top of the jar so steam escapes only through the mouthpiece
options.C: It measures the exact temperature of the water inside the container
options.D: It absorbs excess medication that spills during preparation

explanation: Well done! The cork acts as a tight lid, making sure all the warm steam is forced to travel upward through the central tube and out the mouthpiece where the patient needs it. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h2)

question: Which of these conditions is a classic reason to use a Nelson inhaler?

options.A: Acute sinusitis
options.B: Bacterial pneumonia
options.C: Spontaneous pneumothorax
options.D: Pulmonary edema

explanation: Spot on! Sinusitis brings painful inflammation and blocked nasal passages, which respond wonderfully to the warm, soothing moisture of steam therapy. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h3)

question: A patient has severe laryngitis with a painful, raspy voice and is given steam inhalation. What is the main goal here?

options.A: To deliver systemic antibiotics directly into the bloodstream
options.B: To force deep lung expansion in the lower alveoli
options.C: To soothe inflamed vocal cords and mucosal tissues
options.D: To permanently cure the viral infection overnight

explanation: You got it! Moist heat hydrates dry, raw throat tissues, taking away that scratchy irritation and giving sore vocal cords a chance to rest and heal. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which common substance is often added to hot water in a Nelson inhaler to ease breathing?

options.A: Liquid paraffin wax
options.B: Intravenous saline
options.C: Tincture of benzoin
options.D: Hydrogen peroxide

explanation: Correct! Tincture of benzoin (or menthol) is a classic bedside additive that adds comforting, aromatic vapors to the steam. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why must you carefully check the ceramic jar for cracks before pouring in boiling water?

options.A: To measure the exact volume capacity in milliliters
options.B: To remove leftover food particles from previous treatments
options.C: To ensure the inside is completely sterile for surgical use
options.D: To check for cracks that could leak or shatter from thermal shock

explanation: Safety first! Pouring boiling water into a damaged ceramic jar can cause it to shatter completely from thermal shock, risking severe burns. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h4)

question: How should a patient breathe while using the mouthpiece of a Nelson inhaler?

options.A: Only through the nose with the mouth tightly closed
options.B: In through the mouth and out through the nose
options.C: In through the nose and out through the mouth
options.D: Using rapid, shallow panting breaths only

explanation: Spot on! Inhaling through the mouth draws the medicated vapor straight into the airways, while breathing out through the nose stops them from blowing vapor back into the device. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h5)

question: Up to what level should the nurse fill the Nelson inhaler jar with boiling water?

options.A: All the way to the very top rim
options.B: About two-thirds full
options.C: Only one-tenth full
options.D: Exactly five liters

explanation: You got it! Filling it about two-thirds full leaves plenty of room for steam to build up without the hot water bubbling over into the mouthpiece. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the biggest safety risk you must watch out for when using a Nelson inhaler?

options.A: Acute kidney failure
options.B: Scalding from hot water or steam
options.C: Sudden systemic drug toxicity
options.D: Permanent hearing loss

explanation: Spot on! Because you are working with boiling water, the main danger is accidental spills causing painful burns to the patient's skin or face. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h6)

question: An elderly patient starts feeling dizzy and lightheaded during steam therapy. What is your very first nursing action?

options.A: Stop the treatment and remove the inhaler immediately
options.B: Add more boiling water to increase vapor strength
options.C: Leave the room briefly to fetch a doctor
options.D: Encourage the patient to breathe faster and deeper

explanation: Safety comes first! If a patient feels dizzy or faint, halt the procedure right away to keep them safe from injury. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h6)

question: What should you do right after a patient finishes their steam inhalation session?

options.A: Spray the patient's throat with strong antiseptics
options.B: Assist the patient in wiping their mouth and face
options.C: Immediately place the boiling jar into an ice bath
options.D: Seal the dirty water inside the jar for laboratory testing

explanation: Exactly! Gently wiping their face clears away any condensed moisture or medicine residue so it doesn't dry on their skin and cause irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why should you wait for a Nelson inhaler to cool down before trying to wash it?

options.A: To ensure the plastic cork expands to its maximum size
options.B: To save electricity in the utility room
options.C: To let the medication completely dry into a hard solid crust
options.D: To prevent hand burns and avoid cracking the ceramic from sudden temperature changes

explanation: Spot on! Letting it cool protects your hands from burns and stops cold tap water from cracking the hot ceramic jar due to sudden thermal shock. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary physical form of medication delivered by a nebulizer to the patient's lungs?

options.A: A compressed gas tablet
options.B: A fine mist or aerosolized vapor
options.C: A warm liquid solution
options.D: A dry powder capsule

explanation: A nebulizer turns liquid medicine into a vapor so the patient can easily breathe it deep into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why is nebulization often chosen over other inhalers for patients in acute respiratory distress?

options.A: It requires only normal, quiet breathing instead of a deep, forced inhalation.
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any vital sign monitoring.
options.C: It stops all lung infections within minutes of starting the treatment.
options.D: It works ten times faster than any intravenous medication available.

explanation: Patients struggling to catch their breath cannot coordinate deep inhalers, making normal breathing through a nebulizer mask much easier. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which medication group is most commonly given via nebulizer to relax tightened airway muscles?

options.A: Vasopressors
options.B: Anticoagulants
options.C: Antibiotics
options.D: Bronchodilators

explanation: Bronchodilators open up constricted breathing tubes so air can flow freely in and out of the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h2)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with thick, sticky mucus blocking their airways and causing severe coughing. Which type of nebulized medication is most appropriate?

options.A: A local anesthetic
options.B: A beta-blocker
options.C: A mucolytic agent
options.D: An intravenous fluid

explanation: Mucolytics specifically target and break down thick pulmonary secretions, making them easier for the patient to expel. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h2)

question: What is the main reason for assessing lung sounds before giving a nebulizer treatment?

options.A: To clear out thick mucus plugs before the machine is turned on
options.B: To establish a baseline for evaluating the treatment's effectiveness later
options.C: To find out if the patient has a hidden bacterial chest infection
options.D: To calculate the exact dose of medicine needed for the patient

explanation: Checking lung sounds beforehand helps the nurse compare wheezing or air entry after the treatment ends. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which physical sign indicates that a patient is experiencing severe respiratory distress before treatment?

options.A: A quiet, relaxed breathing pattern while lying flat
options.B: Pink skin color on the cheeks and nail beds
options.C: Use of accessory neck and chest muscles to breathe
options.D: A slow, even heart rate of 60 beats per minute

explanation: Straining neck and chest muscles means the body is working extra hard to pull air into struggling lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is the usual gas flow rate range set on the flowmeter for a standard compressor nebulizer?

options.A: 20 to 25 liters per minute
options.B: 12 to 15 liters per minute
options.C: 6 to 8 liters per minute
options.D: 1 to 2 liters per minute

explanation: A flow rate of 6 to 8 liters per minute provides enough pressure to turn the liquid medicine into a proper mist. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why is sterile normal saline sometimes added to the medication cup during preparation?

options.A: To reach the proper total liquid volume needed for the nebulizer cup to aerosolize correctly
options.B: To permanently neutralize any harmful side effects caused by bronchodilators
options.C: To numb the lining of the throat so the patient does not cough
options.D: To clean the plastic tubing before the medication mist passes through it

explanation: Nebulizer cups need a minimum fluid volume, often 3 to 5 mL, to create an effective aerosol mist. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h4)

question: What position should the nurse place the patient in before starting a nebulizer treatment?

options.A: Flat on their back with no pillows
options.B: Toned flat on their stomach
options.C: Lying strictly on their left side
options.D: Upright sitting or semi-Fowler's position

explanation: Sitting upright lets the chest expand fully, helping the medication travel deep into the lower airways. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why does the nurse occasionally tap the side of the medication cup during the procedure?

options.A: To prevent the plastic parts from overheating while the compressor runs
options.B: To help remaining liquid droplets slide down into the bottom of the cup to be aerosolized
options.C: To signal to the patient that the treatment session is halfway finished
options.D: To clear any dust blocking the outside air filter vents

explanation: Tapping the cup drops clinging fluid back into the reservoir so it doesn't go to waste on the walls. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the best immediate action for the nurse to take after the nebulizer cup runs dry?

options.A: Reassess lung sounds and measure the patient's oxygen saturation
options.B: Immediately start a second dose of medication without waiting
options.C: Disconnect the air flow meter and leave the room quietly
options.D: Instruct the patient to lie flat in bed for one hour

explanation: Checking lung sounds and oxygen levels right after treatment confirms whether the bronchodilator opened the airways successfully. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h6)

question: After a bronchodilator nebulizer treatment, a patient coughs heavily. What should the nurse encourage them to do next?

options.A: Swallow the mucus to keep the throat moist
options.B: Expectorate the loosened mucus into a tissue
options.C: Drink a large glass of ice-cold water immediately
options.D: Lie down flat on the bed to stop coughing

explanation: Coughing brings up the loosened secretions, so spitting them out into a tissue clears the airway safely. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h6)

question: Which common side effect often occurs due to the stimulant properties of bronchodilators like albuterol?

options.A: Rapid heart rate and palpitations
options.B: Uncontrollable drowsiness and sleep
options.C: Severe drop in blood pressure
options.D: Complete loss of the sense of taste

explanation: Beta-agonist bronchodilators stimulate heart receptors, frequently causing a fast heartbeat or jittery feeling. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h7)

question: What should the nurse do FIRST if a patient suddenly develops severe wheezing and increased breathing distress right after starting a nebulizer?

options.A: Wait ten minutes to see if the reaction goes away on its own
options.B: Stop the nebulizer treatment immediately and assess the patient
options.C: Ask the patient to lie flat and take deep, fast breaths
options.D: Turn up the air flow meter to make the mist spray faster

explanation: Worsening distress means a possible paradoxical bronchospasm, so stopping the drug is the immediate safety priority. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h7)

question: Why is proper cleaning and drying of nebulizer equipment so critical for patient safety?

options.A: Dirty equipment will permanently break the air compressor motor
options.B: Washing prevents the plastic mask from changing color over time
options.C: Moist plastic parts easily grow harmful bacteria that can cause lung infections
options.D: Leftover medication residue turns into a solid metal inside the tube

explanation: Wet nebulizer cups are breeding grounds for germs, which the patient would inhale directly into their lungs during the next treatment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the correct way to dry nebulizer parts after washing them?

options.A: Air dry them completely on a clean paper towel or lint-free cloth
options.B: Blow hot air through them using a standard hair dryer on high heat
options.C: Place them inside a sealed plastic bag while they are still soaking wet
options.D: Wipe them dry using a heavily used cloth towel from the laundry bin

explanation: Air drying on a clean surface prevents germ transfer from dirty towels and ensures no moisture is trapped inside. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the main goal of using a steam tent for a patient?

options.A: To provide a cool environment for high fevers
options.B: To administer aerosolized systemic antibiotics
options.C: To increase total body fluid volume rapidly
options.D: To deliver warm, moist air to the respiratory tract

explanation: Great job! A steam tent traps moisture so the patient breathes in warm, humid air, which helps soothe and open up the airways. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h1)

question: How does the high humidity inside a steam tent help a patient with a heavy cough?

options.A: It dilates the tiny air sacs in the lower lungs
options.B: It kills bacterial infections in the upper airway
options.C: It numbs the throat nerves to stop the cough reflex
options.D: It liquefies thick mucus so it is easier to clear

explanation: Spot on! Moisture acts like magic on sticky mucus, thinning it out so the patient can cough it up easily. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which breathing condition is most commonly treated with a steam tent?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism
options.B: Croup
options.C: Pneumothorax
options.D: Pleural effusion

explanation: You got it! Croup causes that classic barking cough, and warm, moist air is one of the best ways to bring relief. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h2)

question: A toddler comes in with a barking cough and noisy breathing (stridor). What should you, as the nurse, prepare for?

options.A: Prepare equipment for a steam tent
options.B: Administer a dry oxygen mask at high flow
options.C: Apply a cold ice pack to the chest wall
options.D: Insert a large-bore intravenous line immediately

explanation: That barking cough and stridor point straight to croup! Setting up humidified steam therapy is a key nursing action here. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h2)

question: Where should you position the steam generator in relation to the patient's bed?

options.A: Underneath the mattress for hidden warmth
options.B: Tied securely to the side rail of the crib
options.C: At a safe distance to prevent accidental burns
options.D: Directly inside the tent canopy next to the pillow

explanation: Safety first! Always keep the hot generator far enough away to protect the patient from burns. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h3)

question: Why is it important to check the electrical cord of the steam generator before turning it on?

options.A: To verify the correct voltage for the hospital room
options.B: To measure how much electricity the unit will use
options.C: To ensure the heating water boils much faster
options.D: To prevent electrical shocks and fire hazards

explanation: Spot on! Water and electricity are a dangerous mix, so checking cords keeps both you and your patient safe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is an important assessment to do BEFORE starting steam therapy?

options.A: Baseline respiratory rate and breath sounds
options.B: Baseline abdominal girth measurement
options.C: Fasting blood glucose level check
options.D: Complete neurological reflex testing

explanation: You need to know how they sound *before* treatment so you can tell if the steam is actually helping! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why should a patient wear lightweight cotton clothing inside a steam tent instead of heavy synthetics?

options.A: Heavy clothes block the steam from reaching the lungs
