options.B: Cotton fabrics absorb all the humidity completely
options.C: Cotton breathes better and prevents overheating
options.D: Synthetic fabrics melt easily when exposed to steam

explanation: Exactly! Cotton keeps the patient comfortable and stops them from getting too hot in a humid space. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h4)

question: How often should you check the patient's breathing during the early phase of steam therapy?

options.A: Every four hours
options.B: Only when the patient rings the bell
options.C: Every fifteen minutes
options.D: Once every shift

explanation: Checking frequently at the start ensures the patient is taking in the moisture well and their breathing is improving. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why do you need to keep a close eye on the water level in the steam generator while it's running?

options.A: To prevent the reservoir from boiling completely dry
options.B: To prevent the plastic tent canopy from melting
options.C: To check if the patient is drinking enough water
options.D: To make sure the steam turns into cold mist

explanation: You got it! Letting the water run dry can ruin the machine and create a safety hazard. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the biggest safety hazard to watch out for during steam tent therapy?

options.A: Hypertensive crisis
options.B: Sudden hypoglycemia
options.C: Scald burns
options.D: Severe hypothermia

explanation: Correct! Because boiling water and hot steam are involved, burn prevention is always a top priority. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h6)

question: You need to add more water to a running steam generator. What is your very first step?

options.A: Ask the parent to hold the steam nozzle away
options.B: Pour cold water slowly while the unit is still boiling
options.C: Turn off and unplug the unit before adding water
options.D: Cover the hot metal parts with a dry towel first

explanation: Always power down and unplug first! This protects you from electrical shocks and nasty steam burns. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the safest way to open the steam tent when the treatment is done?

options.A: Rip open the plastic tent quickly to let fresh air rush in
options.B: Leave the steam running while taking the patient out
options.C: Turn off the generator and open the canopy gradually
options.D: Wait until the room temperature drops below normal

explanation: Opening it slowly prevents a sudden blast of cool air from chilling your damp patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h7)

question: Why should you do a quick physical assessment right after the steam session ends?

options.A: To check if the bed linens need washing
options.B: To evaluate how well the treatment worked
options.C: To see if the patient needs a snack or drink
options.D: To make sure the electrical cord is cool

explanation: Spot on! Comparing your notes now with your baseline check tells you if the therapy did its job. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h7)

question: Which of these details must you include when charting steam tent therapy?

options.A: The brand name of the plastic tent canopy
options.B: The exact electrical voltage of the wall socket
options.C: The name of the manufacturer who built the bed
options.D: Start and end times of the treatment

explanation: You got it! Accurate start and end times give a clear timeline of the care you provided. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h8)

question: Why is it important to write down how the patient tolerated the treatment and how much mucus they cleared?

options.A: It shows how much water the machine used up
options.B: It proves the effectiveness of the treatment
options.C: It determines the hospital room billing costs
options.D: It replaces the need for a physical assessment

explanation: Brilliant! Documenting their response helps the whole healthcare team see that the therapy was successful. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h8)

question: Which common, lightweight device uses two small prongs to deliver low-flow oxygen right into a patient's nostrils?

options.A: Non-rebreather mask
options.B: Venturi mask
options.C: Nasal cannula
options.D: Simple face mask

explanation: You'll see nasal cannulas everywhere in the ward! They're the standard, comfortable choice for giving patients a little extra oxygen through their nose. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h1)

question: As a nurse, why would you start a patient on nasal oxygen therapy?

options.A: To treat tissue hypoxia and raise low blood oxygen levels
options.B: To deliver high-pressure aerosolized medications to the lungs
options.C: To completely replace normal breathing mechanics during sleep
options.D: To prevent the patient from experiencing dry mouth overnight

explanation: Spot on! We give oxygen when the body's tissues aren't getting enough of it (hypoxia), helping to bring those blood oxygen levels back up to a safe place. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h1)

question: What equipment do you attach directly to an oxygen source to control how fast the gas flows?

options.A: Pressure gauge
options.B: Pulse oximeter
options.C: Flow meter
options.D: Humidifier bottle

explanation: The flow meter is your best friend for control—it lets you accurately dial in the exact liters per minute prescribed for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h2)

question: When do you typically hook up a humidification bottle filled with sterile water to an oxygen setup?

options.A: Only when the patient is diagnosed with an active lung infection
options.B: Whenever oxygen is delivered at any flow rate below one liter
options.C: When delivering higher flow rates that can dry the nasal passages
options.D: To cool the temperature of the gas before it enters the nose

explanation: Medical oxygen is very dry and can irritate the nose at higher flows. Adding sterile water for humidification keeps your patient nice and comfortable! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h2)

question: What is the best bed position for a patient struggling to breathe who needs supplemental oxygen?

options.A: Prone position facing down on the bed
options.B: Semi-Fowler's or high-Fowler's position
options.C: Flat on the back with legs slightly raised
options.D: Trendelenburg position with tilted head

explanation: Sitting upright in Semi- or High-Fowler's position lets gravity help expand the lungs fully, making every breath much easier for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h3)

question: You notice raw, red skin inside a patient's nostrils while getting ready to put on a nasal cannula. What should you do first?

options.A: Scrub the irritated skin vigorously with an antiseptic alcohol wipe
options.B: Switch the patient immediately to an invasive mechanical ventilator
options.C: Refuse to start the oxygen therapy until the skin is completely healed
options.D: Document the finding, apply a water-based lubricant if ordered, and monitor the area closely

explanation: Always check and document skin status! Protecting sore areas with safe, water-based lubricants helps prevent further friction without stopping vital oxygen. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h3)

question: How should the little prongs of a nasal cannula face when you put them into a patient's nose?

options.A: Flattened sideways
options.B: Pointing straight up
options.C: Curving downward
options.D: Tilted backward

explanation: They are shaped to match human anatomy! Pointing them downward ensures they slide comfortably along the natural curve of the nasal passages. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why is it smart to check that gas is actually flowing out of the cannula prongs before placing them on the patient?

options.A: To measure the exact oxygen percentage in the room air
options.B: To confirm the equipment works and gas is actively delivering
options.C: To clear out any trapped dust from the manufacturing factory
options.D: To warm up the cold gas before it touches the sensitive nasal lining

explanation: A quick check saves a lot of trouble—you want to make sure there isn't a kinked tube or a closed valve blocking air before it reaches your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the usual maximum flow rate recommended for a standard nasal cannula?

options.A: 2 Liters per minute
options.B: 12 Liters per minute
options.C: 20 Liters per minute
options.D: 6 Liters per minute

explanation: We usually stick to 1 to 6 Liters per minute for standard cannulas. Going higher mostly just dries out the nose without giving extra benefits. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h5)

question: Why does the actual amount of oxygen (FiO2) a patient receives from a nasal cannula vary from person to person?

options.A: Different hospitals calibrate their wall oxygen outlets to different pressures
options.B: It depends on the patient's breathing rate and depth, which mixes room air with the oxygen
options.C: Patients absorb oxygen at different speeds through their skin
options.D: The plastic tubing stretches or shrinks based on the room temperature

explanation: Because a nasal cannula is an open system, patients breathe in regular room air right along with the oxygen. How fast or deep they breathe changes the exact mix! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h5)

question: What is an important daily nursing task for a patient on continuous nasal cannula oxygen?

options.A: Inspecting skin behind the ears and providing nasal hygiene
options.B: Keeping the patient strictly confined to bedrest
options.C: Changing the wall flow meter every four hours
options.D: Washing the entire length of the plastic tubing with soap

explanation: Plastic tubing can rub against delicate skin behind the ears and in the nose. Regular checks and basic hygiene keep your patient safe and comfortable. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h6)

question: Your patient on a nasal cannula complains of a dry, sore throat and a mild nosebleed. What is your best nursing action?

options.A: Increase the oxygen flow rate to flush the nasal passages
options.B: Recommend adding humidification to the oxygen setup as prescribed
options.C: Remove the oxygen permanently and document refusal of care
options.D: Switch the patient to a tight-fitting non-rebreather mask

explanation: Dry medical gas can be tough on delicate mucous membranes. Adding moisture (humidification) is the perfect fix to soothe that dryness and irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h6)

question: Which of these substances should you NEVER use to soothe dry nostrils during oxygen therapy because of fire risks?

options.A: Petroleum jelly
options.B: Aqueous cream
options.C: Water-based gel
options.D: Saline nasal spray

explanation: Never use petroleum-based products around oxygen! They are flammable and can easily catch fire in an oxygen-rich environment—always stick to water-based options. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why do oxygen cylinders and wall outlets always need strict 'No Smoking' safety signs nearby?

options.A: Oxygen strongly supports combustion and makes fires spread rapidly
options.B: Tobacco smoke clogs the small holes in the nasal cannula prongs
options.C: Smoking interferes with the machine's internal electrical circuits
options.D: The smell of smoke ruins the purity of the medical gas supply

explanation: Oxygen itself doesn't burn, but it feeds fires aggressively. Even a tiny spark can turn into a massive flame in seconds around supplemental oxygen! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h7)

question: How do digital (electronic) blood pressure machines mainly measure your blood pressure?

options.A: By placing a small fluid tube inside the artery
options.B: By sensing pulse waves (oscillations) in the cuff
options.C: By feeling the pulse at the wrist directly
options.D: By listening to Korotkoff sounds with a tiny microphone

explanation: Digital machines look for tiny changes or oscillations in pressure caused by your pulse, rather than listening for sounds like we do with a stethoscope. Spot on! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why does a patient moving around during a digital blood pressure check often cause an error?

options.A: Movement stops the battery from sending power to the screen
options.B: Moving completely shuts off the air valve inside the cuff
options.C: Physical activity instantly drops the patient's actual blood pressure
options.D: Movement creates false pressure bumps that confuse the machine's computer

explanation: The machine looks for very steady, specific waves. Any extra shaking or moving creates chaotic signals that mess up the calculation. Keep your patient nice and still! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is one of the best perks of using an electronic blood pressure machine over a manual one?

options.A: They are completely unaffected if the patient moves
options.B: They take very little training to use correctly
options.C: They give exact readings even during serious heart rhythm problems
options.D: They never need new batteries or servicing

explanation: Digital monitors do the heavy lifting for you! You don't need expert stethoscope listening skills to get a quick reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h2)

question: When would a manual blood pressure check with a stethoscope be a better choice than a digital machine?

options.A: When the patient is checking their own pressure at home
options.B: When the patient has a very irregular heartbeat
options.C: When the hospital ward is completely quiet
options.D: When you are in a rush during a busy shift

explanation: Digital machines struggle to calculate properly when the heart rhythm jumps all over the place. That's when your manual auscultation skills shine! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h2)

question: Where should you position the lower edge of the blood pressure cuff on the patient's arm?

options.A: About one inch above the inner elbow crease
options.B: Right up against the shoulder joint
options.C: Directly over the bony wrist
options.D: Halfway down the forearm

explanation: Placing it about an inch above the elbow crease ensures the inner bladder sits right over the brachial artery. Perfect placement! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h3)

question: You get a falsely high blood pressure reading because the cuff you used was way too small for the patient's arm. What should you do next?

options.A: Record the high reading as their true baseline blood pressure
options.B: Switch to measuring the blood pressure on their ankle instead
options.C: Just subtract ten points from the result and write that down
options.D: Grab a larger cuff and repeat the check after giving the patient a short rest

explanation: A wrong cuff size means the reading isn't reliable. Always re-measure with the correct size after letting the patient rest for a minute. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why can crossing the legs during a blood pressure check lead to a falsely high reading?

options.A: It blocks blood flow completely in the arm's brachial artery
options.B: It increases physical tension and blood vessel resistance in the body
options.C: It stops the machine from pumping air into the cuff
options.D: It drains the battery of the electronic device faster

explanation: Crossed legs and slouching temporarily boost your vascular pressure. Always remind patients to uncross their legs and keep feet flat on the floor! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which of these is a MISTAKE when getting a patient ready for a digital blood pressure check?

options.A: Making sure both of the patient's feet are flat on the floor
options.B: Asking the patient to stay quiet while the machine runs
options.C: Allowing the patient to keep a thick sweater on with the cuff rolled over it
options.D: Ensuring the patient rests quietly for five minutes beforehand

explanation: Always put the cuff directly on bare skin! Thick clothing or tight rolling can pinch the arm and mess up your numbers. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is a major giveaway that a digital blood pressure cuff has an air leak?

options.A: The screen flashes bright red and rings a loud alarm
options.B: The battery icon shows full charge the whole time
options.C: The machine shows an error code or cannot finish pumping up
options.D: The device measures the blood pressure twice as fast as usual

explanation: If air is escaping, the machine can't build up the pressure it needs, so it will usually flash an error message at you. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why do electronic blood pressure monitors need to be checked and calibrated regularly?

options.A: Internal sensors naturally drift and lose accuracy over time and with use
options.B: It's just a rule made by manufacturers to keep batteries from exploding
options.C: The internal software wipes its own memory clean every few weeks
options.D: Sensors magically improve their own accuracy without any human help

explanation: Just like weighing scales, electronic monitors can get a bit out of whack over time. Regular checks ensure our numbers stay trustworthy. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h5)

question: A digital monitor shows a very high blood pressure for a calm patient who feels totally fine. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Write down the machine's number and walk away to another room
options.B: Check the reading manually using a stethoscope and manual cuff
options.C: Rush to give the patient strong blood pressure-lowering drugs
options.D: Throw the electronic device away and never use it again

explanation: Machines can glitch! If a result doesn't match how the patient looks or feels, always double-check it manually before panicking or treating. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why is teaching patients how to use home blood pressure monitors such an important nursing duty?

options.A: Patients need to know how to solder broken circuit boards at home
options.B: Good technique prevents false readings that could lead to wrong medication changes
options.C: It stops patients from ever coming back to the hospital clinic
options.D: Home machines are so complicated that only rocket scientists can run them

explanation: If a patient uses poor posture or a bad cuff size at home, their doctor might see bad data and change their prescriptions incorrectly. Your teaching makes a real difference! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is the main reason nurses use portable monitors in the hospital?

options.A: To track vital signs while a patient is moving
options.B: To permanently store a patient's entire medical history
options.C: To deliver intravenous medications automatically
options.D: To replace all stationary equipment in the intensive care unit

explanation: Portable monitors are lifesavers when patients are walking around or being moved between wards. They let us keep a close eye on vitals on the go! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why are portable monitors so great for catching sudden changes in a patient's condition?

options.A: They provide continuous, real-time physiological data outside the bedside
options.B: They eliminate the need for any manual vital sign documentation
options.C: They completely prevent the occurrence of false alarms
options.D: They automatically diagnose underlying diseases without nurse input

explanation: Because they track vitals continuously—even during transport—we can spot sudden warning signs immediately and act fast. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h1)

question: Which portable device does a patient wear to continuously send heart rhythm data to the nurse's station?

options.A: A standard mercury sphygmomanometer
options.B: A handheld blood glucose meter
options.C: A telemetry transmitter
options.D: A basic digital thermometer

explanation: Telemetry packs are worn by the patient to wirelessly beam their ECG rhythm straight to the central monitor. Very handy for cardiac patients! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h2)

question: How is a transport monitor different from a simple, pocket-sized pulse oximeter?

options.A: It does not require a power source or battery to function
options.B: It tracks multiple vital parameters simultaneously during critical movement
options.C: It can only measure the patient's body temperature
options.D: It is strictly used for outpatient home care without nursing oversight

explanation: While a pocket oximeter usually only checks oxygen levels, a transport monitor is built to track several vital signs at once during busy or critical moves. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h2)

question: When are you most likely to hook an inpatient up to a portable monitor?

options.A: During intrahospital transport to diagnostic imaging
options.B: While the patient is sleeping quietly in a stable hospital bed
options.C: During routine discharge education in the room
options.D: When filing physical paper records in the nurses' station

explanation: Whenever we roll a patient out of their room for an X-ray or scan (diagnostic imaging), we hook them up to a portable monitor to keep them safe on the journey. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h3)

question: A recovering heart patient is ready to take their first walk down the ward corridor. What should you do?

options.A: Attach a portable telemetry or wireless monitoring unit
options.B: Keep the patient attached to a heavy wall-mounted monitor with long cables
options.C: Wait until the patient returns to the bed to check vitals
options.D: Disconnect all monitoring devices to encourage normal movement

explanation: Early walks are great for recovery, but we always want a wireless or telemetry unit attached so we can safely watch out for any exercise-related heart issues. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h3)

question: What is an important quick check before you connect a portable monitor to a patient?

options.A: Disconnecting all wireless internet routers nearby
options.B: Resetting the device to factory default settings
options.C: Calibrating the internal clock to Greenwich Mean Time
options.D: Checking the battery charge and power status

explanation: Always make sure the battery is charged! The last thing you want is the monitor dying halfway down the hallway. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h4)

question: Why is it smart to adjust alarm limits on a portable monitor for each specific patient?

options.A: The machine will refuse to record data without personalized input
options.B: Standard defaults are illegal to use in modern hospitals
options.C: Customizing limits stops the battery from draining too quickly
options.D: Factory defaults may be unsafe or cause unnecessary alarm fatigue

explanation: Generic settings can either miss a real problem or beep constantly for no reason (alarm fatigue). Tailoring it to the patient keeps everyone sane and safe! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h4)

question: What should you do FIRST when a portable monitor suddenly lets out a loud, urgent alarm?

options.A: Document a cardiac arrest in the patient chart right away
options.B: Immediately silence the device and walk away to find a doctor
options.C: Turn off the monitor power switch to stop the annoying noise
options.D: Assess the patient's physical condition and check the sensor placement

explanation: Patient first, always! Check the patient and make sure the sensor hasn't just popped off before jumping to conclusions. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h5)

question: What is a very common cause of false alarms on a portable pulse oximeter while moving a patient?

options.A: Normal room lighting brightness
options.B: Fresh battery installation
options.C: High room humidity levels
options.D: Motion artifact and shivering

explanation: Movement or shivering shakes the sensor around (motion artifact), confusing the machine and leading to wild or false readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h5)

question: When is it time to clean and disinfect a portable monitor?

options.A: Whenever the battery runs completely flat
options.B: Only once a week during night shift
options.C: Only if visibly stained with blood
options.D: After every single patient use

explanation: Wiping down the equipment between patients stops germs from spreading and keeps our hospital environment safe. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is your best first step if a portable monitor starts showing crazy, unreadable numbers?

options.A: Throw the equipment into the nearest biohazard bin
options.B: Inspect cable connections and sensor placement
options.C: Take the device apart with a screwdriver to check internal wires
options.D: Ignore the error message until the shift ends

explanation: Usually, erratic data just means a loose cable or a slipped sensor. Always check the physical setup first! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is the main job of wearable health devices in clinical care?

options.A: To deliver oral medications automatically to the patient
options.B: To diagnose complex surgical diseases without a doctor
options.C: To track and transmit health-related data continuously
options.D: To replace traditional laboratory blood testing completely

explanation: Wearables are great because they keep an eye on patient vitals between clinic visits. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h1)

question: Which wearable device is best for continuous, medical-grade heart rhythm monitoring?

options.A: A standard consumer fitness wristband
options.B: A basic smartphone pedometer app
options.C: An adhesive medical-grade patch
options.D: A smart textile running t-shirt

explanation: Medical patches stick securely and are specifically designed to catch every beat of critical heart rhythms accurately. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h1)

question: How do optical sensors in regular fitness wristbands usually measure your heart rate?

options.A: By measuring electrical currents through the skin
options.B: By detecting changes in blood flow using light
options.C: By listening to heart valve closures via tiny microphones
options.D: By calculating body temperature shifts on the wrist

explanation: Think of how a flashlight shines through your fingers—these sensors use light to catch the pulse of blood moving underneath your skin! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h2)

question: What fluid do continuous glucose monitors sample to check a patient's sugar levels?

options.A: Epidermal sweat
options.B: Interstitial fluid
options.C: Capillary whole blood
options.D: Venous plasma

explanation: The tiny sensor sits right under the skin, swimming in the fluid surrounding your cells (interstitial fluid) to estimate blood sugar. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h2)

question: Why is tracking data over time with a wearable better than a single blood pressure check at the clinic?

options.A: It prevents nurses from having to manually record any vital signs
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any laboratory blood tests
options.C: It guarantees that the patient will take all prescribed medications
options.D: It captures daily trends and avoids single-visit anxiety spikes

explanation: Ever get nervous seeing a doctor in a white coat? Wearables show real everyday trends without hospital stress getting in the way. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h3)

question: A heart failure patient uses a wearable at home. Which trend should make a nurse step in early?

options.A: Gradual upward trends in daily weight and decreasing physical activity
options.B: Stable resting heart rates recorded consistently throughout the night
options.C: Occasional reminders to stand up and stretch during sedentary hours
options.D: A slight increase in daily step counts reported over the weekend

explanation: When activity drops and weight creeps up from fluid, it's often an early warning sign that heart failure symptoms are worsening. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is an important nursing duty when giving a wearable device to a patient?

options.A: Writing custom software code to link the device to the hospital
options.B: Calibrating the internal microchips using a sterile surgical kit
options.C: Teaching the patient how to wear, charge, and sync the device
options.D: Replacing the device hardware components whenever the battery dies

explanation: As a nurse, your guidance is key! Patients need to know how to handle, charge, and sync their devices so the data keeps flowing. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h4)

question: Why do nurses set specific alert limits (thresholds) on patient wearables?

options.A: To ensure the device battery never runs out of power unexpectedly
options.B: To stop patients from looking at their own heart rate data
options.C: To comply with government laws regarding smartphone manufacturing
options.D: To prevent alert fatigue from minor, harmless data fluctuations

explanation: Setting smart limits stops alarms from ringing over tiny movements, keeping nurses focused on actual emergencies. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h4)

question: Why is data encryption so important for health wearable devices?

options.A: To increase the physical durability of the wristband strap
options.B: To protect sensitive patient health records from unauthorized interception
options.C: To ensure the step counter measures distance more accurately
options.D: To make the device battery last much longer during daily use

explanation: Encryption scrambles personal health details so hackers can't read or steal confidential patient information. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT an ethical concern when using health wearables?

options.A: Ensuring equal access for patients regardless of income
options.B: Obtaining proper informed consent for data sharing
options.C: Protecting personal health information from data breaches
options.D: Increasing the physical battery weight of the wristband

explanation: Battery weight is just hardware design, while privacy, consent, and equal access are major ethical issues in nursing informatics. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h5)

question: What is a major challenge when using wearable health devices in some Nigerian communities?

options.A: Excessive availability of high-speed fiber optic cables
options.B: Strict government bans on all digital wristwatches
options.C: A complete lack of patients suffering from chronic illnesses
options.D: Unstable electricity supply and limited internet connectivity

explanation: Frequent power cuts and poor network signals can sometimes make it tough to keep live health data syncing smoothly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h6)

question: How can healthcare providers help patients who struggle with technology when using wearables?

options.A: By refusing care to anyone who does not understand technology immediately
options.B: By removing all digital screens from the monitoring equipment
options.C: By forcing all patients to buy the most expensive smartphone available
options.D: By providing simple, guided education and easy-to-use device interfaces

explanation: Patience and clear, step-by-step teaching help bridge the digital gap so every patient feels comfortable using their tracker. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary tool used in tele-nursing to deliver care?

options.A: Information and communication technologies
options.B: Surgical instruments and sterile trays
options.C: Laboratory reagents and microscopy
options.D: Manual blood pressure cuffs and stethoscopes

explanation: Tele-nursing relies fundamentally on electronic communication tools like phones and computers to reach patients remotely. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h1)

question: Why is tele-nursing particularly helpful for patients living in remote areas?

options.A: It brings healthcare services directly to homes without requiring travel
options.B: It guarantees that patients will never need hospital admission
options.C: It provides free medications delivered straight to the doorstep
options.D: It completely replaces the need for any physical doctor visits

explanation: By using technology, nurses can assess and monitor clients who live far away from physical health facilities. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h1)

question: Which device is best suited for automatically sending daily blood glucose readings to a nurse?

options.A: A remote patient monitoring device
options.B: An ordinary paper nursing notepad
options.C: A standard mercury sphygmomanometer
options.D: A hospital bedside surgical tray

explanation: Remote monitoring tools are designed to track and transmit vital health metrics directly to healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h2)

question: How do electronic health records support tele-nursing practice?

options.A: By automatically generating prescriptions without a doctor
options.B: By providing distant nurses with quick access to past patient history
options.C: By allowing patients to perform their own laboratory blood tests
options.D: By replacing the need for any direct verbal communication

explanation: Digital records ensure that nurses caring for patients from afar can easily review previous medical notes and treatments. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of a tele-triage nursing service?

options.A: Conducting mandatory annual physical fitness exams for workers
options.B: Performing emergency major surgeries over a video conference
options.C: Evaluating sudden symptoms and advising on the appropriate level of care
options.D: Dispensing free prescription drugs directly to callers via mail

explanation: Tele-triage involves assessing a caller's symptoms over the phone to guide them on where and how fast to seek medical attention. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h3)

question: A nurse uses a video call to inspect a healing surgical wound for an elderly patient at home. Which model of care does this represent?

options.A: Inpatient intensive care model
options.B: Home care nursing model
options.C: Pure administrative billing model
options.D: Emergency trauma surgery model

explanation: Using video visits to monitor recovery and wound healing at home falls under the home care tele-nursing model. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h3)

question: Which licensing requirement must a tele-nurse always meet when caring for remote clients?

options.A: Holding a valid license in the location where the patient is physically located
options.B: Having a license from any country as long as the nurse has a smartphone
options.C: Possessing a special international internet communication permit
options.D: Registering only with the hospital administration board

explanation: Regulatory bodies require nurses to be legally licensed in the specific jurisdiction where the patient receives the care. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h4)

question: Why is verifying a patient's identity critical during a tele-nursing consultation?

options.A: To ensure the patient is using an approved brand of mobile phone
options.B: To prevent unauthorized persons from receiving confidential health information
options.C: To confirm that the patient has paid their hospital utility bills
options.D: To make sure the patient's internet connection speed is fast enough

explanation: Identity verification protects patient privacy and ensures sensitive medical details are not disclosed to the wrong party. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h4)

question: Which of the following is a common challenge for tele-nursing practice in developing regions?

options.A: Erratic electricity supply and poor internet connectivity
options.B: Patients refusing to use phones for any medical reason
options.C: An overabundance of advanced video monitoring equipment
options.D: Excessive physical contact between nurses and clients

explanation: Unreliable power and weak network signals frequently interrupt remote healthcare delivery in resource-constrained settings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h5)

question: What is a major clinical advantage of tele-nursing for healthcare systems?

options.A: It lowers the cost of medical equipment to zero
options.B: It guarantees that nurses never experience professional burnout
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any laboratory testing
options.D: It reduces overcrowding in physical hospital wards and clinics

explanation: By managing stable patients remotely, hospitals can ease the burden on physical facilities and focus resources where needed most. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h5)

question: What main heart rhythm is an AED built to fix with an electrical shock?

options.A: Ventricular fibrillation
options.B: Sinus bradycardia
options.C: First-degree heart block
options.D: Atrial flutter

explanation: An AED is designed to step in during life-threatening rhythms like ventricular fibrillation, resetting the heart's electrical system so it can beat normally again. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h1)

question: A patient with chest pain is awake and chatting with you in the clinic. Why should you NOT put an AED on them?

options.A: Chest pain medication must be given before applying any emergency electronic device.
options.B: The device only delivers shocks to patients who are unresponsive and in cardiac arrest.
options.C: The AED will automatically call emergency services if turned on near a living person.
options.D: The AED battery will drain too quickly if used on a conscious patient.

explanation: AEDs are smart! They check the heart rhythm and will only give a shock if a dangerous, shockable rhythm is found. If a patient is awake and breathing, the AED won't do anything—and they don't need one. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h1)

question: What is the main job of the sticky electrode pads on an AED?

options.A: To monitor the patient's blood pressure and oxygen levels
options.B: To warm up the patient's skin before the shock is given
options.C: To sense the heart rhythm and deliver the electrical shock
options.D: To manually pump blood through the chest cavity

explanation: Think of the pads as the bridge between the patient and the machine: they read what the heart is doing and carry the shock safely into the body. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h2)

question: How do the speaker and screen on an AED help you during an emergency?

options.A: They record the conversation between family members and healthcare providers.
options.B: They give clear step-by-step directions to guide the rescuer through the rescue.
options.C: They display the patient's exact medical history and home medications.
options.D: They automatically contact the nearest police station for assistance.

explanation: Even if you are nervous, the AED talks you right through it. Just turn it on and listen to the voice prompts! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h2)

question: Where should you place the two sticky pads on an adult patient's chest?

options.A: Directly in the center of the back and over the stomach
options.B: Upper left chest and lower right side of the abdomen
options.C: Both shoulders near the outer edges of the collarbone
options.D: Upper right chest and lower left side of the ribs

explanation: Placing one pad on the upper right and the other on the lower left creates a diagonal path so the shock travels right across the heart muscle. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h3)

question: What is the very first thing you must do when the AED tells everyone to 'stand clear'?

options.A: Check the patient's pulse at the carotid artery.
options.B: Press the shock button immediately without waiting.
options.C: Administer a rescue breath using a bag-valve-mask.
options.D: Ensure nobody is touching the patient.

explanation: Safety first! If anyone is touching the patient, the AED might misread the heart rhythm—or worse, give someone else a shock. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h3)

question: Why is it so important to keep pauses in chest compressions as short as possible when using an AED?

options.A: Pauses reduce blood flow to the heart and brain, lowering survival rates.
options.B: Pauses allow the patient's body temperature to drop too quickly.
options.C: Pauses confuse the AED computer and prevent rhythm analysis.
options.D: Pauses cause the AED battery to drain faster during the rescue.

explanation: Every second you stop pumping, blood stops flowing to the brain. Keeping compressions continuous gives the patient the best fighting chance. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h4)

question: What should you do right after the AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Resume chest compressions immediately.
options.B: Wait for the doctor to arrive and give orders.
options.C: Check for a carotid pulse for ten seconds.
options.D: Remove the electrode pads from the chest.

explanation: Don't wait to check for a pulse right after a shock! Jump right back into chest compressions to keep that blood moving. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h4)

question: What should you do if an AED pad needs to be placed right over a patient's implanted pacemaker bulge?

options.A: Turn off the pacemaker using a magnet before applying the pad.
options.B: Apply the pad directly over the pacemaker to ensure a strong shock.
options.C: Cut a hole in the center of the pad to fit over the pacemaker.
options.D: Place the pad at least an inch away from the pacemaker.

explanation: Putting a pad straight over a metal pacemaker can block the shock. Just shift the pad slightly to the side while keeping the general placement right. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h5)

question: Why must you remove a medication patch from a patient's chest before putting on AED pads?

options.A: The medication will instantly enter the machine and break the processor.
options.B: The patch makes the skin too slippery for the rescuer to press hard.
options.C: The patch will absorb the conductive gel and ruin the AED pads.
options.D: The patch can block the electrical current and cause skin burns.

explanation: Medication patches can interfere with the electricity and even cause nasty skin burns. Always peel them off and wipe the skin clean first! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h5)

question: What does a flashing red light or a chirping sound on an AED usually mean?

options.A: The AED battery is fully charged and ready for an emergency.
options.B: The device has failed a self-test and requires attention.
options.C: The electrode pads are currently connected to a patient.
options.D: The machine is downloading software updates from the hospital.

explanation: That little red light or chirp is your friendly warning that the AED needs a check-up—maybe a new battery or fresh pads—so it's ready when needed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h6)

question: Why do we need to check the expiration dates on AED electrode pads?

options.A: Old pads contain chemicals that become toxic when exposed to air.
options.B: The computer software will refuse to turn on if attached to expired pads.
options.C: Expired pads will automatically trigger a loud alarm that disrupts hospital wards.
options.D: The conductive gel on the pads can dry out over time, preventing proper shock delivery.

explanation: Over time, the sticky gel on the pads dries out. If the gel goes bad, the electricity won't pass through properly during a rescue. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h6)

question: What is an important nursing task for the AED right after a emergency code is over?

options.A: Store the used electrode pads in the patient's bedside cabinet.
options.B: Clean the unit, restock supplies, and return it to its storage station.
options.C: Take the AED apart to clean the internal computer processor.
options.D: Send the AED back to the manufacturer for factory resetting.

explanation: Once the excitement settles, make sure the AED is wiped down, restocked with fresh pads, and put right back in its place so it's ready for the next shift. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h7)

question: Why is it important to document the exact number of shocks the AED delivered during a code?

options.A: It tells the biomedical department when to throw away the machine's battery.
options.B: It provides critical data for the medical team reviewing the patient's clinical course.
options.C: It proves to the hospital administration that the nurse followed the correct protocol.
options.D: It determines how much financial charge the patient receives for equipment use.

explanation: Doctors and the healthcare team need to know how many shocks were given to understand how the patient's heart responded and plan their next steps. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T13#GNS212_U4_T13_h7)

question: Why do nurses love using infrared thermometers on a busy hospital ward?

options.A: It prints out a paper record automatically
options.B: It captures temperature quickly without touching the skin
options.C: It measures core temperature directly from the heart
options.D: It never needs new batteries or calibration

explanation: You'll find these handy on the ward because they let you screen patients fast without needing physical skin contact. Great for keeping things moving! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h1)

question: Why are infrared thermometers a lifesaver when taking a child's temperature?

options.A: Under-fives cannot register a fever on other devices
options.B: Infrared devices block all room drafts completely
options.C: Children are less likely to get scared or fight you
options.D: Kids' skin always radiates extra heat

explanation: Quick, touch-free readings mean less anxiety and crying for the little ones, making your assessment much smoother! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h1)

question: What type of energy do infrared thermometers pick up from the human body?

options.A: Sound wave echoes
options.B: Electrical current
options.C: Ultraviolet radiation
options.D: Infrared radiation

explanation: These thermometers are built to sense the invisible heat energy that naturally radiates from warm human skin. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h2)

question: What is the job of the thermopile inside an infrared thermometer?

options.A: It blocks bright room light from entering
options.B: It warms up the lens to match body heat
options.C: It pumps cool air over the computer chips
options.D: It converts absorbed heat into an electrical signal

explanation: Think of the thermopile as a translator: it takes the focused heat energy and turns it into an electrical voltage that the thermometer's screen can read. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h2)

question: Which part of the ear does a tympanic thermometer aim for?

options.A: The sublingual pocket
options.B: The temporal artery
options.C: The tympanic membrane
options.D: The carotid sheath

explanation: Tympanic thermometers go gently into the ear canal to pick up heat coming straight off the eardrum. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h3)

question: Why is the eardrum (tympanic membrane) such a great spot to check core body temperature?

options.A: It shares a blood supply with the brain's temperature center
options.B: It is completely protected from any room air
options.C: Earwax never affects the reading
options.D: It always shows the highest temperature on the body

explanation: The eardrum shares blood vessels with the hypothalamus (your body's thermostat), giving you a very true picture of core temperature. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h3)

question: Which of these would stop you from using a tympanic thermometer safely?

options.A: A buildup of earwax blocking the ear canal
options.B: The patient just drank some water
options.C: A history of mild seasonal allergies
options.D: Mild dehydration without a fever

explanation: Excess wax blocks the path to the eardrum, meaning the sensor won't catch the right heat radiation. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h4)

question: A patient arrives sweating heavily with thick makeup on their forehead. What should you do for their temperature?

options.A: Use the temporal thermometer right over the makeup
options.B: Use another route, like the ear or mouth
options.C: Wipe the forehead with alcohol and read immediately
options.D: Add two degrees to whatever the temporal reading says

explanation: Sweat and cosmetics mess up forehead heat readings. Save yourself a headache and switch to an oral or tympanic route! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h4)

question: How should you position an adult patient's ear before using a tympanic thermometer?

options.A: Rotate it clockwise three times
options.B: Pull straight down and forward
options.C: Press it flat against the side of the head
options.D: Pull gently up and back

explanation: Pulling the adult pinna up and back straightens out the curved ear canal so the thermometer has a straight shot at the eardrum. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h5)

question: Why should you wait fifteen minutes to take a patient's temperature if they just rushed in from the hot sun?

options.A: To give the patient time to calm down during triage
options.B: To make sure the disposable probe cover doesn't melt
options.C: To let the thermometer warm up its internal sensors
options.D: To let their skin temperature adjust to the indoor air

explanation: Hot or cold weather temporarily changes surface skin temperature. Giving them a few minutes inside ensures your reading is accurate. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h5)

question: What happens to an infant's temperature reading if they are crying or throwing a tantrum?

options.A: It goes up because of increased facial muscle activity and blood flow
options.B: It causes the device to show an error code
options.C: It drops to a false low because of heavy breathing
options.D: It has no effect at all on infrared readings

explanation: Crying pumps up local blood circulation and muscle work around the face, which can push skin temperatures up temporarily. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h6)

question: Which of these does NOT cause an error when using an infrared thermometer?

options.A: Bringing the device straight from a cold room into a warm ward
options.B: Using a brand new disposable probe cover
options.C: Heavy sweat on the patient's forehead
options.D: Accumulated earwax in the ear canal

explanation: A clean probe cover is what you *want* to use! It keeps things hygienic and won't mess up your reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h6)

question: What is the proper way to clean the delicate lens on an infrared thermometer?

options.A: Submerge the whole device in boiling water for five minutes
options.B: Spray high-pressure air directly onto the glass
options.C: Scrub the lens firmly with a scouring pad
options.D: Wipe gently with an approved alcohol wipe following maker instructions

explanation: A gentle wipe with isopropyl alcohol cleans the lens safely without scratching the glass or frying the electronics. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h7)

question: Why is it a big mistake to submerge an infrared thermometer in cleaning liquid?

options.A: It causes the batteries to explode right away
options.B: It ruins the internal electronics and ruins future readings
options.C: It dissolves the outer plastic casing instantly
options.D: It turns the digital display screen permanently black

explanation: Liquid leaking inside will short-circuit the board and mess up the sensitive sensors. Always wipe, never soak! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h7)

question: Why must you always write down the body site (like oral or tympanic) along with the temperature number?

options.A: Different sites use completely different scales like Kelvin
options.B: Electronic health records will lock your chart without it
options.C: Hospital insurance demands the name of the device maker
options.D: Normal body temperature ranges change depending on where you measure it

explanation: Different parts of the body naturally run at slightly different baselines, so knowing the route is vital to read the results correctly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h8)

question: A patient's forehead temperature reads 37.8°C, but they look pale and are shivering hard. What should you suspect?

options.A: The patient has a severe brain injury
options.B: Shivering can make skin feel cold while a real fever is hiding underneath
options.C: The thermometer is definitely broken and should be thrown away
options.D: The patient has no fever at all and needs no more checks

explanation: When shivering causes surface blood vessels to tighten up, skin readings can look normal or low even when core temperature is climbing. Always keep a close eye! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T14#GNS212_U4_T14_h8)

question: What is the main job of a mechanical ventilator in the ICU?

options.A: To replace the function of the human heart
options.B: To assist or take over the work of breathing
options.C: To increase blood pressure in shock patients
options.D: To cure underlying lung diseases permanently

explanation: Think of the ventilator as an extra pair of lungs! It helps or completely takes over breathing to keep oxygen flowing while the patient's body heals. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h1)

question: How can mechanical ventilation affect a patient's blood circulation?

options.A: It has no effect on heart function
options.B: It increases the heart rate in every patient
options.C: It permanently damages heart muscle fibers
options.D: It alters chest pressures, which can impact blood flow

explanation: Because the machine pushes air into the chest using positive pressure, it changes the normal pressures inside. This can sometimes make it a bit harder for blood to return to the heart. Good to keep in mind at the bedside! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h1)

question: Why does carbon dioxide build up in the blood during hypercapnic respiratory failure?

options.A: Sudden loss of red blood cells in circulation
options.B: Primary infection of the heart valves
options.C: Inability to eliminate carbon dioxide effectively
options.D: Excessive oxygen levels in the room air

explanation: Hypercapnic just means too much CO2! When the lungs or breathing muscles are too tired to blow off carbon dioxide properly, it starts backing up in the blood. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h2)

question: An unconscious patient arrives at the emergency unit after a head injury and cannot manage their own saliva. What is the main reason to put them on a ventilator?

options.A: Lowering body temperature
options.B: Airway protection
options.C: Treating high blood pressure
options.D: Correcting severe anemia

explanation: When someone is unconscious, they lose reflexes like swallowing and coughing. Putting them on a ventilator protects their airway so they don't aspirate secretions into their lungs. Excellent clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h2)

question: Which ventilator mode gives a full machine breath whenever the patient tries to breathe, plus a backup rate just in case?

options.A: Assist-Control
options.B: Spontaneous breathing
options.C: Control Mode
options.D: SIMV

explanation: In Assist-Control mode, the machine is right there helping. Every time the patient initiates a breath, the ventilator steps in to deliver a full breath, and a backup rate ensures they never miss one. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h3)

question: What makes SIMV (Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation) different from Assist-Control mode?

options.A: It delivers higher pressures with every single breath taken
options.B: It removes the need for any humidification system
options.C: It completely stops the patient from taking independent breaths
options.D: It allows the patient to breathe spontaneously between mandatory machine breaths

explanation: SIMV gives scheduled breaths but lets the patient do some of the work on their own in between. It's fantastic for exercising their respiratory muscles when they are getting stronger! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h3)

question: You notice a ventilated patient has no breath sounds on the left side and uneven chest movement. What should you suspect first?

options.A: The humidifier water chamber is completely empty
options.B: The ventilator circuit tubing has a small external leak
options.C: The patient is experiencing a sudden drop in blood sugar
options.D: The breathing tube has slipped into the right main bronchus

explanation: Because the right main bronchus is wider and straighter, breathing tubes often slip too far down into it. This accidentally ventilates only the right lung, leaving the left side quiet. Always check tube placement! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h4)

question: What do high-pressure alarms usually tell you about a mechanically ventilated patient?

options.A: The patient is breathing too slowly or not at all
options.B: Changes in lung compliance or increased airway resistance
options.C: A disconnection of the main tubing from the patient
options.D: A power failure in the wall electrical socket

explanation: When the high-pressure alarm sounds, it means something is making it harder to push air in—like mucus plugs, coughing, or the patient biting the tube. Time to put on your detective hat and check the patient! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h4)

question: Why is regular mouth care with antiseptic solution so important for a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: To stimulate saliva production for better digestion
options.B: To check if the patient has a gag reflex
options.C: To reduce bacterial buildup that can lead to lung infections
options.D: To prevent the endotracheal tube from sticking to the lips

explanation: Good oral care clears away harmful germs that could otherwise slide down the breathing tube and cause pneumonia. Simple nursing care saves lives! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h5)

question: When is the best time to perform airway suctioning on a ventilated patient?

options.A: When clinical indicators like secretions or coughing are present
options.B: Every single hour on the exact hour without fail
options.C: Only when the high-pressure alarm rings twice
options.D: Immediately before every meal or tube-feeding cycle

explanation: We don't suction on a rigid schedule because it can irritate the airway and lower oxygen levels. Instead, we listen, assess, and suction only when the patient actually needs it. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h5)

question: To help prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP), at what angle should the head of the patient's bed be kept?

options.A: 60 to 90 degrees upright
options.B: 30 to 45 degrees
options.C: 15 degrees slightly tilted
options.D: 0 degrees completely flat

explanation: Keeping the bed elevated between 30 and 45 degrees uses gravity to stop oral and stomach secretions from trickling down into the lungs. An easy intervention with a huge payoff! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is the main reason doctors order a daily 'sedation vacation' for a ventilated patient?

options.A: To let the ventilator machine calibrate its internal sensors
options.B: To allow the nursing staff to take a scheduled meal break
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of medications in the unit
options.D: To evaluate the patient's neurological status and readiness for weaning

explanation: Pausing sedation for a short while lets us check how the patient's brain is doing and see if they are strong enough to start breathing on their own. Brilliant teamwork! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is the medical term for completely removing the breathing tube after a patient passes a breathing trial?

options.A: Intubation
options.B: Tracheostomy
options.C: Bronchoscopy
options.D: Extubation

explanation: Extubation simply means taking the breathing tube out once the patient's lungs are strong enough to take over. What a wonderful milestone for recovery! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h7)

question: During a breathing trial, your patient suddenly starts sweating, looks restless, and has a fast heart rate. What should you do?

options.A: Increase the sedation medication to maximum dosage immediately
options.B: Turn off all ventilator alarms so they stop ringing
options.C: Encourage the patient to push through the discomfort quietly
options.D: Notify the team and consider stopping the trial due to distress

explanation: Sweating, high heart rate, and restlessness are classic signs that the patient is struggling and getting tired. It's time to pause the trial and give them support. Great assessment skills! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T15#GNS212_U4_T15_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of cardiac monitoring in a hospital setting?

options.A: Measuring exact blood pressure every few seconds
options.B: Calculating the total volume of blood pumped per minute
options.C: Checking the oxygen level inside red blood cells
options.D: Continuous tracking of heart rate and electrical rhythm

explanation: Cardiac monitors are specifically designed to watch the electrical activity and rate of the heart in real time. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is continuous cardiac monitoring especially important for patients recovering from a heart attack?

options.A: It prevents them from moving around too much in bed
options.B: It automatically delivers shock therapy when needed
options.C: It helps catch dangerous rhythm changes early
options.D: It replaces the need for manual pulse checks completely

explanation: Damaged heart muscle after a heart attack can easily trigger erratic rhythms, making early detection through monitoring crucial. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h1)

question: What does the QRS complex on an ECG strip represent?

options.A: Atrial resting phase
options.B: Atrial repolarization
options.C: Ventricular resting phase
options.D: Ventricular depolarization

explanation: The tall QRS complex shows the electrical wave moving through the ventricles, causing them to contract strongly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h2)

question: What happens during the T wave of a normal heartbeat?

options.A: The main heart valves snap shut to trap blood inside
options.B: The electrical signal fires off inside the sinus node
options.C: Blood rushes rapidly from the body into the right atrium
options.D: The ventricles recharge and get ready for the next beat

explanation: The T wave marks ventricular repolarization, which is the electrical recovery or resting state of the lower chambers. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the main function of sticky chest electrodes in cardiac monitoring?

options.A: To warm up the chest skin for better blood circulation
options.B: To measure the exact temperature of the chest wall
options.C: To deliver mild electrical shocks to reset the rhythm
options.D: To pick up the electrical signals generated by the heart

explanation: Electrodes act as sensors that detect tiny electrical currents on the skin surface coming from the beating heart. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h3)

question: A patient with a hairy chest is being hooked up to a telemetry monitor, but the screen shows heavy static. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Replace the entire monitor box with a new unit
options.B: Switch the patient immediately to a 12-lead machine
options.C: Clip the chest hair and prep the skin before placing new electrodes
options.D: Increase the alarm volume so the nursing station can hear it better

explanation: Hair prevents good contact between the electrode and the skin, which causes static and artifact on the screen. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is the normal heart rate range for a healthy adult in Normal Sinus Rhythm?

options.A: 100 to 120 beats per minute
options.B: 60 to 100 beats per minute
options.C: 120 to 150 beats per minute
options.D: 40 to 60 beats per minute

explanation: A normal resting heart rate for adults falls squarely between 60 and 100 beats per minute with regular spacing. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which heart rhythm is considered a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate CPR and defibrillation?

options.A: Normal sinus rhythm
options.B: Sinus tachycardia
options.C: Sinus bradycardia
options.D: Ventricular fibrillation

explanation: Ventricular fibrillation causes the heart to quiver without pumping blood, leading to cardiac arrest within seconds if untreated. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h4)

question: What does the term 'artifact' mean on a cardiac monitor?

options.A: An old model of a monitor no longer used in wards
options.B: A dangerous heart rhythm needing immediate medication
options.C: Unwanted static or interference on the ECG tracing
options.D: A special recording saved for the doctor to review

explanation: Artifacts are false signals caused by movement, muscle tremors, or loose equipment rather than real heart activity. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h5)

question: The telemetry alarm sounds and the screen shows a wild, chaotic line, but the patient is sitting up calmly talking on the phone. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Check the patient and inspect the electrode connections
options.B: Call the doctor immediately to report ventricular fibrillation
options.C: Bring the crash cart to the bedside and prepare to shock
options.D: Turn off the monitor alarm permanently to reduce noise

explanation: Always assess the patient and check the equipment for loose leads before acting on a potentially false reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is it dangerous to leave monitor alarm limits at their default factory settings for every patient?

options.A: It uses up too much electricity in the wall socket
options.B: It stops the doctor from seeing the patient's chart notes
options.C: It can cause unnecessary false alarms or miss personalized warning signs
options.D: It makes the monitor screen too bright to read easily

explanation: Every patient has a different baseline heart rate, so alarm limits must be customized to fit their specific health needs. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h6)

question: Which of the following actions is NOT safe practice when managing cardiac monitor alarms?

options.A: Checking the patient immediately whenever an alarm sounds
options.B: Customizing alarm limits to match the patient's baseline condition
options.C: Permanently disabling noisy alarms so staff can rest
options.D: Changing electrode pads regularly to protect the skin

explanation: Permanently turning off or ignoring alarms puts patients at severe risk if a real emergency occurs. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T2#GNS212_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of using an infusion pump instead of a normal gravity IV line?

options.A: It warms the intravenous fluid before it enters the vein
options.B: It completely removes the need to monitor the IV site
options.C: It delivers fluids at a precise and controlled rate
options.D: It prevents all forms of air embolisms automatically

explanation: Spot on! Infusion pumps give us exact control over how fast fluids run, which is much safer and more reliable than just relying on gravity. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why do we always use infusion pumps for high-risk drugs like chemotherapy?

options.A: These drugs are too thick to flow through gravity sets
options.B: Pumps neutralize toxic drug reactions before they reach the vein
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs must be administered in under five minutes
options.D: Small dosage errors can cause severe patient harm

explanation: You got it! Powerful drugs have a tiny margin for error, so we need pumps to make sure the patient gets the exact right dose—no more, no less. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which device is best for giving tiny amounts of medicine slowly over time, especially for newborns?

options.A: Ambulatory blood warmer
options.B: Gravity drip set
options.C: Large volume pump
options.D: Syringe pump

explanation: Great job! Syringe pumps are brilliant for low volumes because they push the plunger forward in tiny, steady steps. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h2)

question: A post-op patient presses a handheld button on their IV machine to release a safe dose of pain meds. What is this device called?

options.A: Enteral feeding pump
options.B: Large Volume Pump
options.C: Insulin ambulatory pump
options.D: Patient-Controlled Analgesia pump

explanation: That's right! A PCA pump lets patients safely manage their own pain within strict limits set by the care team. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of the air-in-line detector on an infusion pump?

options.A: To measure the exact temperature of the infusing fluid
options.B: To calculate the total fluid volume remaining in the bag
options.C: To stop air bubbles from reaching the patient's bloodstream
options.D: To increase the speed of the fluid if a block occurs

explanation: Spot on! That little sensor is a lifesaver—it catches air bubbles in the tube and stops the pump instantly before air can get into the vein. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h3)

question: How do most electronic infusion pumps push fluid through the tubing?

options.A: By heating the liquid until it expands and moves forward
options.B: By spinning a high-speed internal rotor blade inside the fluid path
options.C: By creating a strong vacuum pull from the distal end of the line
options.D: By using sequential mechanical fingers to squeeze the flexible tubing

explanation: You nailed it! Think of it like fingers gently milking a tube in a wave-like motion to push the fluid forward smoothly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the purpose of the safety limits (guardrails) on smart infusion pumps?

options.A: To automatically calculate patient drug dosages without nurse input
options.B: To track how many supplies are used during each shift
options.C: To lock the pump door so patients cannot change settings
options.D: To warn nurses if a programmed dose is outside safe limits

explanation: Exactly! Guardrails act like a helpful safety net, popping up a warning if a number looks too high or too low. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the best way to catch mistakes before starting a new IV infusion?

options.A: Performing an independent double-check of calculations and pump settings with another nurse
options.B: Bypassing the hospital drug library to speed up the infusion setup process
options.C: Relying entirely on memory to calculate complex weight-based drug doses
options.D: Asking the patient to confirm if the infusion rate feels correct

explanation: Spot on! Two sets of eyes are always better than one. A quick double-check with a colleague helps catch little errors before they become big problems. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why should you keep infusion pumps plugged into the wall socket when patients are resting in bed?

options.A: To allow the pump to automatically clean its internal tubing
options.B: To prevent the pump screen from displaying warning messages
options.C: To increase the speed at which medications are delivered
options.D: To preserve the internal battery for times when the patient is moving

explanation: You got it! Keeping it plugged in saves the battery charge for when the patient needs to walk around or go for a test. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h5)

question: You check an IV site and notice it is swollen, cool to the touch, and painful while the pump is running. What's happening?

options.A: An air bubble has triggered the internal line sensor
options.B: The medication is working at its optimal therapeutic level
options.C: The pump battery is failing and needs to be replaced
options.D: Fluid has leaked into the surrounding tissue (infiltration)

explanation: Spot on! Cool, swollen, and painful tissue around the site means the fluid is going into the arm tissue instead of the vein. Time to stop the infusion and restart! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h5)

question: An infusion pump starts beeping with a 'downstream occlusion' alarm. What should you check first?

options.A: The software version installed on the pump display
options.B: The IV tubing for kinks, closed clamps, or blockages
options.C: The main hospital electrical breaker panel in the hallway
options.D: The expiration date printed on the primary medication bag

explanation: That's correct! 'Downstream' means between the pump and the patient. Always check the line first for bends, pinches, or a closed roller clamp. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why is it dangerous to just silence an infusion pump alarm and walk away?

options.A: Unresolved alarms cause the pump to reverse fluid flow into the bag
options.B: It can delay necessary treatment or fail to catch a dangerous blockage
options.C: Hospital policy fines staff members who touch alarms too quickly
options.D: The pump will automatically erase all patient data if silenced

explanation: You got it! Alarms are there for a reason. Ignoring them without fixing the root cause can leave your patient without their meds or miss a serious line problem. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h6)

question: According to standard infection control rules, how often should primary IV tubing be changed?

options.A: 24 to 36 hours
options.B: Only until the bag empties
options.C: 72 to 96 hours
options.D: Every 7 days exactly

explanation: Spot on! Standard primary lines are generally swapped out every 3 to 4 days (72 to 96 hours) to keep bacteria from building up. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h7)

question: Why must you scrub an IV port with an alcohol swab before hooking up a syringe?

options.A: It prevents the plastic port from cracking under high pump pressure
options.B: It chemically activates the medication inside the attached syringe
options.C: It removes bacteria and prevents microorganisms from entering the bloodstream
options.D: It lubricates the rubber seal so the syringe connects more smoothly

explanation: Brilliant! Friction from scrubbing wipes away germs so they don't hitch a ride straight into the patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T3#GNS212_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of using a syringe driver in clinical practice?

options.A: To flush blocked intravenous lines rapidly with sterile saline
options.B: To deliver a continuous, controlled amount of medication
options.C: To provide intermittent bolus doses every five minutes
options.D: To measure precise hourly urine output in critical care

explanation: A syringe driver is specifically designed to infuse medications slowly and steadily over a set duration. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why do nurses often prefer a syringe driver over intermittent injections in palliative care?

options.A: It works without requiring batteries or electrical power
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any nursing documentation
options.C: It allows family members to freely change drug doses at home
options.D: It avoids painful peaks and troughs by keeping drug levels steady

explanation: You got it! Continuous infusion stops drug levels from bouncing up and down, keeping pain and other symptoms nicely under control without roller-coaster effects. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h1)

question: When is a syringe driver most likely to be used for a patient?

options.A: When the patient refuses all forms of nursing care
options.B: When intravenous access is completely forbidden by law
options.C: When the patient needs rapid blood pressure support
options.D: When oral medications are no longer safe or possible

explanation: Exactly! If a patient cannot swallow, has severe vomiting, or is nearing the end of life, a syringe driver is a lifesaver for giving regular medications smoothly. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h2)

question: What should you do immediately if mixed medications inside a syringe driver turn cloudy?

options.A: Vigorously shake the syringe to dissolve the cloudy particles back in
options.B: Leave the pump running because color changes are completely normal
options.C: Increase the infusion rate to push the cloudy solution through faster
options.D: Discard the mixture immediately because the drugs are likely incompatible

explanation: Well done! Cloudiness means a chemical reaction happened between the drugs, making them unsafe. Never give a cloudy mixture—always prepare a fresh, safe set. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which part of the syringe driver securely holds the syringe plunger and pushes it forward?

options.A: The clear plastic needle cap
options.B: The external wall power plug
options.C: The claw or drive mechanism
options.D: The digital display screen

explanation: Correct! The drive mechanism (or claw) locks onto the plunger and slowly advances it to deliver the exact dose. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h3)

question: Why do modern syringe drivers have security locks on their control panels?

options.A: To prevent the battery from falling out during transport
options.B: To automatically lock the infusion line if air bubbles appear
options.C: To prevent accidental changes to the rate by visitors or patients
options.D: To keep the internal clock set to the correct local time zone

explanation: Spot on! Security locks ensure that inquisitive fingers or accidental bumps don't change the prescribed medication speed. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h3)

question: What safety step must you always do before starting a new syringe driver infusion?

options.A: A complete blood count and electrolyte panel test
options.B: A physical inspection of the patient's heart valves
options.C: A medication double-check with a second nurse
options.D: A mandatory change of the patient's room assignment

explanation: Great job! Independent double-checks with a colleague help catch math mistakes or wrong drug choices before the pump even starts running. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h4)

question: You prepare a total volume of 24 mL to run over 24 hours. What should you set the hourly rate to?

options.A: 1.0 mL per hour
options.B: 24.0 mL per hour
options.C: 12.0 mL per hour
options.D: 48.0 mL per hour

explanation: You're a star at math! 24 mL divided by 24 hours gives you a neat and steady rate of 1.0 mL per hour. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h4)

question: How often should you check the medication insertion site of a syringe driver?

options.A: Only when an alarm starts beeping
options.B: Only once every seven days
options.C: At least every nursing shift
options.D: Every time the patient falls asleep

explanation: Correct! Checking the site every shift helps you spot early redness, swelling, or irritation before it becomes a big problem for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T4#GNS212_U4_T4_h5)
